91.title: Asset extraction — the index goes in, the contents do not
91.content: Skill asset-extraction: Reading a container — a zip, a PDF, a saved web page — into the knowledge graph. What goes in by default (metadata), what does not (contents), the three timestamps that sit near each other and mean different things, and why a producer string is evidence. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links . A container arrives in uploads/: a zip of a saved web page, a PDF, a tarball. Something inside it is wanted. What enters the knowledge graph is the INDEX — what is in there, how big, what type, when it says it was written — and not the files. Contents are extracted only when a person explicitly asks. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-assets.ts <container> bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-assets.ts <container> --extract <path> --because "<why>" . The first writes a folio-extraction/v1 record beside the container. The second additionally writes one named entry, and refuses without a reason.

92.title: Why metadata is the default
92.content: A container’s index is cheap and complete: a zip’s central directory carries every entry’s size, name and timestamp without decompressing a byte. That is enough to answer what is in here, how big is it, and is any of it what I want — which is every question asked before somebody decides to take a file. Extracting by default costs the opposite: a working tree full of files nobody chose, each of which now looks committed-on-purpose to the next reader, and none of which carries a reason. --because is required, and it is the point of the flag. An entry written to disk with no stated reason cannot be told from one nobody authorised. The schema refuses it (ExtractedAsset.superRefine), so this is not a habit that depends on remembering.

93.title: The three timestamps, and the one that gets confused
93.content: |   | says | . | dc.date.issued | when the PUBLISHER published the work | . | materializedAt | when WE brought the bytes local | . | capturedAt | when a TOOL produced this file out of something else | . An extraction timestamp is never a publication date. For example, a WHO IRIS capture: . zip entries 2026-09-20 07:42 (all 11 of them) page PDF CreationDate D:20260920074221 info PDF CreationDate D:20260920074925 . The style guide those files contain was published in 2020. Every timestamp in the capture is 2026, and every one of them is the moment somebody pressed save. Folding the two would date a 2020 publication to 2026 and lose the only evidence the artefact is second-hand. isSingleCapture() computes the distinction rather than asserting it: when every entry shares one minute, ONE ACT wrote the container and no entry’s date says anything about that asset’s own history. When they differ, the container preserved real dates and they can be read as such.

94.title: A producer string is evidence, and is recorded verbatim
94.content: Both captured PDFs carry Producer: Skia/PDF m152. That is Chrome’s print-to-PDF — so neither file is WHO’s own PDF, both are printed web pages, and nothing else in a file listing, a byte count or a checksum shows it. Recorded as written, never normalised to “Chrome”: the version is part of the evidence, and a normaliser is a place for the fact to get smaller. This is the mechanical half of a judgement the IRIS intake already records by hand — the page PDF is filed with role none, because “we looked and it is not what it appears to be” is a different fact from “nobody looked”.

95.title: What is NOT dropped silently
95.content: A zip written on macOS carries a __MACOSX/ shadow per entry. Skipping them quietly makes the asset count disagree with the container’s own, and a reader reconciling the two finds nothing to explain the gap. They go in omitted[] with a pattern, a reason and a count.

96.title: Derived renderings — the artefact we MADE, out of bytes we hold
96.content: A cover thumbnail, an OCR text layer, a page raster, a converted figure: none of these came from the source. They were produced here, from something the source supplied, and the catalogue records an artefact, not where it came from — so a derived file with a plausible name and a materialized state is indistinguishable from one the publisher shipped. DSpace makes this concrete. It generates a THUMBNAIL bundle of its own, so “a THUMBNAIL bitstream on an IRIS item” reads, to anything downstream, as IRIS’s thumbnail. The three WHO IRIS covers in this repository are not those: iris.who.int is egress-blocked here, nothing upstream was fetched, and each is page 1 of a PDF already held, rasterised by cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-cover.py. Three rules, in the order they bite: . | of names what it was DERIVED FROM, not what it is ABOUT. The Handle identifies the item; putting it on a cover we rendered asserts IRIS supplied the image. local:cat-harness/uploads/<file>.pdf#page=1 says the true thing and resolves to the true thing. | The declaration is authored, and the tool refuses without it. the content core’s scripts/gen-covers.ts will not write bytes for a THUMBNAIL whose materialization.note does not declare the derivation. Generating that sentence would make the check circular — a tool cannot attest to its own output. | purpose: working, never archival. A rendering is regenerable from bytes already held and answers no source-loss question; MaterializationSchema already refuses a working copy that claims to discharge sourceLoss, and this is the case that rule was written for. | . Take the determined division, not the clever one. pdf-cover.py renders page 1 and calls it the cover, for the same reason pdf-pages.py sections by page: page 1 is a determined answer and “the cover” is not. Covers differ in shape (portrait, landscape, a scanned title page), and a heuristic has no way to say when it is unsure. Record the geometry. Bitstream.pixelWidth/pixelHeight exist so a listing reserves the box before the bytes arrive. Absent is unmeasured, not square. Check the claim where the check can actually run. A gate that re-renders a derived artefact needs the backend that produced it, and the CI job that runs this repository’s gates installs ruff and nothing else (stated on ingest-stdlib’s Tool node). Do not install a backend in the gate job, and do not degrade to could-not-determine — that would report unknown on every CI run, which is a check nobody can read. Split the claim instead. Of the five things a node asserts about a derived image, four need no decoder at all: . | claim | needs the backend? | . | the bytes exist | no | . | their sha256 is the declared one | no | . | their length is the declared one | no | . | their pixel dimensions are the declared ones | no — a PNG’s IHDR puts width and height at bytes 16..24, big-endian | . | these bytes are what that source renders to | yes | . So the gate keeps its teeth everywhere and gains the last row where the backend happens to be present — and it says in its own output which of the two it ran, because “3 covers verified” would read identically either way and the two are different assurances.

97.title: Where the record lives
97.content: Beside the container, in uploads/. uploads/ is a state graph — a queue that ingestion drains — so an extraction record is not L1 corpus and does not read as one. What a THEME or a LIBRARY entry cites is the extracted file’s localPath, which exists only once somebody asked for it.

100.title: Audit coverage — measured, with denominators
100.content: Skill audit-coverage: Which audits reach which KIND of node, measured rather than inferred. Read before concluding that a corpus is unaudited, before writing a criterion for one, and before building any coverage report — the gate half must be declared, an undeclared declarer is counted, and the stored record holds the relation rather than the census. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . A sidecar count is a fine measurement of sidecars and says nothing about gates. That sentence is the whole skill. Run bun run cat audit:coverage before saying a corpus is unaudited, before writing a criterion for a kind, and before building any coverage report of your own.

101.title: A zero sidecar count is not “unaudited”
101.content: kg-qa sidecars measure kg-audit’s criteria exactly, and KG_SUBJECT_KINDS has no bean — so zero sidecars over the work item store is the right answer to “how many criteria reach this kind” and no answer at all to “is this kind audited”: the check:bean-* gates, check:ready-to-close, check:stale-paths and check:harness-dirs audit work items. This is covered-is-not-reachable one level out: coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for, and the signal in reach is rarely the signal you need. It is not a second answer to check:kind-validators. That asks whether a kind can be typed — does it have a validator that loads. This asks who judges it. A kind can be perfectly typed and audited by nothing, and a validator sweep reports it as covered.

102.title: The gate half is DECLARED, never inferred
102.content: A gate names the kinds it covers in its own module docblock: . * @covers bean-defs, beans * @covers none — .github/workflows/ is not a declared graph typology * @covers computed — it sweeps whichever kinds declare `nodeSchemas` . The tempting alternative is to infer it: grep each gate’s source for a kind’s name or its declared directory. It fails in both directions at once. A gate that mentions beans/defs/ in passing scores as auditing work items; a gate that resolves its directory through directoriesForGraph names no path and scores as auditing nothing. Both answers wrong, neither looking wrong: could-not-determine rendered as clean (directory-conventions). Five states, because three real gates cannot use a static list . | state | what it means | . | declared | names its kinds | . | none | has decided it audits no declared graph — check:workflows reads .github/workflows/ | . | computed | derives its set at run time — check:kind-validators sweeps whatever declares nodeSchemas, so a literal would go stale silently | . | no-script | bun test, eslint, tsc — nothing here to annotate | . | undeclared | has not said | . none and undeclared are different facts and collapsing them would leave a gate that genuinely audits no graph with silence as its only honest answer. computed exists because writing today’s answer as a literal is the snapshot BASE_GRAPH_TYPOLOGIES’ own doc refuses for counts in prose. An undeclared gate is counted and printed, never zero, and every “unaudited” verdict is stated as an upper bound while any remain. That is check:kind-validators’ state 2, for its reasons. All gates declare, so audit:coverage:require-all is wired in CI and the findings are verdicts rather than bounds. The flag is what keeps it closed: a new gate arriving undeclared turns them back into an upper bound, silently, unless something fails. The output still states the caveat whenever the count is non-zero, because the day it reopens is the day a reader needs to be told. When you cannot tell, do not annotate — and then go and read it . A fabricated @covers credits a kind with coverage nobody checked. Under-claiming is recoverable — the count says so out loud. Over-claiming looks like coverage. To resolve an undeclared gate, read its scan set, not its title: check:retired-front-matter is computed, because its set is kgRoots(instance) plus the undeclared .claude/skills/ convention; and check:agents-claims covers code, not docs, because it grades the symbols a prose claim names while AGENTS.md itself is a node of no declared graph.

103.title: Four states per kind, and a single zero cannot tell them apart
103.content: | state | what it means | the case that earns the name | . | no-directory | no layer declares one of this kind | bean-defs, declared inside beans/beans.json, reached through its parent — and carrying gates | . | empty | a directory exists and holds nothing | a determined empty | . | typed-only | a declared validator TYPES its nodes; nothing judges them | none here | . | unaudited | files, and nothing at all — not even a validator | none here | . bean-defs is why the first state is not a gap: it has coverage and no directory of its own. A report that printed 0 for its directory count and left the reader to infer would have manufactured a finding. So every row prints all four counts and names its state rather than leaving it to be read off a zero. typed-only is a finding, and that is the whole reason it exists . A kind whose validator check:kind-validators parses its nodes against looks unreached, because that gate declares @covers computed, which this report counts as neither coverage nor gap. Do not call it covered. --strict fails on typed-only as its own family, because typing is not judging — a kind can parse perfectly against its schema while nothing has an opinion about what it says. What the state buys is telling two different pieces of work apart: a schema parses these nodes and no criterion reads them is not nothing whatsoever reaches this kind. check:harness-state carries one family per kind, and --strict is green and wired in CI. The state stays, because the next kind to arrive will pass through it — and the flag is what stops it resting there. A validator must reach the nodes that are produced . | A kind’s schema must point at the module that holds its shape, not the one that holds its path. A pointer to where a fact is not written is worse than none: a reader who follows it concludes the shape is undeclared on purpose. | Every writer stamps $schema. Consumers route a node by its tag and skip a file that has none, so a writer that omits it leaves only hand-written files validated. A validator over the nodes nobody produces is not coverage. | An untyped node read by a shell script degrades rather than fails: a jq failure branch prints a line nobody acts on. That is why interaction and issue-marks declare validators. | .

104.title: Three rules for building any coverage report
104.content: A measurement must not be a term in itself . If the report’s own sidecar lives in a graph it counts, writing it changes the next run’s answer, and the gate is satisfied only by running the writer twice. Exclude your own output, derive the path from the constants that write it so a relocation cannot leave the exclusion pointing elsewhere, and test that one run converges. Store the RELATION, print the census . The record is stored on the qa-reports branch keyed by commit. Do not record files and sidecars in it: a writer in one graph would turn another graph’s coverage gate red, and a file count that moves whenever anybody adds a page makes the gate stale by default — one people learn to regenerate without reading. What belongs in the sidecar is what defines coverage: declared directories, criteria reaching the kind, gates declaring it, the state. Those move when coverage moves, which is when a reviewer needs the diff. One bit of the census — hasFiles — is all the states need. Recording a count would make the report depend on the signal it exists to replace. A docblock that documents a tag necessarily contains the tag . coversIn read audit-coverage.ts’ own worked examples of @covers as declarations, crediting the coverage report with auditing the work item store. Any parser over docblocks has to tell a use from a mention, and indentation is the distinction JSDoc already provides: ^ \* @covers , exactly one space either side of the star.

105.title: What --check fails on, and what it does not
105.content: --check computes and judges, and writes nothing. It fails on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — a kind that lost its audit, a gate that stopped declaring, in the commit under review — and not on its own sidecar being stale: derived QA results live on the qa-reports branch, so nothing committed is left to be stale. The baseline is read with --against <ref> (a qa-reports ref such as main). A baseline that is not there is UNKNOWN — printed, never a pass, never a failure, because an unwritten baseline is not this change’s defect. A checker that mutates its own subject cannot be falsified (red once, green on the rerun, the file still stale), which is the one property generalise-the-fix (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) Move 3 asks a guard to have. A kind whose directory is declared but absent from the checkout reads unknown, not empty: an absent answer is never printed as a determined zero. A directory that declares storage reads stored instead: its files are on the branch, fetch them with bun run qa:fetch. The findings are reported and do not fail. --strict fails on an unaudited kind and --require-all on an undeclared gate, for the day each gap is meant to close. A gate that refused every push until somebody wrote criteria for interaction/ is a gate that gets switched off within a week.

106.title: Adding a kind, or a gate
106.content: . | A new gate: add @covers in the same change. If you cannot tell which kind its subject is, leave it off — the count is the honest answer. | A new graph typology: it appears in the report the moment it is registered, because the denominator is the registry. Expect it to read unaudited until it declares a validator and typed-only until something judges it — and say in the sidecar why it needs nothing if that is the answer, never by letting the row read clean. | A relocation: nothing to update. Directories resolve through directoriesForGraph. | .

115.title: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
115.content: Skill block-actions: Every block of a rendered document links back to where it can be changed: [edit] opens the block’s Markdown source in GitHub’s editor, and [feedback] opens a GitHub issue about that block, from the folio’s own issue form when it has one, listing the change-sets that already discuss the block. Use when a reader, reviewer or agent needs to propose a change to one block, when setting up a folio’s feedback issue form, or when a document site’s links point nowhere. Named by: Public comment on a review draft . A reader who finds something wrong in a block is one click from proposing the fix or saying what is wrong, and the click lands on the block, not on the repository. The links are per block, because a block is what a comment, a change-set and an edit are about. The code is folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts; the Tool is block-actions; the document build (build-document-site.ts) draws the links on every labelled block, and the public-comment overlay adds the issues that already discuss the block.

116.title: What each link does
116.content: | link | opens | what the person does next | . | ✎ edit | the block’s source (folio/<doc>/<chapter>/<root>.md, or its .ts if it has no .md) in GitHub’s editor, on main | edits and proposes the change; GitHub makes the branch and the pull request, which is reviewed like any content change (content-change-review.bpmn) | . | 📣 feedback | a new issue about the block | describes the problem; the issue is intake, and a public-comment folio triages it like any other comment (public-comment skill) | . | discussed in #n | the issue of each change-set the block’s comments are in | joins the existing discussion instead of opening a duplicate | .

117.title: Every issue is coded with its content
117.content: [feedback] codes the issue with the slug of the document it came from: the title reads Feedback [dpi-h-ra]: <section> — <block> and the body opens with **Content:** \dpi-h-ra``. A folio with several documents, or a repository that takes issues about more than one thing, can then sort feedback by what it is about without opening it. The code is in the title rather than only a label because GitHub silently drops a prefilled label when the reporter has no triage rights, and most public reviewers do not.

118.title: The issue form is the folio’s, and optional
118.content: With no form, [feedback] opens a blank issue whose body already says which block, which section, the source link and the block’s address on the site. It works on day one. A folio that wants structured feedback adds a GitHub issue form at .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/block-feedback.yml (start from the shared templates/issue-forms/block-feedback.yml, whose answers the drafting review sheet imports: skill review-sheet-script) (another name with --issue-template). The link then names the form and prefills only the fields the form declares, matched by id: . | field id | filled with | . | block | the block’s label (its anchor) | . | section | the heading the block is under | . | source | the block’s source path in the repository | . | page | the page it renders on | . | url | the block’s address on the published site (needs --site-url) | . | content | the document’s slug, the code the issue is triaged by | . A form may declare any subset, and fields it does not declare are not sent. Add the questions you want answered (what is wrong, a suggested wording, the reviewer’s organisation) as further fields; they are left for the person.

119.title: Where the repository comes from
119.content: GITHUB_REPOSITORY in CI, else the checkout’s origin when it is on GitHub, else --github <owner/repo>. No repository, no links: a page with no links is honest, a page with broken ones is not. --no-block-actions turns them off for a build that should have none.

120.title: Two forms of the same links
120.content: . | Full (blockActionsHtml): every href written into the page. Used on a one-page document and on index.hydrated.html, so the links work without JavaScript. | Compact (compactActionsHtml + compactActionsScript): the block’s facts as data attributes, and the hrefs built in the browser when a pointer or focus reaches them. Used on a lazy page’s shell, where a prefilled URL per block would bloat the page. The browser builder, BLOCK_URLS_JS, is held equal to editUrl and feedbackUrl by block-actions.test.ts; change both together or the test fails. | . The recipe lives in the harness, cat-harness-tools/src/core/edit-links.ts, so every layer can use it; this package re-exports it. It is published once as assets/js/edit-links.js (held equal to the code by a test). On a page, mark a link data-fa-link="edit|source|feedback" and either give its host the facts (data-src, optional data-repo, data-line, data-block, data-sec) or leave a GitHub blob/edit href, which the runtime reads the facts from. Generators that write Markdown use markdownEditLink. Three places keep their own link on purpose: the public-comment dashboard’s Discuss (it opens a change-set discussion, not feedback on a block), the bootstrap site’s Improve this page (bootstrap-tools may import nothing outside itself), and an IG page’s per-section ✎ / 📣 (SOURCE_LINKS_JS in build-ig-site.ts): a section’s heading can live in an included file, and its issue is titled after the section with the page apart. The IG page’s own Edit this page link does use the recipe. Any page that shows edit or feedback links uses these, not a URL of its own: one recipe, so a change to the issue form or the branch reaches every page at once.

121.title: In the library: edit opens the folio, never the source
121.content: A library entry is a frozen source: the version published for public comment stays in library/ exactly as circulated, and the changes the review asks for are made in folio/. So the library’s Document view (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts, drawn by the platform viewer and by build-library-site.ts on a folio’s site) shows: . | link | on | opens | . | source | the document, each section | the library’s own file on GitHub, read-only | . | 📣 feedback | the document, each section | an issue coded with the entry: Feedback [<entry>]: <section> | . | ✎ edit | each section, and its contents row | the FIRST folio block of the folio section MATERIALISED from it | . A section is matched to the folio by its number, else its title, through the folio-review-anchors/v1 file whose library names the entry. A section the folio has no counterpart for (a PDF’s front matter) gets no ✎ edit, because a guessed link would open the wrong block. The platform’s own library has no materialisation, so it shows source and feedback only. bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-library-site.ts --repo <folio> --out _site publishes a folio’s library at <out>/folio-assistant-core/<library dir>/<entry>/, the same <base>/<handler>/<kind>/<subject> route every viewer follows.

122.title: Using it as an agent
122.content: # one block's links, to hand a reader bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> --block prose:1-1-4-a8e0b3 # every block's, as JSON bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> . When someone in a chat says “this paragraph is wrong”, give them the block’s feedback link, not the repository’s issue page, and the edit link if they can propose the wording themselves.

123.title: What not to do
123.content: . | Do not point [edit] at the frozen review version under library/. Comments cite it, so it is never edited; the folio’s blocks are. | Do not point [edit] at the staging branch. An edit is a proposal to the published text, so it starts from main; a different branch is an explicit --edit-branch. | Do not hand-write issue URLs in a folio’s pages. They drift when a block is renamed; the build recomputes them from the manifests every time. | .

125.title: Relationship first, visualisation later
125.content: Skill board-diagram-interchange: A board is a DIAGRAM OF a folio, not a container of one. The OMG split between the semantic model and its layout, why the arrow runs one way, and what a note may never carry. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Treat a board like the OMG specifications treat BPMN layout: relationship first, visualisation later. BPMN separates the semantic model — bpmn:process, its tasks and its flows — from Diagram Interchange: BPMNDiagram, BPMNShape, BPMNEdge, which say where each of those was drawn. They are two documents about one subject, and the layout one points at the semantic one, never the other way. A folio board is the same shape: . semantic model notes, anchors, content nodes what is true diagram interchange board-positions.json where it was drawn .

126.title: What follows
126.content: A folio is complete with no board. Deleting every board loses layout and no content. That is the test to apply when you are unsure whether something belongs on the board or in the folio: if losing it would lose a fact, it is not layout. A note carries no x, no y, no board, no position — for the same reason a BPMN task carries no coordinates: layout lives on top of notes, not as data within them. One note may sit on several boards, at different places, without the note arbitrating between them. A coordinate on the note could not express that; a layer above it does so for free. An orphan is swept from the LAYER, which is the easy direction: one file, one pass, and nothing edited out of a note a person owns.

127.title: The arrow, and how it is kept
127.content: folio ──▶ board ──▶ position ──▶ note allowed note ──▶ position / board / folio REFUSED . This is a property a future edit can break silently, so it is checked rather than described. schemas/board-positions.test.ts asserts two things against the SOURCE: . | no field named x, y, board or position appears in todo.ts, carried-note.ts, landing-sticky.ts or note-anchor.ts; | board-positions.ts imports zod and nothing else — it names notes by id, and an id needs no type from the layer below. | . The first guards the failure that actually happens: somebody adding coordinates to a note “for convenience”, which makes a content node carry state and gives one note two answers on two boards.

128.title: Two graph typologies, because they are two things
128.content: | kind | holds | what it is | . | boards | content | what a board is and what it shows | . | board-positions | state | where each note was drawn | . content-context-and-state-graphs refuses a content node that carries state, which is the same rule one level up. And check:graph-typology-work asks a sharper question of the second: it is state, written by a running process every time somebody moves a note — but state that records a position in a PROCESS is work, and state that records a position on a CANVAS is not. Both kinds declare recordsWork: false.

129.title: A board declares what it SHOWS, and absent means everything
129.content: schemas/ui/board.ts: an optional filter over pages and kinds, OR within an axis and AND across them. Absent is the default and it means the whole folio — a query rather than a stored list, because a list of content nodes needs something to notice that a listed node was renamed and that a new one was never added, and a query has nothing to fall behind. Every harness above the floor has a board filled with all contents, which is the absent filter — so the minimal board and the total board are the same document.

130.title: Mergeability is the reason for the shape, and its limit is stated
130.content: Positions are the most concurrently-edited state a folio has: two sessions moving two notes is the ordinary case. So the document is sorted and indented, one note per line-block, and the sort is idempotent — a writer that reshuffled on save would conflict with every other save. It is a partial fix. Two notes that sort adjacent still conflict, because the inserted lines overlap. This removes the guaranteed conflict, not every conflict, and it should not be trusted further than that.

131.title: What this skill is NOT
131.content: Not the rendering. How a board draws, when a card becomes its avatar and what an open window does are board-windows. Not the tiles. Which boards and viewers a reader can reach is harness-tiles.

You are in this process when the question is a READER’s — which card is open, what is raised, how to get back. Semantic zoom is in here too and is deliberately not the same mechanism: the threshold is resolved from the kind and applies itself by SIZE, while opening and closing are a person’s acts. The rule the diagram holds is the one about the way back: an action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. i i i i i i i

151.title: Start in the avatar, open into a window
151.content: Skill board-windows: Everything starts as its avatar; opening projects a window onto the board. The two mechanisms that must not be conflated, z-order, and the fixed chrome a content kind fills in. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Everything starts as its avatar, and [x] closes a window back to it. Opening projects a window onto the board; selecting any part of a window raises it. Each content kind controls its own avatar and rendering, and opens into a full-screen panel with fixed controls such as [x], [linksrc] or [edit].

152.title: TWO mechanisms, and conflating them is the defect
152.content: |   | trigger | who | . | semantic zoom | the card’s rendered width crosses a declared threshold | automatic | . | open / close | [x], or opening a card | a person | . An open window is not a zoom state: it is projected onto the board rather than being the card grown large, so it survives zooming out. Only [x] closes it. Collapsing the two gives a board where a card can close itself with no action taken, and where [x] and a zoom-out are indistinguishable. Semantic zoom is the GLASS’s, not the board’s . Every board slot — a landing sticky and a todo sticky alike — is one component: the same closed square tile (--fa-sticky-tile-size) with the theme’s faded art, and the same compact icon row underneath it. A slot is its closed tile at every width, so semantic zoom does not run on the board. It decides what a card shows on the folio glass, where a card is resized freely. Do not add a width observer to the board grid: it would be a zoom with nothing to change, and the next agent would read it as the card’s state.

153.title: One sticky, one icon row, in one order
153.content: Under every sticky, on every panel: view, edit, pin, send to fsh-guts, as icon buttons. An icon-only control carries aria-label (what a screen reader announces) AND title (the same words on hover); they are not interchangeable. No control sits inside the card body. The open window’s bar uses the same icons for the same acts. A link the sticky cannot serve is absent, never dead.

154.title: Pin is a toggle onto the FOLIO glass
154.content: There is one store answering “what is on my glass”: the folio. A second store holding a page-level copy of the card gets no glass tools, no folio geometry and no shelve, and has to be special-cased by the glass filter and count. | Pin makes the sticky a folio asset — todo/<id> (the key the glass’s own Todos panel pulls a todo out under, so the two ways onto the glass agree) or landing/<slot> — with shown: true, drawn by the glass’s own card path and placed by placeOnGlass. A landing sticky’s theme, picture URL and text travel in the entry as data, never as stored markup. | Unpin is shelveFromGlass — the middle of the three states below. The entry stays; the same pin puts it back, where the reader left it. | The pressed state is the store’s answer (folioStateOf(key) === "glass"), never the button’s memory. The glass’s own × shelves too, and the row’s pin follows it. | .

155.title: Send to fsh-guts asks first
155.content: A control a reader has to ask about has not said what it does, so discard is named for where it goes (Send to fsh-guts, the trashcan that is kept) and opens a confirmation that names the sticky, says it is restorable and per-browser, and says where it is restored from — the fish in the navbar’s icon row. Focus starts on Cancel; Cancel and Escape do nothing but close it. A dialog whose dismissal performs the act did not ask. The window bar’s send is the same act and takes the same confirmation. The inverse is Restore in fsh-guts.

156.title: The threshold is declared, inherited, and traceable
156.content: schemas/kg/semantic-zoom.ts (instance data: semantic-zoom.json): a folio default (belowPx) with a per-kind override (byKind) — the repository’s inheritance rule (inherit everything, override anything; a variant states only what it CHANGES). So: . | the folio always has a number, and every kind resolves to one; | a kind that states nothing is complete, not invalid — requiredness is checked after resolution, never on the declaration; | an override carries a required because, and the resolver returns the source alongside the value, so a reviewer can tell a deliberate override from a folio default that does not fit. | . The boundary is stated once. Strictly below the number, so the declared width is the last one that still shows words. A boundary written one way in a comment and the other way in the renderer makes a card flicker.

157.title: Z-order: selecting any part raises
157.content: Windows stack, and selecting any part of one raises it — not a title bar, any part, because a reader who clicks into a window’s content has already said which one they mean. Z-order is session-only. The DI layer carries no z: a committed stacking order would make every raise a file write and every two sessions a conflict, on the most concurrently-edited state a folio has. If that proves wrong, z is one optional field in the positions document.

158.title: The chrome is fixed; the kind fills it in
158.content: A content kind declares which controls it offers, and the platform fixes the frame: . | [x] is always present and always in the same place, so a reader learns the frame once; | a declared control that names nothing known is a finding, not a missing button; | a control the environment cannot perform is hidden, and the reason reported — a dead [edit] 404s for exactly the reader who cannot edit, which reads as “this page is broken” rather than “you cannot do this”. | .

159.title: Closing must have a reachable inverse
159.content: An action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. On an overlay, close may set hidden, because the launcher tile re-opens it. On a board that IS page content, hidden removes a section of the page, so the inline board collapses to a control in its own position, and focus follows it — left alone, focus lands on <body> and the keyboard position is gone. A control two clicks deep inside a collapsed launcher does not count as reachable. A default of “hidden” is allowed only with the inverse on screen. The glass’s tile strip starts slid away; its “Show tiles (N)” tab stays in view, in the strip’s own position, and the same tab hides the tiles again. See harness-tiles §”The glass strip”.

160.title: The floor, which is not negotiable
160.content: This layer’s declared interaction profile is low-dexterity. Every board action is keyboard-operable; drag is an accelerator and never the only way in. Targets are at least the tile size. And the board is ALWAYS collapsible to a linear, tile-based listing — a board that cannot be read linearly cannot be read by a screen reader, printed, or translated. The listing is the ARTEFACT and the board is the overlay . The board is an extra laid over a simple tile-based listing. So the floor must be correct with no JavaScript at all, not merely when the board is toggled off: notes built only by docs-ui.js from a fetch of assets/todos/index.json give a reader with JavaScript off no note, no count, and no hint that notes exist. Three checks follow: . Document order, never the board’s order. The board may stack by BPMN subprocess depth; the floor does not, because document order is what a screen reader and a printout depend on, and a floor that reordered would be a second answer to “what comes next”. Collapsed, never removed. When the board mounts it moves the listing into a disclosure so the page does not show the same notes twice. It does not delete it, hide it from assistive technology, or display: none it: a listing the board removed would have no way back while the board is open. Assert against the SERVED HTML. A test that reads the DOM passes because the board built that DOM. The assertion is on bytes the server sent — a browser context with javaScriptEnabled: false over the same renderer the generator writes with.

161.title: The folio belongs to the HARNESS, not to the library
161.content: A content library is something a reader browses — a replica, a published layer, any folio published as a site. A folio is the reader’s own surface: their notes, the assets they have materialised, the documents they created or linked. So the folio visualisation is cat-harness’s, available by convention on any harness, and a library never implements its own. A library may have its own landing page and its own harness; neither is licence to build a second folio. Consistency is the requirement: a reader moving between libraries must find the same folio, because the point of carrying a folio is that it does not change underneath them. A note or a todo MAY reference nodes in another KG library. The folio is not scoped to the library it is pulled down over, so a renderer must not assume local resolution.

162.title: A tile, or an avatar?
162.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares, an avatar is what the FOLIO holds, and a theme is how either one looks rather than a third kind. The test is in harness-tiles §”A tile, or an avatar?”, and only there, because one rule with two homes is free to drift.

163.title: An asset has THREE states, not two
163.content: Pulling the folio down gives a glass — a surface over whatever is being browsed, carrying sticky notes and the avatars of materialised assets, including materialised KG like cat-bootstrap or cat-harness themselves. | state | where the asset is | how it got there | . | in the library | not the reader’s at all | the default | . | in the folio, not displayed | materialised into the folio’s own reproduce directories — library/ for the bytes, uploads/ for a source — off the glass | the reader closed it, “back in library” | . | on the glass | displayed in the pulled-down folio | the reader pulled it out of the library | . “In the folio” is not folio/. The folio is the reader’s REPOSITORY, of which library/ and uploads/ are declared parts — both carry dependents: "reproduce". folio/ is a different graph typology: renderable authored content. corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a node materialised anywhere else reads as ABSENT to every consumer. Closing returns an asset to the middle state and NEVER to the first. Only its display goes. Putting it back on the glass is a separate act performed from the library, not from the glass it just left. A two-state model would make closing a sticky and un-materialising an asset the same gesture, and a reader tidying their glass would silently discard work; the middle state is what makes closing cheap enough to do freely. When you implement close, check that the library offers the way back — not that the glass does. Close says where the way back is, at the moment of closing. The glass’s [x] opens a confirm that names the layer’s library and links it; Escape and Cancel leave the card where it is, and only the confirm shelves it — after which the glass says, with the same link, where the asset went. Naming the library matters because a reader holding assets from several libraries would otherwise have to remember which one each came from. The place is the card’s own, so there are three. A library card goes back to its layer’s library, a todo to the Todos board, and a landing sticky pinned to the glass to the page it was pinned from; calling a sticky “your Todos” would send the reader to a list it was never on. One function answers “where does this card go back to”, and the confirm, the status after it and the [x] button’s own label all read it, so the three cannot disagree. The confirm is the page’s one confirm dialog, shared with sending a sticky to fsh-guts, so focus-on-Cancel and Escape-cancels are stated once. Opening a library card goes to the asset’s visualizer when its index entry declares one, else to its entry page; resizing is a corner drag, with +/− in move mode and the move bar’s buttons as the non-drag path.

164.title: Two settings panels, two names, each points to the other
164.content: The glass has its own settings (theme, avatars, opacity, blur), and the page has its own under ▦ Actions (scheme, reading preferences, the Discarded fish, Declared kinds). They are named “Glass settings” and “Page settings”, so a screen reader does not read two controls identically, and each panel opens with a link to the other, as its first control, because a reader who opens the wrong panel needs a pointer to the right one. Site chrome and board state are unrelated settings but they are neighbouring places, and a reader moves between places. | The names are declared once (SETTINGS_NAMES in docs-ui.js), because each panel’s link prints the OTHER panel’s name; a panel renamed in one place only would leave the other panel’s link naming something that no longer exists. | The link must OPEN its target, not toggle it, and not open it underneath. The glass’s openPanel closes a panel that is already open, and the open glass covers the sidebar where Page settings lives. So the glass-to-page link shuts the glass first, and the page-to-glass link shuts the launcher first. In both cases focus lands on the target panel’s heading. | No link to nothing. A page with a glass and no sidebar has no launcher. Each panel registers an opener, and the link is drawn only when its target registered one. | . The same holds for any future pair of panels that share a word: name each one for what it acts on, and point each one at the other. scripts/tests/settings-labels-distinct.test.ts checks the source; test/settings-crosslinks.e2e.ts checks the rendered page at 1280×800 and 390×844, by mouse and keyboard.

165.title: Lazy window content fetch and render safety
165.content: Rendering the board with N cards makes 0 per-card detail fetches up front: each board slot (todoSlot / renderBoardTiles) renders only its summary tile/avatar. When a card carries a per-card detail or artifact URL (detailHref, bodyHref, artifactHref, or a non-inlined jsonldHref), opening its window (openCard / createLazyWindowLoader.openWindow) fetches that card’s content lazily on open, caches the result by card id (so re-opening uses the cached result and never pre-fetches the other N - 1 cards), and renders any body or tool/skill output through the declared renderToolOutput (RENDER_AS: text, url, markdown, json) and safeHref boundary (schemas/ui/render-output.ts, site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js). A refused URL scheme (such as javascript:) is never fetched and is shown as escaped text.

168.title: Reading a knowledge graph before you have anything
168.content: Skill bootstrap-kg-navigation: Read and navigate a knowledge graph with nothing installed — no MCP server, no tools, no harness. Named bootstrap- so it cannot be confused with a navigation Skill of a Harness that is installed. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . This skill assumes a text editor and nothing else. No MCP server, no skill-fetching tool, no work-plan store, no build. If those exist they are not yours to rely on yet — see AGENTS.md.

169.title: A graph is files that declare what they are
169.content: Three facts carry the whole model, and every one of them is checkable by reading: . | A layer declares the directories it scans, in its declaration at its root. Each entry is an id, a path, and the kinds of graph found there. | A directory is a place to look, not a type. One may hold more than one part of a graph, so the directory does not say what its files are — the files do, in their own front matter or $schema. | Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. An override matches on an entry’s id, never its path. Matching on path turns one relocated graph into two, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | . Two more words you will meet in a declaration. A field this skill does not describe is an Extension: a Harness added it, and you ignore it. A Harness’s own kind of declaration, which requires everything bootstrap’s does and adds Extensions, is a Subkind of bootstrap’s: read it as bootstrap’s, and it still means what it says. Versions and addresses. A declaration may state its version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and an iriBase. Every identifier it mints, and every page meant for a person, is then <iriBase>v<major>/…: the address carries the major alone, so only a breaking release moves it. The exact release you read is fixed by the pin that brought this repository to you, not by the address. Bootstrap’s own are in its declaration; read them there rather than trusting a copy.

170.title: Do this, in order
170.content: . | Read the repository’s declaration. If there is none, this repository is not a layer yet, and that is the case bootstrap exists for. | Find the entry whose graphTypologies name the kind you want. In bootstrap they are named for what they hold: skills, processes, scenarios (the Roles), schemas and models. The entry’s path is relative to the declaration. | Read the files in that directory. A markdown file declaring name: and description: in front matter is a skill — its body is the instruction you were looking for. A file declaring $schema: is stating that it is something else, and is not a skill however it is named. | Follow a reference by id, not by path. A node that names another names it by id; resolve it through the declaration rather than guessing a filename. | .

171.title: What “I could not determine” means here
171.content: An absent declaration and an unreadable one are different: . | what you found | what it means | what to do | . | no declaration | not a layer yet | this is bootstrap’s case — continue | . | a declaration that will not parse | a layer asserting something broken | stop and say so; do not fall back | . | a declared directory that is not there | the declaration is wrong | stop and say so — scanning nothing and reporting a clean run is the defect | . | no declaration for a kind you want | this layer has none of it | that is an answer, not a failure | .

172.title: What this skill is NOT
172.content: It does not describe what a Harness above bootstrap holds, such as its content or its checks: those belong to the Harness you have not loaded yet. If you need one of them to finish bootstrap, the boundary is in the wrong place — say so rather than importing the definition.

175.title: Inputs and outputs
175.content: schemas/skills/bpmn-authoring/: . | in — processName (required), sourceWorkflow, existingBpmn, participants | out — bpmnFile, diagramFile, taskCount, gatewayCount, participantCount | . graphviz is a declared capability with degradation: skip — layout help degrades, authoring does not stop.

176.title: Diagram Interchange is not optional
176.content: A .bpmn with no DI section — no explicit x/y on its shapes — parses and renders blank, although the XML looks complete. bun run cat render:bpmn renders every diagram to docs/assets/img/workflows/ with bpmn-js in headless Chromium; bun run cat render:bpmn:check fails when an SVG is stale. Run the renderer and look at the SVG before you call a diagram done.

177.title: Readable at 100%: check it before and after (author check)
177.content: Every diagram you write or touch must, when you are done: . | fit 1400 × 900 in diagram units, so its 16px text reads at about 14px in a 1200px band without zooming; every task a fixed 120 × 120 square: boxes never grow to fit their names, and a name that does not fit is shortened (TASK_SIZE in the tools layer); | have no label on another label, on a flow (its own included), on a box or across a lane line: a gateway’s question above the diamond, its answers beside their flows, every label inside one lane; | have right-angled flows and every name inside its box, pool and lane names inside their strips; | have no crossing flows, and the lane order that keeps flows between lanes shortest: each lane sits next to the lanes it exchanges flows with, so no flow crosses a lane it does not stop in. A lane that talks to only one other lane, such as an owner who only approves the merge steward’s card, goes on the outside, next to that lane (owner, 2026-11-07: “swap owner lane down to reduce arrows across non interacting actor lanes”). | . bun run cat bpmn:detangle <file> reports all of it, and --write fixes what it can (lane order, right angles, box and lane sizes, label places). Run it before and after, and put both counts in the PR. Zero findings on every diagram you touch, or it does not merge (owner, 2026-11-02, after 63 of 80 harness diagrams were found with findings: “improve bpmn authoring process/skills so doesnt happen again”). A report nobody has to act on is how they piled up. Run bpmn:detangle <file> --check last; a finding you leave needs a reason in the PR, and only diagram-too-wide / lane-order may be left that way. Then look at the render: the check cannot yet see a box drawn across a lane line or outside its own lane, two flows drawn on top of each other, or a flow that wanders through a lane it does not stop in. Those are found only by looking. The same findings are in render:bpmn’s warnings and the process’s QA report, so a reviewer sees what the author left. The procedure, and why the budget is 1400 × 900, is bpmn-detangle.

178.title: In this repository, a diagram is executable
178.content: processes/**/*.bpmn are not pictures. workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete run them, and workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. That has consequences for how you author: . | Every activity carries <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/> naming the skill that implements it, and <cat-harness.processes:bean store="beans/"/> where it touches the work plan. bun run cat check:workflow-refs fails on a ref that resolves to nothing, and bun run cat kg:audit additionally fails when the named skill exists but no package can serve it. | Every lane names a role. Declare the role once as a top-level <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> (before the collaboration and the process), and set partitionElementRef="<role id>" on the lane; the id is the role’s in scenarios/roles.json, verbatim. Lane names are free text; an explicit ref is the join that does not depend on spelling. <bootstrap.processes:role ref> is the deprecated form. A diagram using any bootstrap.processes: element declares the namespace as the first child of <bpmn:definitions>: <bpmn:import namespace="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns/" location="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns.jsonld" importType="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld"/>. | A store is not a lane. Lanes are for people and agents, the roles that act. A place where things are kept, such as the work plan (work items), a corpus, a session record, an activity log or a published bucket, is a <bpmn:dataStoreReference>. The tasks that read or write it point at it with data associations, and each task sits in the lane of whoever does it. A “Work plan — beans” lane holding “Open the bean” says the store does the work, when the agent does. | The process’s own bpmn:documentation opens with what it is for. Its first sentence is the diagram’s row on the publication-workflow page. kg-export carries it on the Process node as summary (the whole text as description), the page reads it from the published named-subgraph JSON-LD (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) rather than from anything written by hand, and check:process-index fails when a declared diagram’s node has none. So that sentence says what the process does or answers — not who asked for it, which work item or issue it came from, or where the work got to. Those belong later in the documentation, or in the work item. | A gateway may be computed rather than chosen — see dmn-authoring. | Policy is declared on the process. <cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement="strict"/> means workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled; absent policy means strict. Steps marked relaxable="false" may never be relaxed by any package. | .

179.title: Readable diagrams: what the research supports
179.content: These rules are what holds up from the BPMN comprehension research, checked mechanically. kg:audit reports each rule below per process (src/workflow/diagram-quality.ts in the tools layer). The sources, and how strong each rule’s evidence is, are in the process-model-quality methodology. | Separate routing from work. A task never has two outgoing flows: put an exclusive or parallel gateway after it, or a reader must guess fork vs choice (activity-implicit-split, major). A loop-back INTO a task is fine. A gateway either joins or splits, not both (gateway-mixed). A question is a gateway, never a task: a box named “Should it leave now?” or “Separate this graph?” is a decision drawn as work. If someone must judge first, draw that as a task (“Judge whether it should leave”) or a call to Process_AskThePerson, then the question on the gateway after it. | Keep it small. Split by phase into call activities past 20 flow nodes (process-size). That 20 is house style. The only threshold with evidence is 7PMG’s 50 (process-decompose, major), and it predicts modelling errors such as deadlocks, not reading speed. | One start event per process level (process-single-start). Several named end events are fine, and the work item CLOSE pattern needs them. | A decision is a question, its branches are the answers (decision-label-question). | Label activities verb-object: imperative verb, then its object (Review the draft, not Draft review) (activity-label-verb-first). The evidence is one study of how ambiguous labels felt (29 students), so this is reported, never gated. | A name says the step, nothing else. No trailing [skill] slug: the skill is in <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>, and the page links it from there. No step numbers (“1 ·”, “Phase 2:”, “P1.1”): the flows already give the order, and a number in front breaks verb-first. A number that cites a section of a source document goes in the task’s documentation. A list of numbered steps is a sign the diagram copies a document’s outline; group the steps into phases instead. | . Split by phase: how . A diagram can be right in every step and still unreadable on its page. When process-size fires, or a diagram has a start event per lane, split it like this: . | The top-level process shows the phases. Each phase is a <bpmn:callActivity calledElement="…"> to its own process. Keep at the top only what moves the work between phases: who hands off to whom, and the decisions that send it back (rejected → revise). A loop that crosses phases is drawn at the top; a loop inside a phase stays in that phase. | A phase lives in its own file, <parent>-<phase>.bpmn, next to the parent, with its own process id (Process_<Parent><Phase>) and a first documentation sentence that says what the phase does. It becomes the phase’s row on the publication-workflow page like any other diagram’s. | A phase that ends two ways ends in two named end events, and the caller’s gateway right after the call reads which one it reached, as GW_BeanYours reads Process_BeanOpen’s. | Keep the node ids when you move nodes into a phase. A test, a schema or a skill that points at Task_X then changes only its file and process, not its id. | Open and close the work item at the top, once. A process that is only ever called runs on its caller’s work item, so a phase calls neither Process_BeanOpen nor Process_BeanClose (check:bean-calls). “Once” holds for the top as well: a process with several outcomes routes them all into one Process_BeanClose call, which decides itself whether the work item is completed, scrapped or blocked, and only then branches to its named end events. One close per outcome repeats the same box and makes the diagram wide. | A caller’s adjudication accepts looks one level down. If the judgement moves into a phase, put accepts on the call to that phase, and take it off any caller further up. | Name a call activity for the phase, verb-object like any activity (“Review the change”), not for its file. | . A phase that only one parent calls is still worth its own file: the point is the page a reader opens, not reuse. Untangle every diagram you touch . The same discipline as ArchiMate views (archimate-models §”Untangle every view you touch”), and the same geometry: a change never adds a tangle. Run bun run cat kg:audit before and after, and compare edge-crossing, edge-through-node and edge-rectilinear for the diagram, and check that no shape has a flow in and a flow out on the same point and that each lane’s rows sit at k/(n+1) of its height (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”). Say both counts in the PR. Route loop-backs in the channel below the lane (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”), then look at the rendered SVG. What the evidence does NOT support . Do not import these from style guides or model output; each was checked: . | Mandatory left-to-right flow. Figl & Strembeck 2015 (44 people) found no significant difference in accuracy or time across four directions. Lay out left-to-right for consistency, not because it reads faster. | A word cap on labels, a gateway fan-out cap of 4, and a fixed colour palette. No study behind them. Colouring matching split and join gateways made novices more accurate and experts faster, not more accurate (Reijers et al. 2011). | OR-gateways need no rule: the process model refuses inclusive gateways at load. | .

184.title: CI health — a red workflow looks exactly like a green one from in here
184.content: Skill ci-health: A red workflow looks exactly like a green one from inside a checkout. How to read a default-branch health report, the three verdicts that keep it honest, why a watchdog needs both a session-start print and an unattended run, and the separate external question the Pages deployments need. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Record agent step, Review-log watch, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . A workflow’s outcome is invisible from the working tree. Nothing in a checkout says whether the last run passed, so a workflow can fire on every push and fail every time while the repository reads as healthy. Measured here: one publishing workflow fired on every push to the default branch and failed all 30 times over two months. The trigger was fine; the outcome was unobserved, the published site sat stale, and nothing in the repository said so.

185.title: Read the report, and read it by these three rules
185.content: check:ci-health reports each workflow’s state on the default branch — consecutive failures, days since the last green, and whether it has run at all recently. The session-start sweep prints it, so it lands where you already look. | “Could not check” is never rendered as green. A watchdog that has gone blind must not read as good news. | A red that has not re-run in a week is possibly stale, not an active fire. The distinction is what stops a dead workflow consuming attention a live one needs. | A red whose workflow file changed after the failing run is superseded. The version that failed is gone, so the verdict is stale. superseded is never rendered as green and never counted as a live failure: a later edit is evidence the failing version is gone, not evidence the new one works. | . That third rule is not hypothetical. Two workflows here failed to parse on one day — which is why the platform ran them on push despite both being dispatch-only, and why their runs are named by path rather than by their declared name. They were fixed the next day, and they only run on dispatch, so nothing will ever run them on the default branch again. Without the rule they are red forever. Do not “fix” a dispatch-only workflow by dispatching it. Some fail by design in the repository you are standing in — a folio-shaped job preflighting on a manifest the platform does not carry, or a computation step needing a directory only a folio has. A red you caused by running something that was never meant to run here is worse than the stale verdict you were trying to clear.

186.title: For ONE commit, zero checks is not a pass
186.content: check:ci-health reads workflows across history. When the question is one commit (may I merge this PR, must I fix it, or do I not yet know?), the tool is bun run cat ci:watch <sha> or ci:watch --pr <n>. It answers in three states, and undetermined has its own exit code, never 0. The trap it exists for arrives as good news. A conflicted pull request gets no pull_request run at all. GitHub checks out refs/pull/N/merge, which it does not build for a head that conflicts. So the notification that “every check suite completed and none failed” can be true of zero suites. “No suite failed” over nothing that ran is not green, and neither is a partial set (a push-triggered job finished, the PR’s gate workflow never registered). Before reading an event as a pass, ask the head’s merge state. A merge ref that exists can still have been built for an EARLIER head (GitHub leaves the old one in place when a new head conflicts), so the ref must have been built from the current head. The tool enforces this (verdictForCommit, mergeStateForHead); an agent reading PR events without the tool applies it too. qa-publish is a job in the gate workflow, and it is not a gate . Code quality gates carries one job that judges nothing: qa-publish, which runs after gates whatever they concluded and stores the run’s QA results on the orphan qa-reports branch (main/<sha>/ on a push, pr/<n>/<sha>/ on a same-repository PR). Read its outcome as a statement about the evidence, not about the commit: . | red — the record for this commit was not stored. The gates’ verdict is untouched (it is a separate job for exactly that reason), but a later --against this commit will read UNKNOWN, so it is still a red to fix, and a workflow-level red in this report. | green with a ::notice on a fork PR — skipped by design: a fork’s token cannot write. Stated, never silent. | green with the gates red — the red commit’s evidence was stored. That is the point of always(), not a contradiction. | . The merge policy counts it like any job: a PR is handed to the Merge Steward only when CI is green on every job (continual-progress §”Green means handed to the Merge Steward”).

187.title: The report answers about the default branch — and Pages is not on it
187.content: A Pages build outcome is not repository state. It is a fact GitHub holds about the repository, and it changes the repository’s status without changing a single byte of it. So the tool must look external, cache nothing: a committed answer would be right when it was written and silently wrong from then on. The default-branch query cannot see it, for three reasons at once, and all three have to be answered together: . | property | why the default-branch query misses it | . | runs on the publish branch | ?branch=<default> excludes them outright | . | raised by github-pages[bot], event dynamic | there is no file in .github/workflows/ to be a row about | . | its workflow has no file | it is addressable only by a per-repository id | . Measured here on one day: the default-branch page held zero deployments while the publish branch held 51 cancelled and 49 succeeded, of which 25 were self-inflicted. None of it was visible from anywhere. Two more, for the question the three above do not cover . Deliberately not numbered 4 and 5: the three rules are the three rules, for reading the default-branch report, and they are quoted by that count in several places. These are a separate pair for a separate question — which is itself the rule about never letting a count in prose go stale. | cancelled is a THIRD state. A cancelled deployment neither shipped nor broke: the previous preview stays up, so the site is stale rather than down, and nobody is owed a fix. Folded into success the report says the preview shipped; folded into failure it sends somebody after a build that was merely superseded. Both readings are wrong in a way the reader cannot detect — which is rule 1 again, wearing different clothes. Crucial exception: staleness is benign only when falling back to an existing live preview, never when the previous state is a deletion (where “stale” manifests as a 404). When PR N’s merge cleanup removed branches/<slug>/ and PR N+1’s staging deploy was cancelled, the live site serves the deletion rather than a previous preview. Staleness is safe only when what you fall back to actually exists. | Say WHOSE contention it is. One workflow pushing twice and cancelling its own build is a fixed defect; several sessions racing for the publish ref is a different, open one. A merged cancellation count cannot show whether the first fix held — so the self-inflicted ones are named by slug, and a slug still appearing is a branch running the workflow from before the fix. | . Report the counts; grade only a floor . There is no calibrated threshold for “too many cancellations”, so the report states the numbers and does not grade the share — no percentage, no verdict word. That is the same refusal that stopped a PDF heuristic inventing a size threshold with nothing to calibrate against. One statement is graded, because it is a floor rather than a threshold: deployments happened and not one succeeded. That needs no calibration, the way “the build directory is empty” needs none.

188.title: A report is only read by someone in the room
188.content: This is the part that gets designed wrong. The session-start print covers every day somebody is working — and the failure being guarded against is a quiet stretch with nobody looking, which is exactly the stretch in which no session starts either. A report alone cannot cover its own worst case. So the watchdog has a second half: the same check runs on a schedule and maintains one tracking issue, which is . | opened when the default branch has a live failure, | edited in place while it persists — an edit does not notify, so a long outage stays one unread item rather than a stream, | closed automatically when the branch is clean. | . It deliberately does not send another email. The platform already sent 30 and the premise of the whole exercise is that nobody reads them. Live badges at the top of the README are the same state at the front door. Two properties of that scheduled run are load-bearing rather than incidental: . | It needs full history. The superseded rule asks when a workflow file last changed, and a shallow clone cannot answer — which would resurrect exactly the false fires the rule exists to retire. | On “could not check” it leaves the issue untouched and fails its own job, rather than closing it. A watchdog reporting that it cannot see must not read as good news, and its own red is reported by the next scheduled run. | . The second instance: merge-main’s in-place comment . The same edited-in-place doctrine governs merge-main.yml (implemented by cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-main-comment.ts). The workflow fires on every push to main and runs across open PRs; one failing PR must not email the maintainer on every push across the day. So the bot’s PR comment is the record and is edited in place, and a failure whose signature the comment already holds stays quiet. Three conditions stay loud (failing the aggregate step so the run notifies): . | A new failure — the first failure on this PR head. | A changed cause — the failure signature changed even on the same head. | A systemic failure — every selected PR failed, not made up entirely of repeats (or a member failed to classify itself). | . Quiet is not silent. A failure that does not notify still maintains four records: . | Its PR comment (edited in place, carrying the failure signature). | Its line in the job summary. | A warning annotation on the run. | Its own red member job in the matrix (findable in GitHub Actions UI). | .

189.title: The opposite defect
189.content: This covers a workflow that fires constantly and fails every time. The complementary failure — a workflow that never fires at all — is not visible to this check, because a workflow with no runs and a workflow with no failures look identical in the run history. Both are “could not check”, and the first rule applies.

190.title: A superseded PR run is cancelled — and only a PR’s
190.content: A run on a PR head that a newer push replaced judges a commit nobody will merge, and it still waits for and holds a runner. So a workflow that runs on pull_request declares . concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.number || github.sha }} cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }} . Two halves, and the second matters as much as the first. A PR’s runs share one group, so the newer cancels the older. Every other event is grouped by its own sha and never cancelled: a push to main keeps its verdict, so this report’s history of main is not thinned by cancellations, and a cancelled on main keeps meaning contention rather than housekeeping (the third state above). A cancelled run on a PR’s OLDER head is therefore expected and is not a finding. The merge guard judges the head, and the head’s run is never the one cancelled.

191.title: A green step can be a SKIPPED one: the CI cone
191.content: cat-harness-tools/scripts/ci-cone.ts lets a pull request skip a bun run cat <check> gate step whose inputs are unchanged since main’s last green run. Such a step prints SKIPPED — inputs unchanged since <sha>, and the job summary lists it under CI cone. Read it as “not asked here”, never as “passed here”. It is built but NOT wired into the workflow. Measured 2026-10-07 on the 53 candidate steps of gates-kg and gates-docs: . | It saves almost nothing. The 36 checks it could record skip on a beans-only or one-script PR, but they are the cheap ones: about 30 runner-seconds a run. Deciding costs about 0.5 s a step, roughly 22 s for those steps. | Recording would slow main a lot. The expensive checks cannot be recorded: kg:audit:check and kg:audit:all:check read the qa-reports store, and skill:register:check has an unannotated site. Tracing them anyway would add minutes to every main run (kg:audit:all:check: 74 s untraced, 782 s traced). | . Wire it in when those checks become recordable. The rule it follows: an input set is declared or derived, never inferred, and derived is preferred (no drift, no extra data fields). | Declared is a task-io row. It is checked by the input-site audit. | Derived is computed from the run itself and never stored as authored data. A green run on main traces the check under strace and records what that run read: the files, the directory listings, the absent paths it probed, and the read-only git commands it ran, with their answers. A PR skips the check only when every recorded path and every git answer is the same, and so is the script fingerprint (import closure, audited environment, tools and --against baseline). | Inferred is a guess about what a check reads. It is never used. | . Why the derived set is enough. The verdict and its read set come from the same run. A PR run with the same code and the same recorded inputs takes the same path, so it reads the same files and gives the same answer. A data-dependent read is covered by the same argument: the file that chose the path is one of the recorded inputs. What a trace cannot enumerate is never skipped. Each of these is recorded as undetermined, so the check always runs: . | a write inside the checkout; | a git command that is not read-only; | a traced input site the run reached; | a relative path with no known directory; | a trace over 256 MiB; | more than 20,000 paths. | . A failed traced run is asked again untraced, so the verdict is always the check’s own.

192.title: Step names describe what the check does, not merely its passing invariant
192.content: A CI step named solely after its passing invariant misdescribes any failure where the check could not run or the baseline was absent. A step named viewer pages keep the navbar they had that goes red when its audit sidecar is absent misleads a reader to investigate page layouts when zero pages regressed. Where a check has both a subject-invariant branch and an audit/baseline-reachability branch, the step name in the workflow must cover both (e.g. viewer pages keep the navbar they had, and audit is reachable).

193.title: The accidental-repair trap on derived gates
193.content: A green outcome on a derived gate (such as readme:subgraphs:check, docs:harness:check, or other verify/write pairs) must never be read as “was never broken”. Because PR branches run merge:main which regenerates derived files, an unrelated PR branch may happen to carry a freshly generated artefact. When that PR merges into main, it incidentally repairs main, creating an illusion in CI history that the commit before it was clean. The guard: The post-merge regeneration pipeline (.github/workflows/post-merge-regen.yml, scripts/post-merge-regen.ts) audits derived artefacts when dispatched on main and warns when they are stale; dispatched for a PR, it commits the regeneration to that PR’s branch, and the release build regenerates into what it publishes (merge-queue.md §”Where derived artefacts are regenerated”). When inspecting CI health on main, do not treat an accidental green as evidence of health: verify that post-merge checks run and derive their state consistently. Full details in merge-queue.md (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”The accidental-repair pattern”.
