613.title: discussion — settling what an agent cannot read off disk
613.content: Skill discussion: Settle which harness, and which repositories, when no file says: the output is a document conforming to discussion.output.schema.json. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . An agent that has just read bootstrap’s README.md knows the shape of a harness and nothing about this one. Two questions have no answer in any file it can reach: . | which harness this repository should become: bootstrap itself, or any Harness built on it; | which repositories are involved — where the dependency is read from, where the new declaration is written to, and whether they are the same. | . Only whoever asked for the harness can answer them, so the agent asks. This skill says what the asking must produce. processes/discussion.bpmn narrows the candidates and then calls human-agent-discussion, the one reusable way bootstrap asks a person anything, with no default allowed.

614.title: Inputs and outputs
614.content: |   |   | . | in | discussion.input.schema.json: what the agent already knows, and which of the two unknowns is open | . | out | discussion.output.schema.json: harness, repositories[], outcome, determinedBy, answeredBy, and the exchange that produced it | . Both are plain JSON Schema in schemas/, readable with nothing installed. The task is finished when a document conforming to the output schema exists, not when a conversation has taken place. The participant may be a person or a sibling agent that already holds the answer; the output records which (kind: person | agent), as human-agent-discussion says.

615.title: First, say where you are
615.content: Before narrowing anything (A_DetermineWhere), determine the three things human-agent-discussion requires before any question: . | the Process: Initialize a harness, inside Determine the harness and repositories. A Bootstrapping Agent can be nowhere else (FR-2); | the Roles: itself as the Bootstrapping Agent; the person it will ask as the Requestor. A request relayed by somebody else leaves the Requestor undetermined; | the context: what the request said, and what the checkout holds. | . One that cannot be determined is never filled with a default: it is asked about first, and the harness question waits.

616.title: Rules
616.content: Ask the fewest questions that settle it. Narrow the candidate list from context first (a repository whose root already holds a declaration, <name>.json, is not a blank slate) and put the rest as one question with the candidates named. A question a reader must go and research is not ready. Never infer the answer from a default. If nothing is known, the output’s determinedBy is asked, not assumed. assumed is permitted only for a default the README states, and assumption then names it. Record repositories as pairs, not as a list. read from and written to can be the same repository or two; the point of determining them is to know where the declaration lands. Never infer written-to from push access. A remote repository is read-from until the Requestor authorizes writing to it (confirm-harness). A refusal is an outcome. If the participant declines, that is outcome: "unsettled" with what was asked and what is still open — not a guess, and not an error.

626.title: A computed gateway is not a chosen one
626.content: In this repository a DMN table has a second job: an exclusive gateway carrying <cat-harness.processes:decision ref="decisions/<file>.dmn#<Decision_Id>"/> has its branch computed from the table rather than picked by the agent. workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at such a gateway. Asserting the answer would defeat the point of writing the table. You pass facts — e.g. { failCritical: 0, failMajor: 2 } from qa_sweep totals — and the table returns the branch. Adding one means adding the .dmn, the cat-harness.processes:decision ref, and nothing else: the loader checks that every outcome the table can return names a real outgoing flow, so a table that can route somewhere the diagram cannot go is a load error rather than a surprise at the moment of decision.

627.title: The FEEL subset this interpreter implements
627.content: src/workflow/decision-table.ts implements a deliberate subset: - (any), literals, comparisons, and one-of. It refuses ranges, not() and function calls rather than mis-evaluating them. Write within that subset: a table using a construct the interpreter rejects fails at load, rather than being mis-evaluated at the moment of decision.

628.title: Three states belong in the table
628.content: Encode “could not determine” as an outcome in its own right — pages-live-gate.dmn returns live, not-yet and unknown; folio-intent.dmn returns ask when the filesystem cannot decide. A gate whose only outcomes are pass and fail forces an unmeasured input to be rendered as one of them, and it is always rendered as pass. If your decision has an input that may be unavailable, give it a branch.

629.title: Hit policy
629.content: Say it explicitly. FIRST is the usual choice here and is what folio-intent.dmn uses — rules are ordered, the first match wins, and the ordering is then part of the logic and must be reviewed as such.

632.title: document-authoring
632.content: Named by: Authoring a document . Author a document folio: policy guidance, a standard, a report, a handbook — anything whose content is structured prose rather than machine- checked mathematics.

633.title: What a document folio is
633.content: The same content model as a paper, minus the formal layer: . folio/<slug>/ <slug>.ts the document manifest (chapters, in order) <chapter-dir>/ <chapter-dir>.ts the chapter manifest (sections, in order) <block-root>.ts one block manifest <block-root>.md that block's narrative body <block-root>.qa.json QA sidecar (machine-written; never hand-edit) . A block is the unit of authorship, review, feedback and QA. Its .ts carries the metadata — label, title, uses[] — and its .md carries the prose. They are separate files so a reviewer’s diff is over prose, not over a manifest.

634.title: The kinds you may use
634.content: prose, recommendation, example, remark, algorithm, simulator, equation, diagram, figure, table (the document-profile nodes in block-kinds/). Not definition, theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, conjecture, proof. Those seven are the paper profile: their assertion is a formal mathematical claim backed by a .lean sibling, and a document folio has no Lean toolchain to check one. content_profile_check enforces this, and content_validate runs it on every pass. If you find yourself wanting a theorem, you want one of two things: . | a normative statement — a recommendation, a requirement, a rule. See normative-statements for how to carry one in this profile, and read it before reaching for a math kind. | an actual theorem — in which case this folio is a paper. Change the layer’s index.config.json entry to "contentType": "paper" deliberately (the index is the one config), and know that you are taking on Lean and TeX as dependencies. | .

635.title: Adding a block
635.content: . | Find the section it belongs to. content_list shows the tree. A block only reaches the output if a section’s blocks[] names it — writing the files is not enough, and a block nobody lists renders nowhere and is swept by nothing. | Write <root>.ts — the builder call for the kind, with label, optional title, and uses[]. | Write <root>.md — the prose. GitHub-flavoured Markdown; tables, footnotes and raw HTML all survive to the output unchanged, because the document render path assembles Markdown rather than translating it. | Add the root name to the section’s blocks[], in reading order. | content_validate before you consider it done. | .

636.title: uses[] is editorial, and it is yours to maintain
636.content: uses[] lists the blocks a reader must already have read to follow this one. It is a judgement about narrative order, not a mechanical fact — nothing derives it and nothing should. In a paper folio there is a machine-derived formal graph alongside it; in a document folio there is not, so uses[] is the only dependency signal the corpus carries. Every ordering metric, every impact question (“what has to change if this recommendation changes?”), and the reading-order review read it. List direct neighbours only. If A needs B and B needs C, A lists B.

637.title: Rendering
637.content: document_render_md assembles the whole folio into one Markdown file — run it to inspect ordering before you render anything else. document_render_html and document_render_pdf go through pandoc; the PDF path uses an HTML engine (weasyprint, prince, wkhtmltopdf) and never falls back to LaTeX. If no engine is installed it says so.

638.title: What belongs in the folio, and what belongs here
638.content: Subject matter — the actual recommendations, the vocabulary, the chapters — lives in the folio repo, as content. This platform holds the formalism. If you are about to add a domain constant or a subject-specific rule to folio-assistant, you are in the wrong repository.

647.title: Overview
647.content: This skill manages the uploads/ directory as an intake pipeline for converting raw documents into structured content objects. It handles: . | Scanned PDFs / images — OCR extraction → text → blocks | LaTeX source — environment extraction → blocks | Structured / normative guidelines — normative structure → blocks | arXiv papers — fetched source → blocks (delegates to paper-importer) | Arbitrary documents — best-effort structural analysis | . 649.title: uploads/ Directory Convention
649.content: uploads/ <document-id>/ intake.json ← what arrived and where from (folio-intake/v1) <document-id>.dc.json ← what it is: title, type, subject (folio-dublin-core/v1) original.pdf ← raw upload (PDF, scan, etc.) original.tex ← or LaTeX source extracted-text.md ← OCR or parser output (intermediate) extracted-blocks.json ← structured extraction (intermediate) mapping.json ← label/section mapping decisions README.md ← human notes about the document . The two records an upload writes . The description is a Dublin Core record; the intake records the capture and points at it. Both are validated by the registry (check:kind-validators). intake.json — folio-intake/v1, cat-harness-tools schemas/library/intake.ts: . { "$schema": "folio-intake/v1", "doc_id": "example-doc-2016", "record": "example-doc-2016.dc.json", "source": { "upstream": "https://...", "capturedAt": "2026-03-25T10:00:00Z", "capturedBy": "folio-assistant document adapter: the upload form" }, "files": [ { "path": "original.pdf", "bytes": 123456, "sha256": "…", "type": "upload", "role": "original-bitstream" } ] } . An intake names what it is a capture OF: a catalogue item (a folio-catalogue-node/v1 id), a Dublin Core record, or — only when neither exists — its own title. source is ProvenanceSchema (upstream for a URL, absent for a direct upload) plus the capture moment. <document-id>.dc.json — folio-dublin-core/v1: . | upload field | Dublin Core | . | title | dc.title | . | type (guideline, paper, report, standard) | dc.type | . | domain | dc.subject | . | normative level | dc.type qualified normativeLevel | . | detected format (pdf, latex, scan, docx) | dc.format | .

650.title: Pipeline Stages
650.content: Stage 1: Upload (→ uploaded) . Place raw files in uploads/<document-id>/. Create intake.json with source metadata. Files are committed to git for reproducibility. Record the licence in intake.json when you know it. The ingestion pipeline’s licence step runs before any extraction, because library/ is committed content and refusing a source after deriving from it is a deletion nobody may take unasked. That step sees only the upload: the licence record in intake.json (the same stated / unknown record a library manifest carries in meta.licence, cat-harness-tools schemas/library/source-licence.ts) and whether a LICENSE file sits beside it. bun run cat ingest prints its verdict before the first arm runs, and after the arms it writes a recorded licence into the staged entry’s licence.json — the authored sidecar gen-library-jsonld carries into meta.licence (the manifest itself is generated, so a licence written there would not survive a regeneration). It never overwrites a licence.json already there; a mismatch is printed as a conflict. | verdict | when | what to do | . | stated | licence: { status: "stated", id, basis } | nothing — basis says where it is stated | . | unknown | licence: { status: "unknown", searched: [...] } | nothing now; the places tried are the record | . | undetermined | no licence recorded (a LICENSE sibling is named, not read) | ingestion proceeds, and says so — undetermined is never reported as cleared | . It never reads a licence out of extracted text; that is a later check’s job. Supported formats: . | PDF — academic papers, scanned guidelines, reports | LaTeX — .tex source bundles | HTML — web-published guidelines, standards | DOCX — Word documents | Images — scanned pages (PNG, JPG, TIFF) | . For academic papers, prefer the MCP fetch path: when the session network allows the upstream host, use paper-search-mcp (arxiv / PubMed / bioRxiv / medRxiv) or openalex-paper-search (alex-mcp; OpenAlex catalog) rather than curl/WebFetch. The MCP tools return canonical metadata and the PDF in one call, eliminating the OCR-then-extract-then-name dance. See paper-importer.md §Phase 1 (in the science layer) for the per-tool routing table. Sandboxed Claude-Code-on-the-web sessions (github-only allowlist) cannot reach those hosts; in those sessions, queue the fetch onto a normal-network machine per bib-qa/qa-tags.md §Batch intake pipeline. Stage 2: Extraction (→ extracted) . Convert raw format to extracted-text.md: . For PDFs, always start with cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py — do not reach for a Python PDF library directly. It walks a fallback ladder (pdftotext → pypdf → pdfminer.six → a zero-dependency content-stream extractor → OCR) and, when it cannot read a file, tells you which rung failed and why instead of returning an empty string: . python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py FILE.pdf -o extracted-text.md python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py FILE.pdf --diagnose # structure only . Exit 0 = text; exit 2 = no text layer (a scan); exit 3 = a parser problem on a file that does have text. Two failure modes it prevents: . | A silent empty extraction reads exactly like a scan, a broken library, and a malformed PDF. The script separates them by inspecting the PDF structure (CCITTFaxDecode / JBIG2Decode / DCTDecode counts against /Font), so “swap libraries” vs “you need OCR” is decided by evidence rather than guessed. | A broken native extension kills the whole pipeline. pypdf and pdfminer.six both fail via pyo3 PanicException when cryptography’s Rust bindings are broken — and that is a BaseException, so an ordinary except Exception does not catch it. Every rung is guarded accordingly, and the zero-dependency rung exists for this case. | . | Format | Extraction method | . | PDF (text) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py (ladder; pdftotext when available) | . | PDF (scan) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py → exit 2, then cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py (Tesseract) or Claude vision | . | LaTeX | Direct parse (strip preamble) | . | HTML | Readability + turndown | . | DOCX | Pandoc → markdown | . | Images | Claude vision API | . | PDF (tables/figures) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py → tables.json (see Stage 3) | . | PDF (sections) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-structure.py → structure.json + sections/*.md (see Stage 3) | . For scanned documents the script’s OCR rung fires automatically if tesseract and pdftoppm are installed (apt-get install -y tesseract-ocr poppler-utils); it names whichever is missing. Where OCR is unavailable, or where layout carries meaning (headings, lists, tables, boxes), fall back to Claude’s vision capability, which reads structure that OCR flattens. Output: extracted-text.md — raw markdown with preserved structure. Stage 3: Structural Analysis (→ structured) . Analyze extracted text for formal environments and document structure. The three producers this stage actually runs . These scripts build the corpus’s structure.json, sections/ and ocr/ trees. Stage 2’s pdf-extract.py writes loose text, not the greppable sections/ tree the corpus-grep checklist reads. | script | writes | notes | . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-structure.py | library/<doc-id>/structure.json + sections/NN-slug.md | metadata (a page-1 title GUESS, authors, arXiv/DOI from the page-1 stamp, and the PDF Info dictionary as docinfo), TOC from the PDF outline, or else inferred from the layout (see the note below), per-section text split. The page-1 guess is never the entry’s title: l1-document-ingestion §”A manifest’s title” gives the order (catalogue record → referenced.json → PDF /Title → slug) | . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py | library/<doc-id>/ocr/page-NNN.txt | pdftoppm -r 300 -png then tesseract; per-page cache; script auto-detected via Tesseract’s own OSD | . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-candidates.py | library/<doc-id>/candidates.json | pure regex, imports no PDF library; proposals, never content — nothing here writes to content/ and nothing here creates Lean | . python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py FILE.pdf --outdir library/<doc-id>/ # only if scanned python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-structure.py FILE.pdf --outdir library --ocr python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-candidates.py library/<doc-id>/ . How they fit together: . | pdf-structure.py READS OCR, it never runs it. Its --ocr flag consults the cache pdf-ocr.py wrote, gated on text_is_unusable() (under 120 chars/page, or under 55 % letters — mojibake). So on a scanned document the order is pdf-ocr.py first, pdf-structure.py --ocr second. Run them the other way round and the sections come out empty. | An OCR’d document whose structure was never re-run is invisible to the section grep. Its text is in ocr/ but sections/ holds a stub, and its structure.json does not record "text_source": "ocr". Re-run pdf-structure.py --ocr on it. | The backends are optional and their absence is reported, not guessed. pdf-structure.py prefers PyMuPDF (better text on maths, real outlines) and falls back to pypdf; the Dockerfile ships pypdf only, deliberately, so the image stays BSD-licensed against PyMuPDF’s AGPL. Check with python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py --check. | With no outline, the TOC is inferred from the LAYOUT, and the artefact says how. diagnostics.toc_inferred_method is contents (a printed contents page, its page labels moved to physical pages by finding the titles in the body), font (lines set in a heading style: larger, bold, capitals or italic, numbered or not) or regex (text patterns — the last resort, used for OCR’d text, which has no fonts). Weight a regex TOC lowest. Each inferred entry also carries confidence (0..1) and evidence — which independent checks agreed: listed on the contents page, found in the body near the page it names, set in a heading style, numbered. Trust the high ones; look at the flagged ones before citing them. An inferred TOC is used only when it passes the concentration check, its mean confidence is at least 0.6, and no more than a quarter of the sections it would cut are empty; otherwise the entry is split one section per page (granularity: "page", with the reason in structure_note) — l1-document-ingestion §”The route pdf-structure.py takes itself”. The same artefact carries figures — the list of figures and tables, each caption with confidence and evidence (cited in the text, in its numbering run, a graphic on its page) — with numbering gaps in diagnostics.figure_sequence_gaps; and, when the document has a printed contents page, diagnostics.toc_alignment: entries the body no longer carries, numbered sections the contents omits, and page mismatches. On a draft, read these as findings about the document. Every page also has a printed label: pages[] (physical index, the label a reader sees, which sources agreed), page_label on TOC entries and figures, and label_start/label_end on sections. Cite the label, not the physical index; diagnostics.page_label_conflicts lists pages where the PDF’s own labels disagree with what is printed. Before changing cat-harness-tools/scripts/_pdf_headings.py, run python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/toc-benchmark.py before and after: a rule that fixes one document and costs two is visible only there. The numbers, the methods compared and what could not be run are in cat-harness/docs/research-and-analysis/toc-extraction.md. | . For academic papers: . Same as paper-importer Phase 2 — detect theorem/definition/lemma environments, sections, cross-references. For structured / normative guidelines: . This table is for a paper folio only. In a document folio definition is a math kind whose lean field is required, so a guideline recommendation mapped onto it will not validate; and proposition and conjecture are math kinds that content_profile_check rejects. There a normative statement is a recommendation block, with its strength as a code in a declared code list: load normative-statements from the folio-document-adapter package. Many guideline and standards documents have a recurring normative structure that maps onto content-block kinds: . | Guideline element | Content block kind | Notes | . | Recommendation (numbered, boxed) | definition | Normative statement | . | Evidence / rationale summary | prose | Supporting narrative | . | Remarks | remark | Implementation notes | . | Good-practice statement | proposition | Consensus-based | . | Research priority | conjecture | Open questions | . | Background | prose | Context sections | . | Evidence-quality table | diagram | Quality assessment | . When a document distinguishes normative levels (e.g. L1 = what to do, L2 = how to do it), map the normative statement to a definition block and the implementation guidance to a prose block tagged with the level (e.g. ["implementation", "L2"]). The exact level taxonomy is domain-specific; record it in the upload’s Dublin Core record as dc.type qualified normativeLevel. Domain-specific guideline handling (e.g. a particular standards body’s recommendation grammar) belongs in a domain adapter bundle, not the generic paper adapter. This skill detects the shape and hands off the domain-specific mapping rules to the relevant adapter: for prose folios, folio-document-adapter, whose normative-statements holds the recommendation grammar. Tables and figures — run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py . Text extraction destroys tables. A GRADE evidence table or a boxed recommendation comes out of Stage 2 as a run of prose, and nothing downstream can recover that it was a grid. python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py FILE.pdf -o uploads/<document-id>/ python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py --check # which backends are installed . Writes tables.json (pdf-tables/v1) beside structure.json, with each table’s cell matrix, column edges, caption, containing section_id, and a GFM rendering that can be pasted straight into a content block — the LaTeX pipeline already converts a GFM table to \begin{tabular}. Tables split across a page break are rejoined when their column geometry matches; stitched_from records what was merged, so check it on any table whose rows look like two tables. Read status before you read tables. The three ways to get no tables are distinguished on purpose, and tables is null — not [] — whenever nothing actually looked: . | status | Exit | Means | . | ok | 0 | a backend looked; tables: [] means the document has none | . | n/a-no-backend | 5 | pip install pdfplumber (or camelot-py) | . | n/a-no-text-layer | 2 | a scan — its tables are pixels; see Stage 2’s OCR route | . Needs pdfplumber or camelot-py, both pure PyPI installs with no model weights. Docling is the better parser and is not this: its weights come from HuggingFace, which is 403-blocked in sandboxed sessions, so it is a workstation/CI stage whose artefacts get committed — the docling capability probe reports it absent here rather than letting a session believe it ran. Output: extracted-blocks.json — array of detected blocks with provisional kinds, titles, and content; tables.json for the layout-bearing parts that do not survive as text. Figures and captioned tables: describe, keep, transcribe . Owner, 2026-11-11: “actually extract the figures”, “and any tables too”, “need summaries in all 6 UN”, and “make sure all kg extractions happen as part of skills and processes”. This is the method the image and table tasks of processes/library/ingest-derive-content.bpmn point at. It applies to every PDF entry, including one catalogued by reference whose PDF is not held. 1. Judge and describe every extracted image. pdf-images.py and pdf-vector-figures.py give each image a geometry role only; geometry cannot tell a chart from a logo or a 2-pixel fragment of a cover. An agent opens every image (and every vfig- render) and records, in the library’s image-verdicts.json: . | role: figure (carries content), logo, or decorative (ornament, background, blank, or a fragment too small to mean anything); | saw: the reason for the role; | draft: the English description, from the image and its caption only. No number that cannot be read, no interpretation beyond the image; | translations: the same in ar, zh, es, fr, ru, so every figure has all six UN languages (cat-harness-tools#1841). Each becomes its own draft narrative; only a person confirms one (bun run cat narratives); | shows on a vfig- that renders a declared figure or table. | . Put the inspector in attribution.<doc-id>. Images with identical bytes reuse one verdict. Apply with apply-image-verdicts.ts. 2. Keep the figures, small. Only images judged figure are kept, as WebP at quality 80 with the long side at most 1600 px (card Q-FIG-1 = A): about a seventh of the PNG bytes. Logos (the WHO emblem ruling of 2026-09-21 still holds), decorative fragments and page scans are not kept. The sidecar’s file names the .webp. An image pdf-images.py cannot decode is re-rendered from its placed rectangle on the page, never silently dropped. Check the size before committing and flag it on the merge card. 3. Transcribe each captioned table. pdf-tables.py finds grids by geometry and, on WHO layouts, reports many false tables. For every table the structure declares (structure.json figures, kind table), an agent reads the rendered page (and the next, for a continued table), checks cell text against the text layer, and writes it as CSVW (card Q-FIG-2 = A): . | library/<entry>/tables/<label>.csv, header row first; | library/<entry>/tables.csvw.json, folio-tabular-csvw/v1, one table per CSV: fac:group for a two-row header, fac:merged for spanning cells (A1, in CSV rows), plus fac:label, fac:caption, fac:pages, fac:lang (the cells keep the document’s language), fac:notes (footnotes), and fac:narrative: a description of the table in all six UN languages, as draft. | . A caption that points at something that is not a table (a box of prose, a list) is recorded as not a table, with the reason. Stage 4: Mapping (→ mapped) . Interactive step — present extracted blocks to user for review: . | Show block count by kind | Let user rename, reclassify, skip, or merge blocks | Let user define chapter/section structure | Let user set the target paper ID | Generate mapping.json with confirmed decisions | . Stage 5: Content Generation (→ generated) . Generate content objects under content/<paper-id>/: . | .ts manifests via content/schema/builders.ts | .md content in project markdown conventions | Chapter .ts manifests with section structure | Paper .ts manifest (new or updated) | . Tag all generated blocks with: . tags: ["imported", "source:<document-id>"] . Add meta.source referencing the upload: . meta: { source: "uploads/<document-id>", originalSection: "3.2", importedAt: "2026-03-25T..." } . Then publish the extracted statements: every statement taken from the source is published in the artifact’s own pages and in the shared extraction viewer, each linked to its library entry and section, and CI fails when those pages are stale. This is a standard step for every content type: publish-extracted-statements.

651.title: Structured-Document Processing
651.content: Detecting normative structure . Normative guidelines often follow predictable patterns: . RECOMMENDATION N: <recommendation text in bold/box> Remarks: - Implementation note 1 - Implementation note 2 Summary of evidence: <narrative text> Evidence-quality table: <quality assessment> . Label conventions for guidelines . | Element | Label pattern | Example | . | Recommendation | def:<doc>-rec-<N> | def:example-rec-1 | . | Evidence summary | prose:<doc>-evidence-<N> | — | . | Remark | rem:<doc>-remark-<N> | rem:example-remark-1 | . | Good practice | prop:<doc>-gps-<N> | prop:example-gps-1 | . | Research priority | conj:<doc>-research-<N> | conj:example-research-1 | . Cross-referencing recommendations . Recommendations often reference each other and external evidence. Map these to uses[] in content objects: . export default definition({ label: "def:example-rec-3", title: "Recommendation 3: ...", uses: ["def:example-rec-1"], // references Rec 1 tags: ["imported", "source:example-doc-2016", "L1", "normative"], meta: { source: "uploads/example-doc-2016", strength: "strong", quality: "moderate", } }); .

652.title: Integration with Other Skills
652.content: | Skill | Integration point | . | paper-importer | Delegates Phase 5 generation for academic papers | . | content-validation | Validates generated content objects | . | editor | Reviews generated narrative content | . | scientific-accuracy | Checks extracted statements | . | ontologist | Maps terminology to glossary | . | publish-extracted-statements | Publishes the extracted statements, each linked to its library entry and section | .

653.title: Resuming Partial Processing
653.content: Where processing stopped is read from what EXISTS, not from a status field (intake.json has none). To resume: . | uploaded — intake.json is there | extracted — extracted-text.md (or an extraction record) is there | structured — extracted-blocks.json is there | mapped — mapping.json is there | generated — blocks tagged source:<document-id> exist in the content | . Start from the first stage whose artefact is missing. This allows multi-session processing of large documents.

654.title: Checklist
654.content: Before marking intake complete: . | Raw files committed to uploads/<document-id>/ | intake.json and <document-id>.dc.json validate (check:kind-validators) | extracted-text.md reviewed for OCR errors | extracted-blocks.json reviewed and confirmed by user | tables.json written, status checked (not silently n/a), and any stitched_from table spot-checked against the PDF | All content objects generated with correct builders | Blocks tagged with ["imported", "source:<document-id>"] | Chapter/section structure matches document | Cross-references mapped to uses[] | Content validation passes (content_validate) | Extracted statements published with source links, and their pages current (publish-extracted-statements) ``` | .

656.title: document-publishing
656.content: Named by: Authoring a document, Release a draft for public comment . Take a document folio from corpus to published artifact — without a TeX installation.

657.title: The pipeline
657.content: folio/** → document_render_md → build/<slug>.md → document_render_html → build/<slug>.html → document_render_pdf → build/<slug>.pdf . One assembly step, then pandoc. Run document_render_md first and read it: it is the only place the whole document appears in reading order in one file.

658.title: Before rendering
658.content: Run, in this order, and fix what each reports before moving on: . | content_validate — schema, constraints, and profile conformance. A document folio that has acquired a math block or a .lean sibling fails here. | qa_sweep — the QA axes over each block’s sidecar. | document_render_md — read the assembly. Look for: sections that came out empty (a block written but never listed in blocks[]), blocks in an order that does not read, and the > **Missing block:** marker, which means a section names a root that failed to load. | .

659.title: PDF without LaTeX
659.content: document_render_pdf drives pandoc with an HTML engine — weasyprint (recommended), prince, or wkhtmltopdf. If none is installed it reports which are missing and stops. It does not fall back to latexmk, even on a machine that has it: a document folio is defined by not requiring TeX to publish. document_render_html needs only pandoc, so it works when the PDF path cannot. When you are drafting rather than publishing, prefer it.

660.title: Styling
660.content: Both HTML and PDF accept css, a stylesheet path relative to the repo root. Keep it in the folio repo, not here — a house style is content, and the platform ships no default beyond pandoc’s. The same stylesheet drives both outputs, so a print rule (@page, page breaks, running heads) belongs in it alongside the screen rules rather than in a second file that drifts.

661.title: Release files: the public-comment PDF and the offline .docx
661.content: scripts/document-export.ts is the publication pipeline’s FILE step. It runs the same assembly as document_render_md, and it gives the same result locally as on any CI runner, because the commit is the only input that changes: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/document-export.ts release --document <slug> [--out <dir>] [--release <id>] [--date YYYY-MM-DD] . | file | what it is | . | <slug>-public-comment-<sha7>-<date>.pdf | the frozen, line-numbered review draft | . | <slug>-public-comment-<sha7>-<date>.docx | the same draft as Word, whose sha256 goes in the release references (public-comment-channels) | . | <slug>-offline-<sha7>.docx | the editing copy: Track Changes on, one Word bookmark per chapter, section and block | . | <slug>-export-<sha7>.json | document-export/v1: commit, date, tool versions, and each file’s format, filters, parameters, sha256, pages, lines and bookmarks | . | <slug>-…-latest.{pdf,docx,json} | the same files under stable names, overwritten by every export, so a link to one always serves the newest | . | index.html | the Export page: every file above with its format, the filters and parameters it was made with, size, date, and links to this export and to its latest copy | . pdf or docx builds only that half. The PDF is the .docx laid out by LibreOffice (soffice --headless), not a print of the site. That way the two files have the same pages and line numbers (Word line numbering, continuous), and pdf-line-map.py reads the PDF as it reads a Word-made review PDF. It needs pandoc, LibreOffice and poppler (pdfinfo, pdftotext), and never TeX. It refuses a working tree with uncommitted changes under folio/, because the stamp would name a commit the file does not come from (--allow-dirty marks the stamp -dirty). The date defaults to the commit’s date, so two runs at one commit write the same .docx bytes. The PDF differs only in LibreOffice’s creation timestamp. Bringing an offline edit back . An author edits the offline copy in Word with Track Changes on and returns it with every change still pending. A change accepted before upload looks like the original text and carries no author. python3 -I folio-assistant-core/scripts/docx-offline.py changes <edited.docx> --repo . \ --out <changes.json> --summary <pr-body.md> [--apply [--commit]] . | The file’s folio-source-commit must exist in the repository, or nothing is merged (exit 2). | Each paragraph belongs to the last folio_<sha1(label)[:16]> bookmark before it. The name is recomputed from the source commit’s review-anchors.json, so run bun run review:anchors before exporting. | --apply edits the block’s .md in the working tree, carrying each insertion and deletion onto the matching line or table cell so emphasis, links and list markers around it survive. A block whose .md changed since the source commit is a conflict and is left alone. A paragraph that matches no line (a heading, a split or merged paragraph) is manual. Neither is guessed at; both are listed in the summary with the original and the proposed text. | --commit makes one commit per block (`offline edit: (, )`), so a review can take or drop each. Run it on a branch `offline-edit//`, and open the pull request with `--summary`'s file as its body. | Word comments come back on their block, in the report and the summary. Formatting-only changes are ignored. | .

662.title: A large document loads its text as data
662.content: build-document-site.ts publishes a document of 200 or more blocks (LAZY_THRESHOLD) as a shell plus data, because one page of every block is too heavy to use. | file | holds | who reads it | . | en/<slug>/index.html | headings, every block anchor, a placeholder per block, [edit]/[feedback] as data, comment-note counts | readers | . | <slug>/blocks/NNN.json | each block’s rendered HTML, 40 blocks per chunk, in document order | the shell, as the reader nears a block, then the rest in idle time | . | en/<slug>/index.hydrated.html | the whole document on one page | file:// opens (fetch fails, so the shell goes there), readers without JavaScript, tools (block-screenshots.ts) | . | <slug>/pc-notes.json | each block’s comment list (a public-comment folio) | a comment note, when opened | . | outline.json lazy | the hydrated page, the chunk count, and each block’s chunk | the rendered-impact predictor, which names the chunk a change alters | . Pages are under the page locale, en/, and data is not. scripts/document-site-route.ts says where each one goes. The name follows the knowledge graph’s own pair: a subgraph publishes index.jsonld, which references its members, and index.hydrated.jsonld, which holds them inline. The document page is the same pair: index.html references its blocks, index.hydrated.html holds them. A link to a block (#prose:…) or to a term inside one (#term-…) loads that chunk first and lands on it. --lazy always|never overrides the threshold. Two rules for anything that reads the document page: . | Want the text? Read index.hydrated.html when it exists. The shell has placeholders where the text goes. | Find blocks by their anchor (<a id="<label>">). It is on both pages. | . Searching the document’s comments is the dashboard’s job, not the page’s.

663.title: What is not implemented
663.content: The pandoc tools (document_render_*) have no citations, no bibliography, no glossary and no automatic cross-reference numbering: \cite{…} passes through verbatim, so write references as Markdown links or footnotes for that path. The site build (build-document-site.ts) does render \cite{a,b} as a muted [a, b] (each key linked to its entry with --bibliography-url) and :defterm / :refterm as a term and its link; it has no cross-reference numbering either. Cross-references do work: every labelled block emits an HTML anchor, so [see the scope statement](#rec:scope) resolves in both HTML and PDF. Use the block’s label, not a heading-derived anchor, which changes whenever the title is edited.

664.title: Release
664.content: Publication authorisation is the base process’s, not this skill’s: Task_AuthorizeRelease and Task_PublishRelease are non-relaxable in draft-to-publication.bpmn and no content type can opt out of them. Render, review, then take the release decision through the workflow — workflow_next will tell you what is enabled. A public comment release is a full build . A site build is a preview (a pull request’s branches/<slug>/: only what the change reaches, every whole-corpus index borrowed from main) or full (the main deploy, a public comment release, a release: every index rebuilt). See cat-harness skill feature-staging, section “Build types”. Before pc:release freeze, dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, so the frozen copy’s search index and slices describe the draft rather than main. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json.

666.title: document-structure
666.content: Named by: Authoring a document . Decide and maintain the chapter/section skeleton of a document folio.

667.title: Structure is authored, not inferred
667.content: Nothing derives the outline from the prose. Three manifests hold it, and each is an ordered list: . | File | Holds | Order means | . | folio/<slug>/<slug>.ts | chapters: ChapterRef[] | reading order of chapters | . | <chapter>/<chapter>.ts | sections: Section[] | reading order within the chapter | . | a section’s blocks: string[] | block root names | reading order within the section | . A block reaches the output iff some section names it: a block whose .ts and .md exist but that no blocks[] lists renders nowhere. Adding the name to blocks[] is part of adding a block.

668.title: Sections may nest exactly one level
668.content: subsections[] on a section carries another section, whose blocks[] render under a deeper heading. One level only — the renderers flatten at that depth, so a third level silently loses its blocks rather than nesting further. If you need a third level, you need another chapter.

669.title: Chapter granularity
669.content: A chapter is the unit a reviewer is asked to read in one sitting, and the unit the work plan tracks. Prefer more, smaller chapters over few large ones: a chapter is also the unit that gets rewritten.

670.title: Adding a chapter
670.content: . | mkdir folio/<slug>/<chapter-dir> | Write <chapter-dir>/<chapter-dir>.ts — title, optional label, and sections[] (which may start empty). | Add { dir: "<chapter-dir>" } to the document manifest’s chapters[], in the position it should be read. | content_validate. | bun run review:anchors, so the review sheet’s Selected Sections list and every comment’s placement see the new chapter. | . Every document folio declares review:anchors and check:review-anchors from its first commit (review-anchors-from-folio.ts --document <doc>; the --library/--source flags only when it was seeded from a library file). The section list is what a review sheet’s dropdown reads; a folio without it leaves a linked sheet empty. See review-sheet-script, “Linking a sheet to a repository”. The directory name is the chapter’s slug; it appears in build output and in every path a reviewer sees, so name it for what the chapter is about rather than for its position. A ch3- prefix is a rename waiting to happen the first time something moves.

671.title: Back matter: glossary and acronyms go at the end
671.content: Owner, 2026-11-02: every document opens on its title and summary, never on a reference list, and the same skeleton holds across documents: . | Part | Chapters, in order | . | Front | title page and front matter (acknowledgements, publication data), executive summary or abstract, how to use | . | Main | the numbered chapters | . | Back | Annexes or Appendices, then Glossary, then References | . Acronyms are a section of the Glossary chapter, never a chapter of their own. An acronym is a glossary term’s SKOS notation (folio-glossary/v1), so the acronyms list is one view of the glossary graph: the Glossary chapter holds the terms first and the acronyms after them. When a source publication prints its glossary or abbreviations up front (WHO handbooks often do), the folio still puts them at the back. Move the section into the glossary/ chapter by moving its block files (blocks resolve from their chapter’s directory) and keep every label: review comments, review sheets and contributor logs cite them. Then regenerate or update review-anchors.json, and fix any <chapter>/<block> paths in L1-coverage or glossary-table registries. bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/back-matter-order.ts --document <doc> warns when a document breaks this. It is warn-only: moving a chapter in an existing document is its editor’s call.

672.title: Reordering
672.content: Move the entry in chapters[] — nothing else. Do not rename directories to encode order: labels, uses[] targets, feedback records and QA sidecars all key on names, and a rename breaks every one of them for a change that the manifest already expresses. Then bun run review:anchors, as after adding one. After any reorder, re-read uses[] across the moved chapter: an editorial edge that pointed backwards may now point forwards, which is a real finding about reading order rather than a mechanical detail.

686.title: Evidence Appraisal
686.content: Named by: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Translation Workflow, Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Authoring a document, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Board: place a note . Appraise and grade a body of evidence against the grading system the folio declares. This skill supplies the procedure; it does not supply the system.

687.title: Why this skill names no grading system
687.content: Which grading system applies is a methodological commitment of the folio and the body that publishes it; the platform holds no subject matter, and a hardcoded system would leave every folio that uses another one working around the platform. An evidence-retrieval process in the content layer judges certainty “per the grading system the folio declares”. This skill covers what appraisal is, what it attaches to, and what has to survive as a record afterwards. Domain layers supply concrete grading systems as refinement skills and code lists (certainty levels, rating reasons, recommendation strength). Each applies only when declared, never as a default; with nothing declared, appraisal is refused.

688.title: Responsibilities
688.content: . | Appraise the body of evidence assembled for one question, not a citation | Record the grade with its reasons, not as a bare label | Distinguish “the evidence is weak” from “there is not enough to judge” | Re-appraise when the body changes, and say what moved the grade | Refuse to grade when no system is declared, rather than picking one | .

689.title: The unit is the body, not the citation
689.content: The grade attaches to the body of evidence for one PICO question. This is why appraisal sits after retrieval’s parallel join and not inside the fan-out: the three retrieval classes (trusted L1 sources, trusted L2/L3 content, data repositories) contribute to one judgement; grading each branch separately would produce three numbers that answer no question. A single citation does not carry a certainty grade.

690.title: “Cannot appraise” is a third state
690.content: Three outcomes; “not appraisable” is not a low grade: . | outcome | means | . | graded | the body was appraised and carries a certainty | . | not appraisable | too little retrieved, or no declared system, or the question was not framed as PICO | . | gap recorded | nothing authoritative was found, and that is the finding | . Never collapse “not appraisable” into the lowest grade: “we looked and the evidence is poor” is not “we could not look”. A recommendation resting on the first is weak; one resting on the second is unsupported.

691.title: Inputs
691.content: . | The framed PICO question — without it the search is not reproducible and the appraisal is not checkable | Candidates that passed an authority check, so authority is a resolved fact rather than an assertion in the citation | The grading system declared by the folio | .

692.title: Outputs
692.content: . | A certainty judgement for the body, in the declared system’s own vocabulary | The reasons, in enough detail that a later reader can tell whether they would still hold (decision-audit); a grade without them cannot be reviewed, only re-litigated | Any gap, recorded as a gap rather than as a low grade | .

693.title: This has nothing to do with formal content
693.content: A graded body of empirical evidence is never an input to a formal deductive proof. In a content type with a formal proof layer, a formal claim’s assertion is discharged by its machine-checked proof sibling and by nothing else; certainty grading belongs to empirical guidance about the world, where the question is what the evidence supports. An empirical grade in a formal proof obligation is a category error.

694.title: Actors
694.content: . | Author / guideline developer (lead) | Domain SME (domain judgement, supplied by the content-type layer) | Content Reviewer (checks the grade’s reasons survive, not the grade itself) | .

702.title: Evidence review — the same rule, a second instance
702.content: Skill evidence-review: Evidence review as an instance of untainted verification — the separation of the appraising party from the drafting party, what recurring surveillance in a living guideline shares with a stale QA verdict, and which of guideline methodology’s rules are fenced rather than shipped. Named by: Contributor feedback on a working draft, Make a decided public comment change . Skill id: evidence-review · Package: folio-core . untainted-verification states a generic discipline. Evidence review — the appraisal of the evidence behind a recommendation — is one instance of it; the translation round trip is another. Two unrelated instances are evidence that the discipline is generic, where one would only be an example.

703.title: The rule
703.content: The party that drafted the recommendation does not write the evidence appraisal for it. Guideline methodology already separates the systematic review team from the guideline development group for the same reason: a party assessing its own output is comparing a thing with its own paraphrase of itself. | untainted-verification | here | . | producer | whoever drafts the recommendation | . | checker — given the artefact, and nothing that would let it shortcut | the appraisal, given the question and the evidence, not the draft’s conclusion | . | adjudicator — given the intent and the checker’s output, never the artefact | the evidence-to-decision judgement | . An appraiser shown the drafted recommendation is told the answer before being asked the question; its “the evidence supports it” measures the instruction, not the literature.

704.title: Recurring surveillance is staleness, generalised
704.content: A living guideline is updated as evidence appears, so its appraisal is a verdict with an expiry. A QA verdict is hashed to its subject and stales when the subject is edited; a living-guideline verdict stales when the evidence base changes, even though the subject did not. The field_hash covers only inputs in the repository; an external corpus is not covered. Either way, “verified on DATE against THESE inputs” is a different claim from “verified”, because a reader given the second cannot tell a current verdict from a lapsed one. A folio implementing surveillance gives each verdict an explicit expiry, as bean-blocking (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) does for a block: a verdict with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one.

705.title: The fencing analysis — which rules are the platform’s, and which are not
705.content: Run through domain-fencing (opt-in cat-harness.kg-ops)’s three questions, in order, first-to-answer wins: . | candidate rule | Q1 rationale survives translation? | Q2 domain in mechanism or vocabulary? | Q3 needs the domain installed? | verdict | . | appraiser ≠ drafter | yes, word for word | vocabulary | no | platform — it IS the spine | . | a verdict carries what it was verified against, and when | yes — it is the field_hash argument | vocabulary | no | platform | . | a finding is upheld by opening the cited source, never by trusting the rule’s wording | yes | vocabulary | no | platform — and already the practice in voice-who-guideline-development | . | certainty rated across the GRADE domains | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | PICO question formulation | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | evidence-to-decision framework tables | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | a search strategy is re-runnable — databases, dates, query recorded | yes in rationale | mechanism is bibliographic | yes | fence the mechanism, keep the rationale (it is the row above) | . Three rows are platform rules; the four fenced rows are a folio’s methodology, not a backlog. Nothing is shipped for the fenced rows — empty criteria would let a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run. A folio that wants them declares them in its own repository.

706.title: What this skill does NOT do
706.content: It asserts no clinical or empirical claim, and the platform must not. The mechanism carries process — who may rule on what, given what. The evidence is the folio’s and the judgement is the guideline group’s; a platform that shipped a default answer to either would be asserting on their behalf.

Read it first; this skill adds only what evidence review instantiates. | translation-manager §”The agentic round trip” — the other instance. | voice-who-guideline-development in the IRIS replica’s style guide — how a recommendation is worded: the language of normative statements, not the process that produces them, which is this skill. | domain-fencing — the three questions, and why a fenced rule is correctly located rather than missing. | .

709.title: External registry — the role’s contract
709.content: Skill external-registry-contract: The contract the external-registry role is held to: what a trusted registry outside this layer must provide for a portal to verify what it received, and what the verifier does when it cannot. The narrowest contract the diagrams require. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: KG to public portal, Evidence for a recommendation . external-registry in scenarios/roles.json is played by an external actor: trusted registries and observatories outside this layer’s control. A role played by something we do not run is still a role, and its skills are its contract: what we rely on it to do. A contract is not an instruction; it is what the diagrams assume.

710.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
710.content: One lane names this role: Lane_Portal in processes/kg/kg-to-portal.bpmn, holding P_Verify and GW_Verified. What that lane’s documentation, the task’s, and kg-to-portal §”Trust” require of the registry is the whole contract — nothing more is claimed.

711.title: What it must do
711.content: . | Publish the trust anchors a verifier resolves a signer’s key from — for GDHCN, a WHO SMART Trust DID trustlist (did.json), served as static JSON (PROD: tng-cdn.who.int/v2/trustlist/…). | Serve a slice by its hierarchical path, …/$domain/$participant/$usage/did.json, with - as a wildcard, so a verifier fetches only what it needs. | Nothing else. Whether a package signature can be expressed for GDHCN verifiers at all is an open question in kg-to-portal, not a promise of this role. | .

712.title: What the verifier does when the contract is not met
712.content: An unreachable registry is unknown, never a pass: GW_Verified routes it as it routes a mismatch, to the last good version (End_Rejected). This side of the contract is ours, and it is what makes relying on a party we do not control safe. Needs the owner’s review: this contract is inferred from one diagram. The test in tested-by: holds the side of it that is ours: one lane names this role, it holds P_Verify and GW_Verified, and GW_Verified serves the bytes only on a match, sending every other answer to End_Rejected. Lines 1 and 2 above are the registry’s own behaviour on a network this repository does not reach, and nothing here tests them.
