3001.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3001.title: Skill-pipeline subject indexing: decompose the cataloguer’s stages and validate each
3001.content: Adopted 2026-09-26 (work item 0js9). All three sources were ingested through the library pipeline, and the primary was read whole before this node was written.

3002.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3002.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
3002.content: Prior systems found the right topics and still got the headings wrong. The failures were in applying the rules, and a single prompt gives rule application nowhere to happen. The source reviews the earlier LLM studies and states the diagnosis directly (its section “Present Contribution”): the documented accuracy failures “are not primarily failures of topic identification — they are failures of rule application”. The models “produce unauthorized heading forms, omit required subdivisions, use deprecated subfield practices, and fail to verify headings against authority files”, and every prior study “treats subject assignment as a single-step task”. The remedy is structural. A professional cataloguer works through distinct stages, so the pipeline gives each stage its own skill, and each skill passes a structured intermediate output to the next. The source’s own framing is “an externalized, architecturally enforced form of chain-of-thought reasoning”: the intermediate outputs are “inspectable and correctable at each step before proceeding to the next”, and that is what a single prompt “cannot” provide.

3003.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3003.title: The four stages, as the source defines them
3003.content: Section “The Four-Skill Pipeline” and its Figure 1. Each stage names the policy it encodes, which is the point: every stage is small enough to be checked against its own source document. | # | stage | receives → emits | what it encodes | . | 1 | Conceptual analysis | title, abstract, table of contents → an aboutness statement and a flat list of candidate concepts, each justified | Wilson’s four methods of subject determination (purposive, figure-ground, objective, cohesion), Langridge’s three questions, the Joudrey–Taylor framework, via Holley & Joudrey’s review | . | 2 | Quantitative filtering | concept list → an ordered list of candidate headings, each with its intended MARC field | SHM H 180: the 20 % rule, the rule of three, specificity, depth of indexing; H 80: order by predominance; the 2026 LC genre/form policy | . | 3 | Authority validation | candidates → authorised forms, with variants redirected through their UF references | a local index over the LCSH and LCGFT authority files; a live query against LCNAF for names; H 830 for geographic subdivision | . | 4 | Field synthesis | validated headings → MARC 21 6xx fields | H 1075 subdivision order, H 830 indirect geographic subdivision, H 405 and H 430 for name headings, J 105 and J 110 for genre/form | . Two design choices inside the stages are part of the method, not details: . | Stage 1 over-generates on purpose. The source: “The skill intentionally over-generates at this stage — filtering is deferred to Skill 2.” Recall is one stage’s job and precision is the next stage’s. A stage 1 that filtered as it went would be doing stage 2’s job with none of stage 2’s rules. | Authority validation is a lookup, not a judgement. Stage 3 asks whether each candidate exists as an authorised form in the file. It does not ask the model whether the candidate looks authorised. That makes it the one stage whose output is deterministic given its input. | .

3004.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3004.title: How the skills were made: the construction discipline is part of the method
3004.content: Section “Source Material and Skill Construction”: each of eleven LC policy documents and one review article was “read in full and its normative content — rules, exceptions, decision criteria, and worked examples — was translated into structured instructions”. The resulting skills “are not simply prompts; they are multi-section documents that define terminology, enumerate decision steps, specify output formats, and include validation checks.” . This is what makes the method survive a change of vocabulary. The pipeline shape stays fixed, and moving to another vocabulary means re-reading that vocabulary’s policy manual into the same four stages. The source names MeSH, AAT and FAST as the next candidates. A stage whose instructions cannot be traced back to a clause in the vocabulary’s own policy is not this method.

3005.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3005.title: What it refuses
3005.content: . | Never go from the work to the finished fields in one pass. That is the failure the method exists to correct. | Never rely on the model’s internalised knowledge of the vocabulary. The source contrasts itself with single-prompt approaches on exactly this point: it “explicitly encodes SHM rules at each stage rather than relying on the model’s internalized knowledge of LCSH conventions”. | Never emit a heading that stage 3 did not find in the authority file. If a validator is never allowed to say no, the stage is only there for show. | Never ship the output as final. The source’s conclusion: the output “would serve as a draft for review by a subject cataloger rather than as a final product, consistent with the human-in-the-loop workflow advocated throughout the literature”. | Never read a difference from an existing record as an error. The source’s baseline records “may reflect subject indexing decisions made years or decades ago — potentially under different LC policies”. Its largest systematic difference, genre/form in 655 fields rather than as $v subdivisions, is the pipeline applying the current policy correctly. | .

3006.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3006.title: The parallel tracks, and why they are not this node
3006.content: methodology-adoption: parallel tracks are recorded, not blended. Two ingested sources take a different route to the same task. Each is recorded here as it presents itself. Trained extreme multi-label classification, with LLMs in support (Annif, arXiv:2504.19675v2). A toolkit of XMTC backends is trained on catalogued records, and its suggestions are merged by ensemble. Omikuji uses partitioned label trees; MLLM does lexical matching; XTransformer is a fine-tuned transformer. Language models are used around the classifier and do no classifying themselves: they translate records between languages and generate synthetic training records. It placed first in the task’s all-subjects quantitative ranking. It needs a large body of already catalogued records to train on. Chow names this as the line: the skill pipeline “does not require training data or corpus-level pattern learning”. Use Annif’s track where that corpus exists and the vocabulary’s policy is not written down in a form a stage could encode. Retrieve, then let a model judge each candidate (Homa / OntoAligner, arXiv:2504.21474v1). Subject indexing is recast as ontology alignment: embed the record, retrieve the top 30 subjects by cosine similarity, and ask a small fine-tuned model whether each one matches. The authors report that recall held up and precision did not: “the system retrieves a broad set of candidate subjects, but many are not relevant”. The retrieval step does real work. What this track lacks is any stage that applies the vocabulary’s rules: nothing in it filters by policy, orders by predominance, or constructs a subdivided heading. For a flat vocabulary that may not matter. For LCSH, it is exactly the gap Chow diagnoses. Neither is refused as wrong. They answer the same question under different conditions, and which one applies depends on the context. Composing them into “Annif’s candidates, filtered by Chow’s stage 2” would be a house method that cites nobody.

3007.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3007.title: Against hybrid-llm-deterministic
3007.content: These are parallel nodes, and the difference is worth stating because the two look alike. hybrid-llm-deterministic has the model emit a rule that machinery then executes. The model never touches the data at scale, because a generated result would have to be checked item by item. This method has the model emit results, the headings themselves, and checks each one. That is sound here, and it is sound for a reason the other node does not cover: checking a result costs one authority-file lookup when the answer must come from a closed, enumerable vocabulary. The expensive per-item verification that the rule/result inversion avoids becomes a membership test here. Where results come from an open space, that argument fails and hybrid-llm-deterministic is the node to reach for.

3008.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3008.title: Where this rendering stops
3008.content: methodology-adoption step 2 requires both halves, so both are given here. Adopted: the diagnosis (rule application, not topic identification); the decomposition into four stages, each with a structured output; the over-generate-then-filter split; authority validation as a lookup; the construction discipline of reading each policy document into a stage; and the refusals above. Not adopted, and deliberately: every tool in the paper. Claude Code, its skill file format, the local TF-IDF index over NDJSON dumps from id.loc.gov, the LC suggest2 API, and MARC 21 as the output encoding are one instantiation. The owner’s instruction on ingesting a tool paper, 2026-09-23: “do not need to match tools in paper, start with process, determine most appropriate tools (known or which can be added).” The same holds for the specific LCSH rules: they are the content of stages 2–4 for LCSH, and another vocabulary’s policy supplies its own. Not assessed: the source’s evaluation is ten titles, one or two per discipline, compared with existing Harvard records along four dimensions. The source calls the comparison “interpretive rather than strictly quantitative” and says ten comparisons “are insufficient for statistical generalization”. No claim about how well this method performs rests on this node. It also cites a 26–35 % alignment figure for single-prompt approaches from Tang & Jiang (2025). That paper is not ingested here, so the figure is second-hand and is not repeated as a finding. Named by the source as open, and left open here: under-subdivision (geographic $z and chronological $y), choosing among overlapping authorised headings, the missing step of consulting peer records for the same ISBN, and overlapping population groups in conceptual analysis. These are the source’s own stated limitations (section “Limitations and Areas for Improvement”). They are listed so that a skill built on this node does not rediscover them.

3009.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3009.title: How this platform applies it
3009.content: It does not apply it yet, and says so. No skill here assigns controlled vocabulary terms. Library entries produced by the L1 ingest (epic slw1) carry structure, sections, images and labels, but no subject field. This node exists so that the day one is added, the method is chosen by adoption and not improvised. A skill that implements it names this node and does not restate it.

3010.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3010.title: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3010.content: ← All methodologies . skill-pipeline-subject-indexing — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Assigning terms from a closed, rule-governed controlled vocabulary to a work: deciding what it is about and saying so in the vocabulary’s own authorised form. Use it when the vocabulary comes with a written policy manual (LCSH has the Subject Headings Manual; MeSH, AAT and FAST are the source’s own named candidates) and an authority file that can be queried, and a wrong but plausible term would be acted on in cataloguing, retrieval or linking. It answers how to produce the assignment. It does not answer how to tell whether an assignment is good: that is consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation, which is a parallel node and is not folded into this one. Not for choosing between options (kepner-tregoe), a recurring decision rule (dmn), or making a model emit a rule instead of a result (hybrid-llm-deterministic); §”Against hybrid-llm-deterministic” explains why the last is a separate method and not this one’s parent. Not for free keywording with no vocabulary to validate against, because the authority step is what the method rests on. Origin. Eric H. C. Chow, “A Skill-Based Agentic Pipeline for Library of Congress Subject Indexing” (arXiv:2605.03537v1), School of Humanities, The University of Hong Kong. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. The method is rendered from that paper alone. Two parallel tracks, both entrants in SemEval-2025 Task 5, were ingested beside it and read so that §”The parallel tracks, and why they are not this node” rests on the papers and not on how Chow summarises them: Suominen, Inkinen & Lehtinen, “Annif at SemEval-2025 Task 5: Traditional XMTC augmented by LLMs” (arXiv:2504.19675v2), National Library of Finland; and Bayrami Asl Tekanlou et al., “Homa at SemEval-2025 Task 5: Aligning Librarian Records with OntoAligner for Subject Tagging” (arXiv:2504.21474v1). Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2605.03537v1 | library/arxiv-2504.19675v2 | library/arxiv-2504.21474v1 | . Applied by skills: . | mesh-subject-indexing | mesh-subject-indexing | . Node file: skill-pipeline-subject-indexing.md .

3011.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3011.title: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3011.content: This methodology node completes work item folio-assistant-qh1s (Issue #1164): a literature search over requirements-management practice across the five lifecycle dimensions (organisation, identifiers, traceability, change, and retirement), the explicit adoption or rejection of candidate methodologies through methodology-adoption, and the proposed executable BPMN filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) put to the owner before automation is built. Whereas sibling methodology requirements-standards-assessment.md (work item folio-assistant-1gf7) assessed open interchange and syntax standards (ReqIF, OSLC RM, EARS, RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, IEEE 29148, Planguage, SysML, Gherkin) to map their constructs onto bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json, this node governs how requirements are organised, identified, traced, amended, superseded, and retired as they are filed into docs/requirements/ once docs/requirements/ grows past a flat hand-maintained list.

3012.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3012.title: 1. Literature search over requirements-management practice
3012.content: Per literature-search, every surveyed source is recorded below with its provenance/access status (ingested library/<bib-slug> node where held on disk, or external standard / open-source specification where copyright or scope keeps the full text outside library/) and with what it offers here across the five dimensions of work item folio-assistant-qh1s: . | Organisation — how a growing corpus of filed requirements is structured and navigated without breaking path stability. | Identifiers — how requirements and sub-clauses receive durable, collision-free, human- and machine-addressable IDs in a distributed Git workflow. | Traceability — how backward lineage (to proposals, user needs, and L1 sources), horizontal dependencies (between requirements), and forward verification (to work items, skills, processes, and test attestations) are recorded and checked. | Change — how in-scope amendments versus scope-altering replacements are distinguished, reviewed, and versioned. | Retirement — how obsolete or superseded requirements leave active force without breaking historical links or audit trails. | . 1.1 Summary matrix across the five filing dimensions . | Source | Provenance / library status | Organisation | Identifiers | Traceability | Change | Retirement | . | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering, Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, 6.5) | Proprietary ISO/IEEE standard; assessed via public clause structure (no full-text redistributable PDF in library/) | Separates stakeholder requirements (StRS) from system/software requirements (SyRS/SRS); organises by system architecture or functional domain | Unique, persistent requirement identifier (id) independent of document section position | Clause 5.2.7 mandates bidirectional traceability: backward to source/parent need, forward to design elements and verification records | Clause 6.5 requires formal change control, impact analysis over dependent items, and baseline sign-off | Explicit lifecycle status attribute (retired / obsolete / superseded); historical records retained for audit | . | Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson, Mastering the Requirements Process, 4th ed.) | Commercial book / template; assessed via published Volere atomic “Snow Card” specification | Groups requirements by functional area / business event / concern rather than implementation module; pairs functional with non-functional categories | Atomic requirement number + type code + event/use-case reference on each Snow Card | Each card records Source / Originator, Supporting Materials, Dependencies, and a mandatory measurable Fit Criterion | History log on the card tracking creation, amendments, and re-verification | Explicit archived / retired state with reason when business rules change; card number is never reused | . | IREB CPRE Foundation Level (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals, 3rd ed.) | Standard RE body of knowledge; external textbook | Contrasts tree-structured chapter hierarchies against faceted / attribute-driven views over atomic requirement objects | Recommends immutable object identifiers decoupled from chapter headings so restructuring views never renumbers requirements | Defines three explicit trace link directions: pre-RS / backward (to origins), post-RS / forward (to artefacts/tests), and within-RS / horizontal (dependsOn, refines, conflictsWith) | Configuration management and baseline versioning; change impact propagation along trace links | Status state machine (draft → agreed → validated → implemented → deprecated/retired) | . | Doorstop (Browning & Adams, Doorstop: Text-Based Requirements Management Using Version Control, JOSS 2014; github.com/doorstop-dev/doorstop) | Open-source Git-native requirements tool (lgpl-3.0); external software reference | Stores one text file per requirement (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter) inside version-controlled directories representing document trees | Prefix + identifier per file, addressable in git diffs; supports sub-links and hierarchical parent pointers | Parent/child trace links stored directly in requirement front matter; detects suspect links when a parent requirement changes | Git commits and pull requests are the change-control log; review happens in PR diffs alongside code and tests | active: false / normative: false front-matter flags retire an item in place without git rm, keeping git blame and incoming links intact | . | Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (Nygard 2011; Kopp et al., adr.github.io/madr/, already adopted in methodologies/madr.md) | Adopted harness methodology (methodologies/madr.md) | Flat directory of Markdown files (docs/decisions/ or docs/proposals/), indexed by concern or status in index.md | Filename slug (<slug>.md) serves as the stable human-readable identifier | Cross-references related decisions, issues, and motivating forces in front matter and body | Append-only / immutable intent: minor clarifications edit in place; substantive reversals file a new record that supersedes the old | Explicit status transitions: proposed → accepted → deprecated | superseded by ADR-XXXX; old files are never deleted | . | W3C PROV-O (PROV-O: The PROV Ontology, W3C Recommendation 2013, adopted in methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md) | Ingested in library/w3c-2013-prov-o | Graph of prov:Entity nodes linked by typed provenance relations independent of filesystem nesting | Stable IRIs (req:<slug>, req:<slug>#<key>) identifying each entity | prov:wasDerivedFrom (parent/source lineage), prov:wasGeneratedBy (filing/test activity), prov:wasAttributedTo (actor/sign-off) | prov:wasRevisionOf and prov:specializationOf distinguish revisions from distinct derived entities | prov:wasInvalidatedBy and prov:invalidatedAtTime model retirement/supersession without erasing the entity from the provenance graph | . | RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017 — BCP 14 key words) | Ingested in library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | Separates normative statements (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) from explanatory prose within a specification | Statement-level addressing (statements[].key → req:<slug>#<key>) so each normative keyword clause is individually citable | Pairs each uppercase keyword statement with its own successCriteria and verification witness | Changing a statement’s modality (SHOULD → MUST) is a normative change requiring re-sign-off | Retiring or relaxing a MUST statement requires explicit normative adjudication | . | Specification-Compiled Agents & Issue-Driven Work Plans (arxiv-2404.04834v4; hmans-2026-beans-readme) | Ingested in library/arxiv-2404.04834v4 and library/hmans-2026-beans-readme | Connects declarative specifications to executable agent work items (beans/) and automated verification gates | Cross-graph IDs: req:<slug> linked to work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) and process IDs (Process_*) | Closed-loop compilation: requirement statement → work-plan work item → implementing skill/process → test attestation | Specification edits trigger deterministic re-check (check:requirements) across all linked sets and attestations | Completed work items archive when closed; filed requirements remain in-force as the persistent invariant until superseded or retired | . | IEEE Std 830-1998 (IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) | Historical IEEE standard (superseded); external baseline | Monolithic single-document SRS organised by deep numbered outline (3.1.1.1 Functional Requirement 1) | Positional section numbers (§3.2.4.1) tied to document outline location | External traceability matrices (spreadsheets) mapping section numbers to test cases | Document-level revision history table at the top of the monolithic SRS | Striking out or deleting sections in a new SRS edition, causing section renumbering unless placeholder sections are kept | . 1.2 Detailed source notes: what each source offers this harness . 1.2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, and 6.5) . | What it offers here: . | Attribute canon (Clause 6.5): Defines the essential metadata attributes every managed requirement needs beyond its statement text: unique identifier, requirement status, source/origin, rationale, priority/modality, verification method/criteria, and trace links. Our bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json directly embodies this attribute set (id, title, status, proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, statements[], beans, skills, processes, supersededBy). | Bidirectional traceability (Clause 5.2.7): Establishes that forward traceability alone (requirement → test) is half a system; backward traceability (requirement → originating proposal/need/source via proposedIn and derivedFrom) is what prevents gold-plating (orphan requirements with no stakeholder origin) and explains why a constraint exists when an agent later considers changing it. | Change and retirement discipline: Distinguishes an approved baseline from working drafts (RequirementSet.stage: draft → proposed → approved → accepted in bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json) and requires any transition into or out of active force to carry human sign-off. | . | . 1.2.2 Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson) . | What it offers here: . | Atomic “Snow Card” structure with Fit Criteria: Volere’s primary contribution is insisting that a requirement is not filed until its Fit Criterion (our statements[].successCriteria) is written beside the description (statements[].statement). A requirement whose fit criterion cannot be stated is still a proposal or open question. | Organisation by semantic concern / business domain: Rather than organising requirements by the code file they touch or chronological filing date, Volere organises requirements by functional domain / concern area so a reader auditing one domain sees all governing invariants together. In cat-harness, the eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) already partition skills, processes, schemas, and tests; projecting filed requirements under those same eight concern groups in docs/requirements/index.md aligns requirement navigation with the rest of the knowledge graph. | . | . 1.2.3 IREB CPRE (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals) . | What it offers here: . | Decoupling identification and storage from presentation views: IREB highlights the classic failure mode of hierarchical specifications: when chapter structure is used as both the file path and the requirement ID, reorganising chapters breaks every incoming reference. Storing atomic requirements at stable paths with immutable IDs (docs/requirements/<slug>.md → req:<slug>) while providing faceted views (grouped by concern group, by RequirementSet, or by lifecycle status in docs/requirements/index.md) gives both stable URIs and structured human browsing. | Three-axis trace topology: Clarifies the distinction between backward trace (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal trace (dependsOn between peer requirements), and forward trace (beans, skills, processes, and verification attestations). | . | . 1.2.4 Doorstop (Browning & Adams, JOSS 2014) . | What it offers here: . | Git-native file-per-requirement architecture: Doorstop proved that storing requirements as individual text files with YAML front matter and Markdown prose in the same Git repository as the implementation eliminates external ALM database drift. Every requirement filing, amendment, or retirement travels in the same pull request as the code, process diagram, and test attestation that implements or verifies it. | In-place retirement (status: retired / superseded): Doorstop retires requirements by flipping a front-matter status field rather than deleting the file (git rm), ensuring that historical commits, test runs, and child requirements never point to a missing file. | Suspect-link awareness: Doorstop flags downstream items when an upstream requirement changes. In our harness, check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts) provides the deterministic equivalent: it verifies that every derivedFrom, dependsOn, and supersededBy target exists, that no cycle exists in derivedFrom, that no in-force requirement depends on a retired or superseded requirement without updating its own lineage, and that every RequirementSet at approved or accepted has a matching human requirement-signoff attestation and only in-force members. | . | . 1.2.5 Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) . | What it offers here: . | Proposal-to-Requirement continuity (git mv + proposedIn): In cat-harness, a feature starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (where options are weighed using Kepner-Tregoe, SWOT, and MADR). When the feature ships and is signed off, git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md promotes the file in place, preserving its slug, its git log --follow history, and the options analysis that justified it, while proposedIn records the commit SHA and path of the proposal before the move. | Immutable supersession chain: When a shipped requirement’s fundamental contract is replaced by a new design, the old requirement file is not overwritten into a different contract; instead, the new proposal is filed as docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md, and the old requirement’s front matter is updated to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | .

3013.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3013.title: 2. Candidate methodologies: adopted vs rejected with reasons
3013.content: Following skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md, we do not invent an unattributed house method. We adopt four orthogonal practices from the surveyed literature—naming their origins, what is taken, what is left behind, and how each binds into bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and check:requirements—and we explicitly reject five candidate practices with documented reasons. 2.1 Adopted methodologies . M1 — Doorstop + MADR git-native file-per-requirement and two-level semantic identifiers (req:<slug> and req:<slug>#<key>) . | Origin: Doorstop (Browning & Adams 2014) for one-file-per-requirement in Git with YAML front matter + Markdown body; MADR (methodologies/madr.md) for human-readable <slug>.md filenames; RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md) for statement-level normative clauses. | What is adopted: . | Each filed requirement lives in its own Markdown file at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> matching its filename stem (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Individual normative clauses inside a requirement are declared in statements[] (key, modality, statement, successCriteria) and addressed as req:<slug>#<key> (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, every <slug> is globally unique: a slug exists either as an unshipped proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md or as a filed requirement in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, never both (check:requirements refuses a collision). | . | What is left behind and why: . | Doorstop’s auto-incremented numeric filenames (REQ001.yml, REQ002.yml) are left behind because concurrent feature branches in a multi-agent repository collide on sequential integers and opaque numbers hide meaning in prose and test logs. | Doorstop’s content-hash “fingerprint” clearing on whitespace edits is left behind because explicit lifecycle status + human requirement-signoff attestations (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/) provide stronger, semantically intentional governance than raw byte hashes. | . | . M2 — Faceted concern-group organisation (code-lists/concern-group.json) over flat docs/requirements/<slug>.md storage (Volere + IREB faceted view) . | Origin: Volere functional-area grouping (Robertson & Robertson) combined with IREB CPRE’s separation of stable storage identifiers from faceted navigation views (Pohl & Rupp), bound to the harness’s eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json. | What is adopted: . | Physical storage stays flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md: Every filed requirement sits directly in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, preserving 1:1 path parity with docs/proposals/<slug>.md for git mv, keeping req:<slug> → docs/requirements/<slug>.md resolution O(1) without directory searches, and ensuring check:requirements (mdFilesIn) reads 100% of filed requirements. | Logical organisation in docs/requirements/index.md groups by two orthogonal views: . | By Concern Group (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct from code-lists/concern-group.json), so a reader or agent working in a concern domain sees every in-force invariant governing that domain. | By Requirement Set (RequirementSet) and Lifecycle Status (in-force vs superseded / retired), so CRD baselines and historical records are cleanly separated from active invariants. | . | . | What is left behind and why: . | Physical subdirectory nesting (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) is rejected (see R3 below) so that reclassifying a requirement’s concern group or cross-cutting scope never breaks markdown links or requires a second git mv. | . | . M3 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 + IREB + W3C PROV-O three-axis bidirectional traceability . | Origin: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Clause 5.2.7 (bidirectional traceability), IREB CPRE (backward / horizontal / forward trace links), and W3C PROV-O (library/w3c-2013-prov-o, methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md). | What is adopted: . | Backward traceability (to origin and parent sources): . | proposedIn: required on every requirement promoted from docs/proposals/<slug>.md (commit SHA + path: docs/proposals/<slug>.md), binding prov:wasDerivedFrom to the exact pre-move proposal revision. | derivedFrom: array of parent req:<slug> IDs or library/<bib-slug> L1 sources from which this requirement is derived (checked for existence and acyclicity by check:requirements). | . | Horizontal traceability (between peer requirements): . | dependsOn: array of req:<slug> IDs that this requirement relies on at runtime or design time (checked for existence by check:requirements). | . | Forward traceability (to work items, implementation, and verification): . | beans: work-plan work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) that delivered or amended the requirement. | skills and processes: the Skill and Process (Process_*) nodes that implement the requirement. | Verification & Sign-off: test runs (test/runs/) and attestations (test/attestations/) citing req:<slug> or req:<slug>#<key>, plus RequirementSet membership and human sign-off attestations in test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json. | . | . | . M4 — MADR / ISO 29148 immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired) . | Origin: MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 6.5 configuration & change control. | What is adopted: . | Four lifecycle states (status in requirement.schema.json): . | proposed: drafted in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or in a RequirementSet at draft / proposed / approved stage) awaiting final delivery and acceptance sign-off. | in-force: shipped, verified, and accepted by human BA/owner sign-off; actively binds the codebase and knowledge graph. | superseded: replaced by a newer requirement; must carry supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (enforced by requirement.schema.json allOf rule and check:requirements). | retired: no longer applicable (the feature or constraint was intentionally removed without replacement); supersededBy is omitted, and the retirement rationale and authorising issue/bean are recorded in the document body. | . | Change decision rule (Amendment in place vs Supersession): . | In-scope amendment (edit in place, keep req:<slug>): When clarifying prose, adding a statements[] sub-clause, tightening a successCriteria check, or updating skills/processes/beans links without reversing the core invariant, edit docs/requirements/<slug>.md in place and record a fresh requirement-signoff attestation if its RequirementSet is approved or accepted. | Scope-reversing replacement (file req:<new-slug>, mark old superseded): When a new proposal reverses or fundamentally replaces an in-force requirement’s contract, file the new proposal at docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md (status: in-force, derivedFrom: [req:<old-slug>]), and update docs/requirements/<old-slug>.md to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | Set membership consistency: Because check:requirements enforces that an approved or accepted RequirementSet may only contain in-force (or proposed at approved stage) members, superseding or retiring a requirement requires updating any RequirementSet that lists it (replacing the old ID with req:<new-slug> or removing the retired ID under a re-signed set amendment). | . | . 2.2 Rejected candidate methodologies (with reasons) . | Candidate methodology | Verdict | Reason for rejection in this harness | . | R1 — IEEE Std 830-1998 monolithic SRS & positional section numbering (§3.2.1.4) | Rejected | Tying a requirement’s identifier to its outline position in a single monolithic file causes cascading renumbering whenever a section is inserted, split, or reordered. Renumbering breaks req: URIs in test runs, attestations, and work items, and a single monolithic SRS file creates constant Git merge conflicts across parallel agent branches. | . | R2 — Centralised sequential integer IDs (REQ-0001, FR-0042) | Rejected | In a distributed multi-agent Git workflow (worktrees, branches, subagents), two branches filing requirements concurrently will allocate the same next integer (REQ-0043) unless gated by an external lock server. Even when unique, opaque integers convey no domain meaning in test logs or prose compared to req:<slug>#<key>. (Note: FR-NNN may still appear as a local table label inside a single CRD proposal during discussion, but the canonical graph identifier is req:<slug>#<key>.) | . | R3 — Physical subdirectory sharding (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) | Rejected (kept as faceted index view in docs/requirements/index.md instead) | 1. check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts, mdFilesIn) scans docs/requirements/ and docs/proposals/ non-recursively and enforces a 1:1 slug namespace between docs/proposals/<slug>.md and docs/requirements/<slug>.md.2. Many proposals span multiple concern groups (e.g., sdlc + process); forcing a single directory path would make paths brittle when concern boundaries evolve.3. Faceted grouping in docs/requirements/index.md delivers the navigational benefit of Volere/concern-group organisation with zero path churn. | . | R4 — ReqIF XML / OSLC RM RDF triples as the primary authored store | Rejected (consistent with requirements-standards-assessment.md) | XML UUID graphs and raw RDF triples are unreadable in GitHub PR reviews and cannot be naturally co-authored as prose + front matter by humans and agents. Our YAML front matter (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) exports cleanly to JSON-LD (bootstrap/ns.jsonld) without burdening authors with XML. | . | R5 — Destructive deletion (git rm) of superseded or retired requirements | Rejected | Deleting docs/requirements/<slug>.md when a requirement is retired or superseded breaks historical provenance: past test/runs/, test/attestations/, beans/, and derivedFrom links would become dangling references. Keeping the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md with status: superseded (supersededBy: req:<new-slug>) or status: retired preserves referential integrity across the graph. | .

3014.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3014.title: 3. Proposed filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn)
3014.content: To fulfil Criterion 3 of work item folio-assistant-qh1s (“a filing PROCESS proposed as BPMN, to be put to the owner before it is built”), the executable BPMN diagram sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (Process_RequirementsFiling) models the end-to-end process for filing, organising,superseding, or retiring a requirement in docs/requirements/. 3.1 Where Process_RequirementsFiling sits in the lifecycle . In the CRDM lifecycle (skills/process/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md): . | Phases 1–4 (crdm-needs.bpmn, crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn, crdm-data-model.bpmn, crdm-signoff.bpmn) produce and sign off a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and optionally a RequirementSet moving from draft → proposed → approved). | Phase 5 (crdm-deliver.bpmn) builds and verifies the MVP in code, skills, and processes. | At Phase 6 (crdm-close.bpmn), when the feature ships and stakeholders/BA confirm acceptance criteria are met, Process_RequirementsFiling (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) governs the transition of the proposal into docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or the amendment, supersession, or retirement of an existing filed requirement). | . 3.2 Lanes and responsibilities . | Lane | Role (partitionElementRef) | Responsibility in Process_RequirementsFiling | . | BA / Feature Requestor (Lane_BA) | business-analyst | Reviews the filed requirement’s organisation, traceability links, normative statements, and any supersession/retirement transition (BA_ReviewFiling), and issues the human sign-off decision (approve, amend, reject, defer, cancel) required by check:requirements before a RequirementSet can reach accepted. | . | Authoring Agent (Lane_Agent) | authoring-agent | Executes the deterministic filing steps: classifies the requirement’s concern group and filing mode (A_ClassifyFiling), moves or updates the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (A_PromoteOrUpdate), binds the Requirement front matter (A_BindFrontMatter), updates superseded/retired records (A_UpdateLifecycle), indexes the requirement in docs/requirements/index.md (A_UpdateIndex), runs check:requirements (A_RunCheck), and records the human sign-off attestation (A_RecordFilingSignoff). | . 3.3 Step-by-step walkthrough of sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn . | A_ClassifyFiling — Classify filing mode, concern group, and req:<slug> identifier (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Determine which of the three filing modes applies: . | New filing from proposal: promoting docs/proposals/<slug>.md → docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | In-place amendment or supersession: amending an existing docs/requirements/<slug>.md or superseding req:<old-slug> with req:<new-slug>. | Retirement: retiring an obsolete docs/requirements/<slug>.md (status: retired). | . | Assign the primary concern group from code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) for indexing in docs/requirements/index.md. | . | GW_FilingMode — Which filing transition? (cat-harness.processes:judgement): . | Branches on the three modes: promote (from docs/proposals/<slug>.md), amend-or-supersede (on an existing requirement), or retire (marking an active requirement retired). | . | A_PromoteOrUpdate — git mv proposal to docs/requirements/<slug>.md and capture proposedIn (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | On the promote branch, record the pre-move commit SHA (git log -1 --format=%H -- docs/proposals/<slug>.md), execute git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md so Git history stays unbroken, and populate proposedIn: { commit, path: "docs/proposals/<slug>.md" }. | . | A_BindFrontMatter — Bind Requirement front matter, statements, and 3-axis lineage (skill: specification-management): . | Validate or author the YAML front matter against bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>, title, status: in-force (or proposed prior to acceptance sign-off); | statements[] with stable #<key>, RFC 2119 modality (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), normative statement, and measurable successCriteria; | Backward lineage (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal dependencies (dependsOn), and forward implementation links (beans, skills, processes). | . | . | A_UpdateLifecycle — Update superseded or retired requirement records and RequirementSet membership (skill: specification-management): . | When superseding req:<old-slug> or retiring a requirement, set status: superseded + supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (or status: retired with retirement rationale in prose) on the old file without deleting it, and update any RequirementSet in docs/requirements/*.set.json so no approved/accepted set retains a non-in-force member. | . | A_UpdateIndex — Organise entry in docs/requirements/index.md under its concern group and status (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Add or update the requirement’s row in docs/requirements/index.md under its code-lists/concern-group.json section (for in-force requirements) or the Superseded and Retired Requirements archive table, and regenerate directory READMEs (subgraph-readmes.ts). | . | A_RunCheck — Run check:requirements gate (skill: specification-management): . | Execute bun run cat check:requirements to verify schema validity, slug uniqueness across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, derivedFrom acyclicity, resolution of all derivedFrom / dependsOn / supersededBy / skills / processes references, and RequirementSet invariants. | . | GW_CheckPassed — Does check:requirements pass?: . | If fail, loop back to A_BindFrontMatter to fix schema, collision, or broken-link findings before asking a human reviewer. | If pass, proceed to BA_ReviewFiling. | . | BA_ReviewFiling — BA / Owner reviews filed requirement, organisation, and sign-off (calledElement: Process_Adjudication, skill: adjudication, fulfilment: person): . | The Business Analyst / Owner reviews the filed requirement, its concern-group placement in docs/requirements/index.md, its traceability links, and its verification evidence, deciding approve, amend, reject, defer, or cancel (adjudication-requirement-set). | . | A_RecordFilingSignoff — Record requirement-signoff attestation and set stage (skill: adjudication): . | Append the human decision to test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json and update the RequirementSet stage (accepted on approval). | . | GW_FilingAccepted — Filing accepted?: . | approve / amend → End_RequirementFiled (“Requirement filed and indexed in docs/requirements/”). | reject / defer / cancel → End_FilingHeld (“Filing held or deferred — recorded with reason”). | . | . 3.4 Open design choices put to the owner before automation is built . Before any new CLI subcommand or schema extension is built on top of check:requirements, the following three design choices from this proposal are put to the owner: . | Concern-group tagging — index-only vs schema field: . | Option A (current zero-schema-change baseline): Keep bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json unchanged (additionalProperties: false) and organise requirements by concern group in docs/requirements/index.md. | Option B (optional schema field): Add an optional "concernGroup" (or "concerns": string[] referencing code-lists/concern-group.json) to bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json so docs/requirements/index.md can be generated deterministically from front matter. | . | Enforcing in-force dependency health in check:requirements: . | Today check:requirements verifies that every dependsOn and derivedFrom target exists. Should check:requirements also fail (or warn) when an in-force requirement dependsOn a requirement whose status is retired or superseded? | . | Standalone requirement sign-off vs RequirementSet sign-off: . | Today test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json attaches to a RequirementSet (*.set.json), and a standalone docs/requirements/<slug>.md promoted via git mv only needs proposedIn. Should every filed requirement belong to a concern-group RequirementSet (docs/requirements/<group>.set.json), or remain standalone unless grouped by a CRD? | . | .

3016.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3016.title: Automatic term extraction: candidates from prose, ranked, judged by a person
3016.content: Adopted 2026-11-10 (cat-harness#1144 follow-up, owner card Q-IDX-1 = A), so that the glossary skills that read prose for terms rest on a published method rather than on a house heuristic.

3017.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3017.title: Its sources: what is held
3017.content: | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | Tran et al. 2023, survey | ✅ library/arxiv-2301.06767v1 | the task and its two steps (§1), the feature families (§5.1, Fig. 2), the evaluation methods and measures (§6, Fig. 4), nested terms as the main open problem (§8.1) | . | Frantzi & Ananiadou 1996 | ✅ library/frantzi-ananiadou-1996-c-value | the C-value measure and its algorithm (§3, equations 1–3), and the human judge as the last step | . | Frantzi, Ananiadou & Tsujii 1998; Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima 2000 | ❌ not held | C-value applied to terms, and NC-value’s context weighting. Nothing here depends on them; they are named so that a reader does not take this node’s C-value for theirs | .

3018.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3018.title: The task, in the survey’s words
3018.content: “ATE systems usually employ a two-step procedure: (1) extracting a list of candidate terms, and (2) determining which candidate terms are correct using supervised or unsupervised techniques.” (§1) . The candidates come from preprocessing (tokenisation, lemmatisation, POS tagging, chunking). The second step scores them with features from six families (§5.1, Fig. 2): shape, linguistic, frequency, statistical, contextual and variational. The statistical family splits in two. Some measures need no reference corpus, such as C-value, TF-IDF and lexical cohesion. Others compare the domain text with a general one, such as weirdness, domain relevance and termhood.

3019.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3019.title: C-value, as Frantzi & Ananiadou define it (§3)
3019.content: C-value scores a candidate string a by how often it occurs, how long it is, and how often it occurs inside longer candidates. It exists for nested units: a phrase such as “Wall Street” that occurs mostly inside longer ones (“Wall Street Journal”) and would score low on its own frequency. | case | C-value(a) | . | a has the same frequency as a longer candidate that contains it (it only ever occurs inside that one) | 0: not a candidate | . | a is not a substring of any extracted candidate | (|a| − 1) · n(a) (eq. 2) | . | a occurs inside one or more longer candidates, not always the same one | (|a| − 1) · (n(a) − t(a) / c(a)) (eq. 3) | . n(a) is the frequency of a, |a| its length in words, t(a) its total frequency inside longer candidates, and c(a) the number of those longer candidates. The algorithm visits n-grams from the longest down, after a minimum frequency cut-off, and revises t and c of every substring as it goes. The more different longer candidates contain a, the smaller t(a)/c(a) and the higher its C-value. Two limits the paper states itself. It measured no precision or recall, because those “depend on the definition of collocation and they are domain dependent” (§4). And it presents the method as semi-automatic: “It is the human judge that will give the final decision” (§3). The 1996 paper is about collocations; applying it to terms is its own stated future work (§6), done in the papers that are not held.

3020.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3020.title: How a result is judged (survey §6)
3020.content: Three evaluation methods: human judges, a dictionary, or a gold standard list. Three scopes: all results, part of them, or the top k. With a gold standard the measures are precision, recall and F1. The survey notes that “the performance of different approaches is often not directly comparable” because the setups differ. Here, the gold standard for a layer is its own authored glossary terms: precision is the share of candidates a person accepted, and recall is the share of authored terms that the extractor proposed.

3021.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3021.title: Nested terms are the hard case (survey §8.1)
3021.content: Nested terms are “words or phrases that are both terms themselves and parts of longer terms”. The most common error the survey reports for current systems is that they predict only the shorter, nested term instead of the whole multi-word term, or the other way round. This is the case C-value was built for, and it is why C-value is the statistical measure this node names.

3022.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3022.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
3022.content: Adopted: . | the two steps, candidates then scoring; | C-value as the first scoring measure, because it needs no reference corpus and it addresses nested terms; | evaluation against the layer’s authored terms, reported as precision and recall, and never as one score. | . Refused: . | An extracted term is never a definition. It enters the glossary as candidate, with no definition until a person writes one. This is the 1996 paper’s human judge, and it is glossary-terms’ existing rule. | A score is not a decision. The ranking orders the review queue. A cut-off may shorten the queue, but it never promotes a term. | A measure the sources do not define is not added under this node’s name. NC-value’s context weights, or the log-length variant of C-value, come in with their own held source or not at all. | .

3023.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3023.title: How it is performed here
3023.content: The glossary skills that read prose for terms name this node in their uses-methodology, and the Tool that computes C-value satisfies them. Both live in the content layer, which links down to here. The Tool’s test reproduces Table 2 of the 1996 paper. By default it applies the paper’s method as published, which on ordinary prose ranks function phrases such as “it is” first (the paper: many candidates “may seem unimportant”, §4).

3024.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3024.title: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3024.content: ← All methodologies . automatic-term-extraction — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Finding which words and phrases in a body of prose are the TERMS of its domain, so that a glossary can be proposed from the text rather than typed from memory. It answers which strings are candidate terms, ranked. Every output is a candidate: a person decides what is a term and writes its definition (glossary-terms: an extractor writes candidate, only a person moves one to authored). Not for assigning terms from a closed controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), not for keywords that summarise one document against the others (lsi, correspondence-analysis, the keyword graph), and not for reading definitions a source already states in its own glossary section, which are copied verbatim and need no extraction. Origin. Automatic term extraction (ATE) as surveyed by Hanh Thi Hong Tran, Matej Martinc, Jaya Caporusso, Antoine Doucet and Senja Pollak, “The Recent Advances in Automatic Term Extraction: A survey” (arXiv:2301.06767v1, CC BY 4.0), ingested whole and read. The C-value measure for nested multi-word units is Katerina T. Frantzi and Sophia Ananiadou, “Extracting Nested Collocations”, COLING 1996 (ACL Anthology C96-1009, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), ingested whole and read; its equations were checked against the printed page, because the Anthology’s own text layer is a poor OCR. The later C-value/NC-value papers that apply the measure to terms (Frantzi, Ananiadou & Tsujii 1998; Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima 2000) are not open access and are not held. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2301.06767v1 | library/frantzi-ananiadou-1996-c-value | . Applied by skills: . | glossary-terms | glossary-terms | ontologist | ontologist | . Node file: automatic-term-extraction.md .

3025.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3025.title: WireGen: from a written intent to a reviewed, mid-fidelity wireframe
3025.content: Adopted in part, 2026-09-23, by the owner’s direction. In the owner’s words: “make methodology/utilize/integrate into existing processes. need both web and mobile layouts in usability reviews. wireframe is part of design process for adjudication”. Integrated into CRDM, 2026-10-14. crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn calls Process_WireframeDesignReview (Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built; the candidates become assets of the request’s proposal, and the requester or BA chooses one at BA_ReviewReqs. See wireframe-design-review. Placed in cat-harness (owner, 2026-09-23: “put wireframe in cat-harness, not folio-assist(-core)”). The method is domain-neutral, and methodology-adoption §4 puts a domain-neutral method in the harness. It was first drafted in litlfred/ihris, and its first use was that folio’s data-model site. Issue #1023.

3026.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3026.title: What the method says (rendered faithfully)
3026.content: Section numbers below are the paper’s. | Design intent comes first, as language (§3, §5.2). A short natural-language description of what the screen is for and what it holds. | Mid-fidelity is the target (§3.1.1). The wireframe is monochrome and simplified, but it carries real content, semantic icons and interactive elements, not boxes and placeholder text. | HTML is the carrier (§3.1.2, §3.3). The screen is expressed as a UI-specific HTML-like language. Raw output is post-processed against UI guidance: icons chosen by meaning, typography, and layout guidelines (§3.3). | Evaluation is blind and comparative (§4.3). Independent raters with design background see the description and a shuffled grid of candidates, without knowing which generator produced which. They mark candidates significantly better or significantly worse. | Usefulness is asked separately (§5.2): whether a wireframe is effective for inspiration, whether it relates to the description, and whether the candidates are diverse. These are rated on a 5-point scale. | Refinement is iterative (§6). Intent, then wireframe, then a revised intent, then a revised wireframe. | .

3031.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3031.title: Specification-compiled agents
3031.content: Adopted 2026-09-23, on the owner’s “ingest into library for use as evidence and skills as subgraph on processes in cat-harness”. The authors’ own sentence for the mechanism: . “we compile an industry standard BPMN 2.0 process model into a ReAct style control graph. Each BPMN node provides a typed tool contract and a node local policy, while the control plane enforces branches and joins, scopes context per node, and applies contract derived runtime validation with targeted retries.” .

3032.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3032.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
3032.content: The control flow is COMPILED from a specification the model did not write, so the model never rediscovers the plan at runtime. Everything else in the paper follows from that. The model still reasons — it is a ReAct agent, not a state machine — but it reasons locally, inside a node, against a typed contract, with the branches and joins enforced by something that is not it.

3033.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3033.title: Three principles, and they are separable
3033.content: The paper names them together; they are three distinct commitments and a reader may take one without the others. | principle | what it does | what it costs | . | constrained execution | branches and joins come from the diagram, not from a plan the model produced | the diagram must exist and be right | . | targeted context management | each node sees the minimum it needs, rather than the accumulated transcript | somebody must decide, per node, what that minimum is | . | modular decomposition | prompt, tools and orchestration are generated as separate artefacts | more upfront authoring than a single prompt | . The second is the one with an argument behind it rather than an intuition. The paper cites evidence that model performance degrades as more of the context window is consumed, and observes that a generalist system cannot scope context per subtask because it does not know, at construction time, what each subtask will need. A specification does know — which is why scoping is available to this design and not to the other.

3034.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3034.title: What the paper measured
3034.content: Ten workflows, 9 to 52 nodes, all deterministic, spanning e-commerce, costing, risk, labelling, news, social, promotion, tournament registration and weather. Ten successful agents per workflow per system, evaluated across all control-flow paths — 300 agents over 30,543 test cases, from 371 generation attempts. Baselines: Roo and Cline. AutoGen, MetaGPT and FLOW were tried and produced nothing executable — MetaGPT emitted prompts and tools but no agent, AutoGen needed manual wiring even with GraphFlow, FLOW produced decompositions rather than code — so they were excluded rather than scored, which is the honest handling. Aggregates (Figure 4), specialist vs Cline vs Roo: . |   | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | tool-use exactness ↑ | 57.7 % | 48.6 % | 38.1 % | . | tool-call errors ↓ | 1.27 | 3.19 | 3.22 | . | latency (s / effective step) ↓ | 2.49 | 6.59 | 9.08 | . | process adherence ↑ | 54.7 % | 51.6 % | 42.4 % | . | repair iterations ↓ | 0.00 | 1.85 | 2.04 | . | total tokens | 53.8 k | 1 021.8 k | 1 468.6 k | . The two robust results are the last two rows, and they are robust because they are not close: zero repair iterations across every successful generation, and an order of magnitude in tokens. Those are properties of the pipeline rather than of the generated agent, which is why they do not vary the way the run metrics do.

3035.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3035.title: What the figures say that the prose does not
3035.content: Read off Figure 3 directly, 2026-09-23, as part of ingesting the images. This is a reading of the paper’s own chart, not a claim about the authors’ work, and it is recorded because the surrounding text does not say it. The paper writes of tool-use exactness that “the per-workflow breakdown in Figure 3(a) confirms this advantage holds consistently across all ten workflows regardless of complexity.” Figure 3(a) does not show that. On three of the ten the specialist system is not best: . | workflow | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | Cost | 49.6 | 76.0 | 67.6 | . | Tournament | 46.2 | 99.4 | 94.9 | . | Weather | 81.8 | 90.1 | 61.0 | . Tournament is not a near miss — it is 46.2 against 99.4. The same two workflows invert in panels (b) and (d): on Cost the specialist has the most tool-call errors (1.43 against 0.55 and 0.34) and the lowest process adherence (57.2 against 87.1 and 76.2), and Tournament repeats both. And the aggregate advantage is carried disproportionately by two workflows. On Risk the specialist shows 0.20 tool-call errors against 13.19 and 11.94, and 98.6 % exactness against 0.4 % and 0.9 %; Social contributes a smaller version of the same. A mean over ten workflows, two of which contain an order-of- magnitude gap, is a mean dominated by those two. Separately, §4.3.1 gives the aggregate repair figures as “2.08 for Roo and 1.89 for Cline” where Figure 2(d) is labelled 2.04 and 1.85. Small, and noted only because this node quotes one of them. None of this makes the method wrong. It makes the aggregate run metrics the wrong thing to quote, and it is the reason the section above marks the generation metrics as the robust pair. It also suggests a real question the paper does not ask: what do Cost and Tournament have in common that inverts the result? Looking at their diagrams, both are shallow and branch-heavy — the regime where a compiled control graph has least to contribute, because there is barely a plan to rediscover.

3036.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3036.title: What this checkout already does, and where it differs
3036.content: methodology-adoption §”Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools” requires this comparison before any tool is proposed. Read from the repository, not assumed: . | the method asks for | this checkout has | gap | . | BPMN 2.0 as the authored control flow | processes/, 69 diagrams, .bpmn as the source of truth | none — this is already the premise | . | a control plane that enforces branches and joins | workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_gate / workflow_complete, with workflow_complete refusing a step that is not enabled | none of substance | . | a node-local policy | cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement, relaxable, cat-harness.processes:decision, cat-harness.processes:judgement — four mechanisms, already finer than the paper’s one | this checkout is AHEAD | . | a typed tool contract per node | <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> names the instruction body; there is no typed input/output contract | the real gap | . | context scoped per node | not modelled. A step returns a skill; nothing says what the agent may or must see | the second real gap | . | contract-derived runtime validation with targeted retries | nothing. A step that goes wrong is not caught by the control plane | follows from the first gap | . | compilation to an executable agent | nothing, and deliberately: the diagrams here govern agents rather than generating them | out of scope, not a gap | . The last row is the one to be careful about. The paper’s system emits a deployable service; this repository’s engine runs alongside an agent doing the work. Those are different products of the same specification, and adopting the method here means taking the first three principles, not the code generator.

3037.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3037.title: Where this rendering stops
3037.content: . | No implementation is adopted. ReAct, FastAPI, LangGraph and Langfuse are the paper’s tools, not obligations. | The benchmark is not adopted. Ten workflows the authors built themselves, and they say so: “author-constructed workflows may introduce design bias”. A benchmark of somebody else’s processes measures their processes. | The numbers are not adopted as evidence for anything here. See the figures section: three of ten workflows invert, and the aggregate is dominated by two. What survives is the shape — zero repair iterations and an order of magnitude in tokens — and even those were measured on that corpus. | The deterministic scope is inherited, not argued away. Every workflow evaluated is deterministic by construction. The authors state the limit plainly; this node does not extend the result past it, and deterministic-and-agentic is where the open question lives. | “Specialist beats generalist” is not a conclusion this node draws. The paper compares one specialist pipeline against two general coding assistants operating unconstrained at their defaults, and says future work will examine “more heavily optimised baseline configurations”. That is a fair comparison of realistic low-configuration usage and it is not a claim about ceilings. | .

3038.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3038.title: The owner’s own statement of the two ends
3038.content: library/kg-folio-asst-2026-09-30 is the owner’s deck of 2026-09-30. It is cited as evidence of intent, not of effect. Slide 7 draws the axis this node sits on: “BPMN Execution Skill: given a Process, Context, State, Role utilize one or more Skills in order [to] execute a Task”, run by either of two Tools. One is an open-source BPMN engine with “state and swimlanes strictly enforced”. The other is “an agentic swarm with ungoverned state”, mitigated by mechanical and agentic QA/QC reports. This node is the method for the first end. The deck measures nothing, so it says where the owner wants the harness to go and nothing about how well either end works. That is what the paper above is for. The diagrams this method executes are OMG BPMN 2.0.2 (formal/2013-12-09), recorded as library/omg-2013-bpmn-2-0-2. The entry identifies the exact specification and its clause outline, so a citation can name a clause and page. It holds none of the text, because OMG’s licence forbids posting copies on a network.

3040.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3040.title: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3040.content: ← All methodologies . specification-compiled-agents — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A process is already written down as a diagram, and something must now EXECUTE it. Use it when the control flow is external and authored — a BPMN process, a DMN table, a pipeline someone drew — and the question is how an LLM should act inside it. It answers where the plan comes from, never what the plan should be: authoring the diagram is bpmn-authoring, deciding a branch from a table is dmn, and choosing between options is kepner-tregoe. Its companion is hybrid-llm-deterministic, and the two are the same shape at different grains: that one has the model emit a RULE that machinery validates and runs; this one has the model act inside a CONTROL GRAPH that machinery derived from a specification. Reach for this one when the artefact that constrains the model already exists as a diagram. Do NOT reach for it where no specification exists, or where the process is genuinely open-ended. The paper’s own evaluation is scoped to deterministic workflows and says so; a setting with ambiguity, stochasticity or open-ended human decision-making is outside what it measured, and outside what this node claims. Origin. Harris Borman, Herman Wandabwa, Fusun Yu, Sandeepa Kannangara, Justin Liu, Anna Leontjeva and Ritchie Ng, “Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution”, Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Published as a workshop paper at SCALE, ICML 2026 (PMLR 306); arXiv:2607.14456v1 [cs.SE], 16 July 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. It is a SYSTEM paper reporting one implementation against a benchmark its own authors built, so what is adopted below is the METHOD, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. §”What the figures say that the prose does not” carries a reading of the paper’s own charts that changes how its headline numbers should be used, and it is the reason this node quotes almost none of them. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2607.14456v1 | library/kg-folio-asst-2026-09-30 | library/omg-2013-bpmn-2-0-2 | . 3042.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
3042.title: Its sources: what is held, what is not
3042.content: | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | ODRL Information Model 2.2 (W3C REC, 2018) | ✅ library/w3c-2018-odrl-model-2-2 | the model, its classes and every MUST quoted below | . | ODRL Vocabulary & Expression 2.2 | ❌ not held | the Common Vocabulary actions (display, modify, …) and their includedIn; the JSON-LD context. 3043.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
3043.title: The load-bearing idea, in the standard’s words
3043.content: “The ODRL Information Model represents Policies that express Permissions, Prohibitions and Duties related to the usage of Asset resources. The Information Model explicitly expresses what is allowed and what is not allowed by the Policy” — §2. Its terms (§1.3): a Policy is “A group of one or more Rules”; an Action “An operation on an Asset”; a Permission “The ability to exercise an Action over an Asset”; a Prohibition “The inability to exercise an Action over an Asset”; a Duty “The obligation to exercise an agreed Action”; a Party “An entity or a collection of entities that undertake Roles in a Rule”; a Constraint “A boolean/logical expression that refines an Action and Party/Asset collection or the conditions applicable to a Rule”. Three mechanisms carry the method, and the platform uses all three: . | Actions inherit through includedIn. “a Permission or Prohibition of an encompassing Action is inherited by all Actions with an includedIn relationship”, and every action other than use and transfer “MUST have one includedIn property value” (§2.4). | Constraints conjoin. “When multiple Constraints apply to the same Rule … they are interpreted as conjunction and all MUST be satisfied” (§2.5). | Conflicts are resolved by a declared strategy: “perm: the Permissions MUST override the Prohibitions; prohibit: the Prohibitions MUST override the Permissions; invalid: the entire Policy MUST be void” (§2.10). | . And one that makes extension legitimate: a policy may “Use an ODRL Profile that declares the supported vocabulary” (§2.1), and new actions are made by creating “an instance of an Action and define its includedIn parent Action” (§3.3).

3044.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
3044.title: What this platform adopts — class by class
3044.content: | ODRL | here | where | . | Policy (Set, Offer, Agreement), uid, profile, inheritFrom, conflict | adopted; both live policies are Sets with conflict: odrl:prohibit | OdrlPolicySchema, policies/*.jsonld | . | Permission | adopted: one rule per (actor, action), migrated from the old per-actor lists | policies/folio-defaults.jsonld, policies/http-gateway.jsonld | . | Prohibition | adopted in the schema and the evaluator; no live policy states one — both files’ prohibition is [] or absent | permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts | . | Action + includedIn | adopted: the folio profile’s actions each name a broader action, ending at ODRL’s odrl:display/modify/annotate/derive/translate/execute under odrl:use | skills/permissions/permissions.json, ODRL_ACTIONS, broaderOrSelf() | . | Party — assignee, assigner | adopted as the assignee of each rule, an actor id from scenarios/actors/, plus the profile party cat-harness:anyone for an unauthenticated reader | OdrlRuleSchema, ANYONE | . | Asset — target | adopted as an optional target string | ruleApplies() | . | Constraint | adopted for three profile leftOperands — cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task, cat-harness:role — and four operators eq, neq, isAnyOf, isNoneOf, conjoined | OdrlConstraintSchema, constraintHolds() | . | Profile | profile is required; the action half of the profile is permissions.json | OdrlPolicySchema | . The evaluator is the question every caller asks — the BPMN task gate (src/workflow/authorize.ts, action perform-task), the HTTP routes (src/core/rbac.ts), and the auth_whoami tool (src/tools/auth.ts) — all through decide(), over policies loaded by src/core/access.ts.

3045.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
3045.title: What it refuses or departs from, with reasons
3045.content: Each item is a place where the code differs from the held text. They are stated so nobody reads @conformsTo w3c-odrl as full conformance. | Duty, obligation, consequence, remedy — refused. No reader exists, and .strict() rejects the keys “because a rule that silently means less than it says is exactly the failure a permission file must not have” (schemas/content/odrl.ts). A Permission carrying an unfulfilled duty would be read as unconditional, which is worse than refusing it. | Refinements, AssetCollection, PartyCollection, LogicalConstraint, rightOperandReference, dataType, unit, status, implies, partOf, hasPolicy, transfer — refused, for the same reason: no reader. | target is optional; ODRL requires it. §2.6.1: “A Permission MUST have one target property value of type Asset” (Prohibition likewise, §2.6.2). Here an absent target means the layer’s whole graph. Every live rule omits it. | The default conflict strategy is prohibit; ODRL’s is invalid. §2.10: “If the conflict property is not explicitly set, the default of invalid will be used.” The code names this as “OUR rule rather than claimed as ODRL’s”; both live policies set odrl:prohibit explicitly, so the difference does not fire today. Kept by owner ruling, 2026-10-01 (work item jcet): an unstated clash denies rather than voiding the policy — a deliberate profile departure, not an oversight; odrl.test.ts pins it. | Across policies, any deny wins. decide() evaluates each policy and lets a prohibition in one beat a permission in another. ODRL’s merge rule is different — inherited conflict values are replicated and “If a Policy has multiple conflict property values … then the entire Policy MUST be void” (§2.10). Only the child’s conflict is read by permits(). | A circular inheritFrom is tolerated, not refused. §2.9: “Inheritance MUST NOT be circular.” effectiveRules() walks with a visited set, so a cycle terminates silently instead of failing. (Cycles are deliberately allowed in the action graph — the owner’s “doensnt necc need to be rooted acyclic graph”. That sits uneasily with §2.4, which calls includedIn transitive, says “the Actions form ancestor relationships”, and requires every action to reach use or transfer; a cycle among profile actions is a departure, not a reading.) | No-match answers unknown, a third value. This node found no held text that defines the outcome when no rule matches; unknown — never permit, never deny — is the platform’s rule (Decision in schemas/content/odrl.ts), so task-authorization can report it as a finding. | Role eligibility is added on top. permits() denies a permitted request whose cat-harness:role the actor is not eligible for. That is role-model’s separation of what a lane needs from what an actor may do; it is not ODRL. | Cardinalities not enforced: an empty policy validates (§2.1: “MUST have at least one permission, prohibition, or obligation”); an Offer needs no assigner and an Agreement needs no policy-level assignee (§2.1.2, §2.1.3); and the profile IRI is never checked, although §3.2 says a processor that “does not recognise the ODRL Profile identifier(s) … MUST stop processing”. | The profile is not published as RDF. §3.3 asks that new terms “must also be defined as a skos:Concept”; permissions.json is plain JSON with id, title, description, includedIn, and the profile IRI https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/ns/folio-odrl is not shown to resolve. | .
