3133.title: Q
3133.content: QA gate: check dispositions against the people and the pull request candidate, extracted Before Ready for merge. Reads: the change set's Disposition (change set), each comment's Blue Disposition on Review Public Comments, the PR's diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every comment number has one disposition; that each agrees with the people's Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted comment has its change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Deferred, Duplicate or Out of scope one has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set), first line "Passed <head sha>: …" or "Failed <head sha>: <why>", and QA report (change set), the report's link. The sheet shows both under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. BPMN activities of folio-assistant-core · source folio-assistant-core/processes/content/public-comment-change.bpmn#Task_QaGate . QA gate: check dispositions and PR candidate, extracted Reads: the change set's Disposition (change set), the people's Blue Disposition and feedback, the pull request's diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every feedback item has one disposition; that each agrees with the people's Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted item has the change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate or Out of scope item has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set) on the Agent tab, first line "Passed <head sha>: …" or "Failed <head sha>: <why>", and QA report (change set), the report's link. The sheet shows the gate under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. 3135.title: Glossary: BPMN activities
3135.content: Candidate terms extracted from every BPMN task and call activity: name as the label, its own <documentation> as the definition, the element id as the code. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap 38 (SKOS) · bootstrap-tools 7 (SKOS) · cat-harness 376 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 229 (SKOS). Split by first letter. 650 terms are too many for one page within its budget of 1.0 MB, so they are on 3 pages by the first letter of the label. The ranges are fixed, so a term’s address does not move as terms are added. A label that does not start with a letter is on the first page. | A–D: 198 terms | E–Q: 206 terms | R–Z: 246 terms | .

3137.title: quality of the evidence
3137.content: In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. Also called: certainty of the evidence, confidence in the estimates of effect . The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout.

3159.content: Training that is beyond clinical update and includes wide-ranging competences like research and scientific writing; multidisciplinary context of patient care; professionalism and ethical practice; communication, leadership, management and behavioural skills; team building; information technology; auditing; and appropriate attitudinal change to ensure improved patient service, research outcomes, and attainment of the highest degree of satisfaction by stakeholders. 3217.content: One who provides services to patients and communities (practising health worker) or whose medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of the job (e.g. education, research, public administration) even if the health worker is not directly providing services (professionally active health worker). 3253.title: Public Health Workforce candidate
3253.content: The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. Also called: Public health workforce . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 3287.title: Facility/Institution Ownership Type candidate
3287.content: Classification for ownership type: • Publicly-owned: Facilities owned or controlled by a governmental unit or a public corporation (where control is defined as the ability to determine the general corporate policy) corresponding to the institutional sector “government units” defined in the System of National Accounts 2008. • Not-for-profit privately-owned: Facilities that are legal or social entities created for the purpose of producing goods and services, whose status does not permit them to be a source of income, profit, or other financial gain for the unit(s) that establish, control or finance them, corresponding to the institutional sector “non-profit institutions serving households” defined in the System of National Accounts 2008. • For-profit privately-owned: Facilities that are legal entities set up for the purpose of producing goods and services and are capable of generating a profit or other financial gain for their owners corresponding to the institutional sector “non-financial corporations” defined in the System of National Accounts 2008. Also called: Facility/institution ownership type . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 3317.doc: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution
3317.title: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution candidate
3317.content: An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. Also called: Health workforce education and training institution . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 3329.title: Facility Type candidate
3329.content: Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. Also called: Facility type . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 89; PDF page 103). 3373.title: Remuneration candidate
3373.content: Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 3466.title: Status in Employment candidate
3466.content: One of two categories of the total employed: (a) wage and salaried workers (employees): workers who hold a job defined as “paid employment”, with explicit (written or oral) or implicit employment contracts that give them a basic remuneration that is not directly dependent upon the revenue of the unit for which they work, and (b) self-employed workers: workers who, working on their own account or with one or more partners or in a cooperative, hold a “self-employment job”, i.e. one in which the remuneration is directly dependent upon the profits derived from the goods and services produced. Also called: Status in employment . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 93; PDF page 107). 3474.title: Gender candidate
3474.content: Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. This includes norms, behaviours and roles associated with being a woman, man, girl or boy, as well as relationships with each other. Candidate definitions (3) . | Accreditation (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))In a health workforce context, the evaluation of educational institutions and programs of study against pre-defined standards required for the delivery of education. The outcome of the process is certification of the suitability of education programmes and the capability of education institutions to deliver initial and/or continuing education. The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 69 for this entry. | Health Workforce Education and Training Programme (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))A “coherent set or sequence of educational activities or communication designed and organized to achieve pre-determined learning objectives or accomplish a specific set of educational tasks over a sustained period” with the objective to improve health knowledge, skills and competencies applied to health and enable the training of new health workers. Health workforce education and training programmes will often have a numerus clausus that restricts the number of places for a given programme. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 91; PDF page 105). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 108 for this entry. | Health Workforce Education and Training Institution (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). Facility Type candidate Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. 4203.content: Gender candidate Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. This includes norms, behaviours and roles associated with being a woman, man, girl or boy, as well as relationships with each other. As a social construct, gender varies from society to society and can change over time. Gender is hierarchical and produces inequalities that intersect with other social and economic inequalities. The handbook cites its reference 48 for this entry. | Facility Type (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 4210.content: National Capacity to Monitor Key Metrics for Health Workforce Planning and Global Monitoring Frameworks 4-05 candidate Capacity of national human resources for health information systems to monitor key metrics relevant for national health workforce planning and policy-making and for global monitoring frameworks . NHWA indicator 4 – 05. The definition is the sheet's "Indicator name"; the label is its "Abbreviated name". Candidate definitions (7) . | International Health Regulations (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))An international legal instrument that is binding on 196 countries across the globe, including all Member States of WHO. Its aim is to help the international community prevent and respond to acute public health risks that have the potential to cross borders and threaten people worldwide. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 91; PDF page 105). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 109 for this entry. | Subnational Level (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))To be defined according to the specific conditions, governing structures, and constitutional provisions existing in a given country. Disaggregation based on administrative boundaries down to the first or second subnational level is recommended (depending on the structure of administrative boundaries and the size of subnational territories), without overlaps between the administrative units. Examples for subnational administrative units are states, regions, provinces, counties, and districts. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 93; PDF page 107). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 47 for this entry. | Active Health Worker (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))One who provides services to patients and communities (practising health worker) or whose medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of the job (e.g. education, research, public administration) even if the health worker is not directly providing services (professionally active health worker). If data are not available for practising or professionally active health workers, data with the closest definition can be used, such as “health worker licensed to practice”. Categories of level are based on the definitions of OECD/Eurostat/WHO-Europe Joint questionnaire on non-monetary health care statistics. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 88; PDF page 102). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 48 for this entry. | Occupation (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))The concept of occupation is defined as a “set of jobs whose main tasks and duties are characterized by a high degree of similarity”. A job is defined as “a set of tasks and duties performed, or meant to be performed, by one person, including for an employer or in self-employment”. The National Health Workforce Accounts covers health and health-related occupations grouped according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations 2008. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 46 for this entry. | Remuneration (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 58 for this entry. | Status in Employment (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))One of two categories of the total employed: (a) wage and salaried workers (employees): workers who hold a job defined as “paid employment”, with explicit (written or oral) or implicit employment contracts that give them a basic remuneration that is not directly dependent upon the revenue of the unit for which they work, and (b) self-employed workers: workers who, working on their own account or with one or more partners or in a cooperative, hold a “self-employment job”, i.e. one in which the remuneration is directly dependent upon the profits derived from the goods and services produced. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 93; PDF page 107). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 93 for this entry. | Gender (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. This includes norms, behaviours and roles associated with being a woman, man, girl or boy, as well as relationships with each other. As a social construct, gender varies from society to society and can change over time. Gender is hierarchical and produces inequalities that intersect with other social and economic inequalities. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). Public Health Workforce candidate The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. 4213.title: Q
4213.content: quality of the evidence In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout. Remuneration candidate Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 4303.title: clinical
4303.content: A guideline whose recommendations address the care of individual patients by health workers: assessment, diagnosis, treatment and management of a condition in a person. Also called: clinical guideline, clinical health . Looked up against the MeSH RDF API (id.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/, 2026-10-23): closeMatch to MeSH D017065 ('Practice Guideline', Publication Type; entry terms 'Clinical Guideline', 'Clinical Practice Guideline') and D015510 ('Clinical Medicine', Topical Descriptor). Neither is an exactMatch because this concept classifies a guideline's domain within a three-way partition (clinical, public health, health system strengthening) rather than publication form or the medical discipline as a whole.

4308.content: A guideline whose recommendations address how the health system itself is organised and resourced — service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, access to medical products, financing, and leadership and governance — rather than a particular condition or population intervention. 4415.title: A
4415.content: ArchiMate model from the glossary candidate, extracted Make an ArchiMate model agree with the instance's folio-glossary/v1 terms whose focus is an ArchiMate element: elements matched by their skosConcept property (never by name) take the term's prefLabel and definition, a term with no element gets one on no view, and the relationships the terms list are added. A type that disagrees is reported, never changed. A relationship between two linked elements that no term lists is reported, and removed with --prune along with the lines that draw it. No box or line is moved. Without --write it only reports; --check fails when anything would change. --seed goes the other way once, and only from an ingested model held under library/ (--from): an authored model is never a source of the glossary. Build the review sheet's Apps Script and a document's Config tab candidate, extracted Builds Code.gs (--script), the one Google Apps Script every review sheet runs (from review-sheet.gs), and one document's Config tab rows (--config), filled from the folio's review/public-comment/sheet-sync.json, its review anchors and the draft's pdf-line-map.json. The script keeps a public-comment review sheet's links and joins current: each comment No. links to its comment page; Sections, Page and Line no(s) link to the page of the frozen review draft; Review Change Sets joins its comments, suggested revisions, feedback and dispositions, each No. n linking to its row; and on both tabs Agentic status lists each pull request of the change-set, linked, with its status and what it changed, from the Agent tab. It reads the document's URLs, tab and column names and data from the sheet's Config tab (visible, locked to the owner), which the agent writes from these rows. A person pastes the script (one file) into the sheet once (Extensions > Apps Script) and runs installTriggers; from then on the sheet rebuilds itself within about a minute of an edit, with no agent. With "mode": "drafting" in the config it builds the drafting sheet instead: one Contributor Feedback tab where each row is a change set (ids assigned by the script), Sections picked from the document's table of contents and linked to it, and Issue and Agentic status from the Agent tab. 4417.title: C
4417.content: Catalogue a library from its bibliography candidate, extracted Write one folio-dublin-core/v1 record and one folio-catalogue-node/v1 item per library entry that the source ledger joins to a CSL-JSON reference, into the folio's declared catalogue directory, so gen-library-jsonld reads the title from the catalogue's dc.title instead of falling to the PDF or the slug. The join is exact: a ledger row naming the entry's structure.json source file, one reference id, and the same sha256 where both record one. Unjoined entries are reported and left alone. Never touches a node it did not write. Tools of folio-assistant-core · source folio-assistant-core/tools/catalogue-from-references/catalogue-from-references.ts#catalogue-from-references . Check a review log and its repository's issues for changes candidate, extracted The mechanical check a review-log watcher runs on every poll. Given a drafting sheet's Contributor Feedback values and the folio repository, it reads the repository's open and closed issues (leaving out pull requests, issues labelled no-sheet and, with --author, issues someone else opened) and compares a digest of them and of the cells people set (Title, Selected Sections, Contributor Feedback, Disposition, Ready for agent, Ready for merge, Dispositions confirmed; on a public-comment log also Committee Feedback, TWG (CS), TWG (human) and Change Set (human)) with the last check's. Unchanged: it prints {"status":"unchanged"} and exits 0. Changed: it exits 10 and lists what changed (issue opened, updated or closed; a cell's old and new text), the Contributor Feedback rows to append, one per issue that no row's Issue cell links yet (Title the issue's title, the first Contributor Feedback column @login (#N): first paragraph, Issue the issue's URL; a closed issue's row marked closed), and closedRows, the rows linking a closed issue, which the watcher hides with their text struck through. A read with no Issue column (a public-comment log's Review Change Sets) tracks only issues labelled change-set unless --label says otherwise, and appends no rows: each open issue is reported as an issue-unlinked change instead. It writes no sheet and no issue: the watcher appends the rows and does the agent pass. With --accept it stores the new state for the next poll to compare against. Tools of folio-assistant-core · source folio-assistant-core/tools/review-log-watch/review-log-watch.ts#review-log-watch . 4425.title: S
4425.content: Spreadsheet tabular metadata candidate, extracted Read a workbook into a folio-tabular-csvw/v1 record, one CSVW table per rectangular block of cells. 4452.content: web-apps candidate, extracted Interactive web apps as knowledge-graph content: a layer holds an app's source in a directory of kind web-app (one web-app.json), its UI strings go through the harness's translation process like any template, and the harness's apps visualiser (Tool web-app-build) builds it at publish and writes it to its own route with no site chrome, loaded only when a reader opens it. 4455.title: Glossary: Schema fields, A–C
4455.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2523 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 507 terms and is 304 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. 4460.title: Glossary: Schema fields, M–O
4460.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2523 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 219 terms and is 131 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 219 shown . M N O

4465.title: Glossary: Schema fields, D–E
4465.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2523 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 204 terms and is 122 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 204 shown . D E

4469.title: Glossary: Schema fields, T–Z
4469.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2523 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 520 terms and is 303 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 520 shown . T U V W

4475.title: Glossary: Schema fields, F–L
4475.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2523 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 509 terms and is 301 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 509 shown . F G H I J K L

4484.title: Glossary: Schema fields, P–R
4484.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2523 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 552 terms and is 325 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 552 shown . P Q R

4489.title: Glossary: Schema fields, S
4489.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2523 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 264 terms and is 153 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2718 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 264 shown . S

4513.title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems
4513.content: World Health Organization (2023). Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. World Health Organization. TitleDigital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-12-21 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240085138 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis second edition of the digital adaptation kit for HIV provides operational, software-neutral requirements to support the incorporation of WHO clinical, public health and data use recommendations into digital systems. Developed within the SMART Guidelines approach, it focuses on the content requirements for person-centred digital tracking and decision support systems used by health workers for HIV services in primary health care settings. The kit is intended to facilitate transparent, consistent and adaptable translation of narrative guidance into digital implementations while supporting interoperability and local customization. The publication organizes HIV-related requirements into eight components: health interventions and associated recommendations; generic personas; illustrative user scenarios; business processes and workflows; core data elements; decision support and scheduling logic; indicators and performance metrics; and high-level functional and non-functional requirements. It covers processes including HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis, care and treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, infant diagnosis, diagnostics, client follow-up, referral, and aggregate reporting and data use, with complementary operational resources provided in web annexes. 4519.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis
4519.title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis
4519.content: World Health Organization (2025). WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis. World Health Organization. TitleWHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2025-4-10 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization DOIhttps://doi.org/10.2471/B09341 Languageen AbstractThis web annex to the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 3: Diagnosis, compiles the evidence synthesis and analyses used to inform WHO recommendations on diagnostic technologies for tuberculosis and drug-resistant tuberculosis. The publication presents systematic reviews, meta-analyses, qualitative evidence syntheses and economic evaluations examining the diagnostic accuracy, safety, cost–effectiveness and implementation considerations of multiple diagnostic approaches, including low- and moderate-complexity nucleic acid amplification tests, targeted next-generation sequencing technologies and Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests. The annex describes the methods applied to identify, assess and synthesize evidence across diverse populations and settings, including adults, adolescents, children and people living with HIV. It addresses the detection of pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis, rifampicin resistance and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis using respiratory and non-respiratory specimens. The document also examines stakeholder and user perspectives, operational feasibility and factors influencing implementation. 4541.content: World Health Organization (2024). Digital adaptation kit for immunizations: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. World Health Organization. TitleDigital adaptation kit for immunizations: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-12-31 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240099456 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis publication presents the World Health Organization’s digital adaptation kit (DAK) for immunizations, developed within the SMART Guidelines framework to support the implementation of WHO immunization recommendations in digital systems. The document provides operational and software-neutral specifications intended to facilitate the translation of immunization guidance into interoperable digital health applications, particularly person-centred point-of-service systems and electronic immunization registries. It outlines the role of digital adaptation kits in strengthening digital health systems by improving the consistency, transparency and standardization of health content, workflows, data structures and decision-support logic used in immunization programmes. The publication also situates the DAK within broader digital health strategies and interoperability standards. The document describes eight core components of the immunization DAK, including health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and functional requirements. It incorporates WHO guidance related to routine immunization, electronic immunization registries and digital health interventions, while emphasizing adaptability to country-specific policies and implementation contexts. Additional sections address interoperability, data standards, workflow optimization and the use of digital systems to support longitudinal tracking, reporting, decision support and communication within immunization services. The publication is intended for immunization programme managers, digital health teams, software developers and implementers involved in designing and deploying digital immunization systems. 4549.content: World Health Organization (2021). Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring: recommendations for a public health approach. World Health Organization. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring: recommendations for a public health approach AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-7-16 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240031593 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThese consolidated guidelines provide comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and programme monitoring across the continuum of HIV care. Updating the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines, this edition integrates guidance issued between 2016 and 2021 and reflects major advances in clinical practice, diagnostics and service delivery. Developed using the GRADE approach and informed by expert consultation and country experience, the guidelines aim to support countries in implementing high-quality, person-centred HIV services while advancing universal health coverage and progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. The publication addresses HIV testing strategies, prevention interventions, antiretroviral therapy, management of advanced HIV disease, care for common coinfections and comorbidities, differentiated service delivery, procurement, laboratory services and programme monitoring. It incorporates updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, dolutegravir-based treatment, rapid antiretroviral therapy initiation, viral load monitoring and community-based models of care. Intended primarily for national HIV programme managers, policy-makers and health-care providers, the guidelines also serve as a resource for technical partners, community organizations and people living with HIV to support the implementation of effective, equitable and people-centred HIV programmes. 4551.doc: Lignes directrices de l'OMS : recommandations sur les interventions numériques pour le renforcement des systèmes de s…
4551.title: Lignes directrices de l’OMS : recommandations sur les interventions numériques pour le renforcement des systèmes de s…
4551.content: Organisation mondiale de la Santé (2022). Lignes directrices de l'OMS : recommandations sur les interventions numériques pour le renforcement des systèmes de santé. Organisation mondiale de la Santé. TitleLignes directrices de l'OMS : recommandations sur les interventions numériques pour le renforcement des systèmes de santé AuthorsOrganisation mondiale de la Santé Issued2022-5-19 Typebook PublisherOrganisation mondiale de la Santé ISBN9789240046641 (version électronique) Languagefr AbstractCes lignes directrices de l’OMS présentent des recommandations fondées sur des données probantes concernant l’utilisation des interventions numériques pour renforcer les systèmes de santé et soutenir les progrès vers la couverture sanitaire universelle (CSU). Élaborées en réponse à l’adoption croissante des technologies numériques et à la résolution sur la santé numérique approuvée par l’Assemblée mondiale de la Santé en 2018, elles répondent à la nécessité d’évaluer rigoureusement les interventions de santé numérique afin que les investissements reposent sur des données probantes relatives à leurs avantages, leurs inconvénients, leur acceptabilité, leur faisabilité, leurs implications en matière de ressources et les considérations d’équité. Les lignes directrices soulignent que les technologies numériques doivent compléter, et non remplacer, les composantes fondamentales de systèmes de santé performants. Les recommandations portent sur un ensemble prioritaire d’interventions de santé numérique, principalement accessibles au moyen d’appareils mobiles, notamment la notification des naissances et des décès, la notification des stocks et la gestion des produits de base, la télémédecine entre client et prestataire ainsi qu’entre prestataires, la communication ciblée avec les clients, le suivi numérique de l’état de santé et des services reçus, les outils d’aide à la décision destinés aux professionnels de santé et l’apprentissage numérique. Les lignes directrices présentent également des considérations relatives à la mise en œuvre, recensent les principales lacunes en matière de recherche et visent à aider les ministères de la santé, les responsables des politiques de santé, les professionnels de santé, les partenaires du développement et les autres parties prenantes à prendre des décisions éclairées concernant l’adoption, le déploiement à grande échelle et l’institutionnalisation des interventions de santé numérique efficaces. 4555.content: World Health Organization (2013). WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention. World Health Organization. TitleWHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2013-11-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241548694 Languageen AbstractThese guidelines provide recommendations for screen-and-treat strategies to prevent cervical cancer by detecting and treating precancerous cervical lesions. The screen-and-treat approach bases treatment decisions on screening results, allowing treatment soon or ideally immediately after a positive test, rather than requiring histological confirmation. The guidelines compare strategies using human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), and cytology, linked to treatment with cryotherapy or loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP). They are intended primarily to support policy-makers, programme managers and other health professionals in selecting appropriate cervical cancer prevention strategies according to available resources and existing programmes. Nine recommendations are provided. HPV-based screening is generally preferred where feasible, while VIA is suggested where HPV testing is not feasible; cold knife conization is not recommended as part of a screen-and-treat strategy. Recommendations apply to all women, with specific guidance for women living with HIV. Decision-making and implementation flowcharts support adaptation of the recommended strategies to country and regional contexts. Issued2007-12-31 Typedocument Languagefr AbstractA cross-sectional survey was conducted among 112 HIV positive patients who had received antiretroviral therapy for > 3 months to assess the efficacy of treatment [viral load < 400 copies/mL]. The median age at enrolment was 36 years, 90% of patients were at the AIDS stage and median CD4 rate was 118/mm[3]. Patients received a combined treatment of 2 NRTI +1 NNRTI [51%], 3 NRTI [45%] and 2 NRTI+1 PI [4%]. Virological efficacy was seen in 74% of the patients, irrespective of the prescribed protocol and the initial clinical and immunological profile. Mean improvements measured were 20% on the Karnofsky index [KI], 2.1 kg/m[2] in body mass index and 82 cells/mm[3] in CD4. The prevalence of side effects was 84%. TitleNational health workforce accounts: a handbook AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-11-23 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240081291 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThe National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Handbook, second edition, provides the conceptual framework, standards, methods and indicators that support the systematic collection, analysis and use of health workforce data for evidence-informed policy-making and planning. Developed by the World Health Organization, the handbook supports implementation of the National Health Workforce Accounts as a country-led system to strengthen human resources for health information systems, improve data quality and availability, and monitor progress towards universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other global health objectives. It describes the rationale, principles and applications of NHWA at national, regional and global levels and outlines a modular approach to health workforce monitoring. The handbook presents guidance on implementation and reporting methods and defines a set of standardized indicators organized into four modules covering workforce stock and flows, education, finance and expenditures, and working conditions, governance and leadership. It explains indicator metadata, calculation methods, disaggregation requirements and reporting standards, and illustrates how NHWA data can be used to support workforce planning, policy development, retention strategies, equity analyses and monitoring of health workforce trends. The revised edition incorporates updated indicators, occupational classifications, tools and guidance to address evolving health workforce priorities and emerging global health challenges. TitlePandemic influenza preparedness framework: annual progress report, 1 January – 31 December 2022 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-8-4 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240076907 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThe Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework: annual progress report, 1 January–31 December 2022 presents technical and financial progress in implementing the PIP Framework, which aims to strengthen the sharing of influenza viruses with human pandemic potential and improve developing countries’ access to pandemic vaccines and other response supplies. The report assesses progress under the High-Level Implementation Plan II (2018–2023), including activities financed through the industry-funded Partnership Contribution mechanism. The report documents achievements and challenges in influenza laboratory capacity and surveillance, virus sharing, disease burden estimation, regulatory preparedness, risk communication and community engagement, deployment planning, and national pandemic preparedness. In 2022, 91% of Partnership Contribution recipient countries reported influenza data to FluNet, 48 countries had implemented regulatory approaches for pandemic influenza products, and 37 countries had developed or updated pandemic preparedness plans. It also presents progress in securing pandemic response products through benefit-sharing agreements, alongside financial allocations, expenditures and implementation milestones. 4583.doc: The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance
4583.title: The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance
4583.content: World Health Organization (2016). The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance. World Health Organization. TitleThe use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-8-8 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241511186 Languageen AbstractTuberculosis remains a major global public health challenge, and the WHO End TB Strategy emphasizes the need for early diagnosis and universal drug-susceptibility testing. This policy guidance presents evidence-based recommendations on the use of the commercial loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis. Developed following a systematic review of studies conducted since 2012 and assessment using the GRADE approach, the document evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of TB-LAMP as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy, as an add-on test after negative smear microscopy, and in comparison with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, while also assessing the frequency of indeterminate or invalid results. Based on the available evidence, WHO recommends that TB-LAMP may be used as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy in adults with signs and symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis and as a follow-on test when further investigation of smear-negative specimens is required. The guidance emphasizes that these conditional recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence, apply to sputum specimens from patients with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, and should not replace rapid molecular tests capable of detecting rifampicin resistance. It also highlights the limited evidence for use in people living with HIV, notes the extrapolation of recommendations to children, and provides implementation considerations and priorities for future research. Европейское региональное бюро Languageru AbstractОценка лечения и ухода в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом выполнена с учетом стратегии или концепции ВОЗ/ЮНЭЙДС «Лечение 2.0», где указаны пять приоритетных областей: оптимизация лекарственных схем, обеспечение доступа к диагностике в местах оказания помощи, снижение стоимости, адаптация систем оказания услуг и мобилизация сообществ или гражданского общества. TitleDigital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-11-4 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240093362 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides practical guidance for countries seeking to digitally transform primary health care through the development and implementation of person-centred point of service systems (PCPOSS). It addresses the transition from paper-based and fragmented digital systems towards integrated, interoperable digital solutions that support service delivery, continuity of care, data use and health system strengthening. Grounded in WHO recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening and aligned with the SMART Guidelines framework, the publication outlines approaches for translating clinical and public health guidance into digital systems while maintaining fidelity to normative standards. The publication presents a stepwise methodology covering assessment of digital readiness, identification of user requirements, workflow and business process mapping, system design and adaptation, software selection, testing, deployment and scale-up. It emphasizes person-centred care, interoperability, longitudinal health records, decision support and the use of standards-based digital architectures. Through practical tools, worksheets and implementation guidance, the publication supports policy-makers, programme managers, digital health practitioners and software developers in designing and optimizing digital systems that improve service quality, strengthen accountability and enable more effective, integrated and responsive primary health care services. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations: optimizing health worker roles to improve access to key maternal and newborn health interventions through task shifting AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2012-12-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241504843 Languageen AbstractThis WHO guidance provides evidence-based recommendations on optimizing health worker roles through task shifting to improve universal access to key maternal and newborn health interventions. Developed in response to health workforce shortages and inequities in access to care, it assesses whether specific interventions can be delivered safely and effectively by different health worker cadres, including lay health workers, auxiliary nurses and nurse midwives, nurses, midwives, associate clinicians, advanced level associate clinicians and non-specialist doctors. The guidance presents 119 recommendations, ranging from practices recommended for implementation to those requiring targeted monitoring and evaluation, rigorous research, or not recommended. It emphasizes that task shifting should complement efforts to increase skilled care and should aim to expand access while maintaining safety. Implementation should consider health-system capacity and local sociocultural, political and financial conditions, with recommendations adapted through national dialogue and considered as packages of interventions rather than in isolation.
