4893.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease
4893.title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease
4893.content: World Health Organization (2021). WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease. World Health Organization. TitleWHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-3-22 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240022676 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractTuberculosis remains one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent despite being largely preventable and curable. This updated WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on systematic screening for tuberculosis disease to support earlier diagnosis, timely initiation of treatment and reduced transmission. It revises the 2013 guidance in light of new evidence on the effectiveness of screening interventions and the performance of screening tools, using the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The document is intended to assist countries in planning and implementing screening strategies adapted to their epidemiological and health system contexts. The guideline presents recommendations for systematic screening in the general population and in groups at increased risk of tuberculosis, including people living with HIV, household contacts, prisoners, miners, migrants and other vulnerable populations. It also reviews the use of symptom screening, chest radiography, computer-aided detection software, C-reactive protein and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests as screening tools, together with guidance on monitoring, evaluation and implementation considerations. The publication identifies research gaps and is accompanied by an operational handbook providing practical guidance for applying the recommendations in national tuberculosis programmes. TitleWHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 1: prevention: tuberculosis preventive treatment AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2020-3-23 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240002906 Languageen AbstractThis operational handbook provides practical guidance for the programmatic management and scale-up of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in line with WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. The publication addresses the global burden of tuberculosis infection and the need to expand preventive interventions among populations at high risk of developing TB disease, particularly people living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients and other vulnerable groups. It supports implementation of commitments made at the United Nations High-Level Meeting on Tuberculosis and outlines strategies to strengthen national responses through integrated, people-centred approaches. The handbook describes the cascade of care for TPT, including identification of target populations, exclusion of active TB disease, testing for TB infection, treatment options, management of adverse events, adherence support, monitoring and evaluation, and ethical considerations. It also provides operational guidance for contact investigation, integration of preventive services with active TB case finding and HIV services, health system strengthening, and resource mobilization. Practical implementation tools, policy considerations and monitoring indicators are included to assist national TB programmes, policy-makers and health-care providers in adapting and scaling up TPT services in diverse epidemiological and health system settings. World Health Organization. TitleClassification of digital health interventions v1.0: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2018-3-14 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis publication presents version 1.0 of the World Health Organization’s Classification of Digital Health Interventions (DHIs), a taxonomy developed to provide a shared and standardized language for describing how digital and mobile technologies are used to address health system needs. Intended primarily for public health audiences, the framework supports communication among policymakers, programme planners, implementers, researchers, donors and technology specialists by defining digital health interventions as discrete digital functionalities linked to specific health objectives. The classification was developed to facilitate evidence synthesis, landscape analyses, planning processes and the articulation of digital solutions to identified health system challenges. The framework organizes digital health interventions into four primary groups according to the main user: clients, health-care providers, health system managers and data services. It links digital interventions to broader health system challenges and to system categories such as electronic medical records, logistics management information systems and telemedicine platforms. Developed through technical consultations, literature review and public feedback, the classification builds on existing mHealth and eHealth frameworks while providing a simplified and practical reference for health programmes. The document is intended to support the design, implementation, evaluation and interoperability of digital health initiatives and will be periodically updated to reflect emerging technologies and evolving practices in digital health. 4911.content: World Health Organization (2017). WHO recommendations on maternal health: guidelines approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations on maternal health: guidelines approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2017-10-17 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis publication compiles WHO recommendations on maternal health that have been approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee into a single, accessible reference for WHO staff, policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals. It brings together current WHO guidance covering the continuum of maternal care during pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period, with the dual purpose of facilitating access to recommendations and helping identify areas where further guideline updates are needed. The document indicates newly issued and updated recommendations since 2013 and provides, for each recommendation, its strength, the quality of supporting evidence and the corresponding source guideline. The compilation addresses interventions to promote, prevent and protect maternal and perinatal health, including antenatal care, prevention and management of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, peripartum infections, labour and childbirth, postpartum haemorrhage, postnatal care and health promotion, as well as the management of maternal conditions such as HIV infection, malaria and tuberculosis. Developed according to WHO’s guideline development process using the GRADE approach and structured evidence-to-decision frameworks, it presents evidence-informed recommendations intended to support consistent policy development, clinical practice and programme implementation across diverse health-care settings. 4929.doc: Directriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud
4929.title: Directriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud
4929.content: Organización Mundial de la Salud (2022). Directriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud. Organización Mundial de la Salud. TitleDirectriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud AuthorsOrganización Mundial de la Salud Issued2022-5-19 Typebook PublisherOrganización Mundial de la Salud ISBN9789240046993 (versión electrónica) Languagees AbstractEste documento presenta las recomendaciones de la OMS, basadas en la evidencia, sobre el uso de intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud y apoyar el avance hacia la cobertura sanitaria universal (CSU). Elaborada en respuesta a la creciente adopción de las tecnologías digitales y a la resolución sobre salud digital aprobada por la Asamblea Mundial de la Salud en 2018, la directriz aborda la necesidad de evaluar rigurosamente las intervenciones de salud digital para garantizar que las inversiones se fundamenten en evidencia sobre sus beneficios, riesgos, aceptabilidad, factibilidad, implicaciones en materia de recursos y consideraciones de equidad. Asimismo, subraya que las tecnologías digitales deben complementar, y no sustituir, los componentes fundamentales de unos sistemas de salud sólidos y eficaces. Las recomendaciones se centran en un conjunto priorizado de intervenciones de salud digital accesibles, como mínimo, mediante dispositivos móviles, entre ellas la notificación de nacimientos y defunciones, la notificación de existencias y la gestión de suministros, la telemedicina entre pacientes y profesionales y entre profesionales, la comunicación dirigida a los pacientes, el seguimiento digital del estado de salud y de los servicios recibidos, las herramientas de apoyo a la toma de decisiones para el personal sanitario y el aprendizaje digital para los trabajadores de la salud. La directriz también presenta consideraciones para la implementación, identifica las principales lagunas de investigación y proporciona orientación a los ministerios de salud, los responsables de salud pública, los asociados para el desarrollo y otras partes interesadas para adoptar, ampliar e institucionalizar intervenciones de salud digital eficaces sobre la base de la mejor evidencia disponible. 4933.title: Global hepatitis report 2026
4933.content: World Health Organization (2026). Global hepatitis report 2026. World Health Organization. TitleGlobal hepatitis report 2026 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-4-24 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240122383 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis report provides a comprehensive assessment of the global burden of viral hepatitis and progress towards the goal of eliminating hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. Drawing on data reported by Member States and modelled estimates, it analyses trends in incidence, prevalence and mortality associated with hepatitis B and C, covering the period from 2015 to 2024 based on the latest available data. It also situates these trends within the context of global commitments, strategies and targets. The publication reviews the coverage and impact of key interventions for prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including vaccination, infection prevention and control, harm reduction and access to antiviral therapies. It identifies persistent gaps in testing and treatment, marked regional disparities, and the need for accelerated scale-up of services, particularly in high-burden settings. The report concludes that progress towards the 2030 elimination targets remains off track despite the availability of effective interventions. Intended for policymakers, programme managers and public health stakeholders, it serves as an analytical and strategic resource to guide national and global responses to viral hepatitis. 4941.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
4941.content: World Health Organization (2016). WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-11-7 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241549912 Languageen AbstractThis guideline presents the World Health Organization’s evidence-based recommendations on routine antenatal care to support a positive pregnancy experience for pregnant women and adolescent girls. It aims to provide a comprehensive, consolidated framework for antenatal care that complements existing WHO guidance on the management of specific pregnancy-related complications. The recommendations promote a person-centred, rights-based approach that extends beyond the prevention of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality to enhance women’s physical, psychological and sociocultural well-being, support healthy pregnancies, and improve the quality and utilization of antenatal care. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals, the guideline informs the development of national policies, clinical protocols and service delivery models. Developed according to the WHO guideline development process, the document draws on systematic reviews and applies the GRADE and GRADE-CERQual approaches together with the DECIDE evidence-to-decision framework. It contains 49 recommendations covering nutritional interventions, maternal and fetal assessment, preventive measures, management of common physiological symptoms, and health system interventions to improve antenatal care utilization and quality. The guideline also introduces the 2016 WHO antenatal care model, recommending a minimum of eight contacts during pregnancy, and emphasizes implementation, dissemination and periodic updating as new evidence becomes available. TitleGuidelines for the prevention and control of infection with LAV/HTLV III AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Control Programme on AIDS Issued1986-12-31 Typedocument PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThese guidelines provide recommendations for preventing and controlling infection with LAV/HTLV-III, the retrovirus recognized at the time as the etiological agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Developed as part of the WHO AIDS Control Programme, they are intended primarily for public health authorities and health professionals, who are responsible for adapting the guidance to different populations and settings. The document summarizes available knowledge on transmission, clinical manifestations, laboratory detection, surveillance, notification and confidentiality, and case definitions for AIDS. The guidelines emphasize routine precautions to prevent exposure to blood and other potentially infectious body fluids, particularly among health care workers, laboratory personnel and providers of home and emergency care. They address prevention and management of needlestick, parenteral and mucous-membrane exposures, safe handling of specimens and contaminated equipment, and precautions for non-health-care workers. Guidance is also provided on disinfection, sterilization, and the safe processing of reusable needles, syringes and other instruments. 4949.doc: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006
4949.title: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006
4949.content: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia (2006). Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006. WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia. TitleEnumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006 AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia Issued2006-12-31 Typedocument PublisherWHO Regional Office for South-East Asia Languageen AbstractDescription: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes is essential for initiation of antiretroviral therapy for a person with HIV as well as for monitoring the response to treatment. The techniques for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes are evolving. The flow cytometry continues to be the gold standard of CD4 T lymphocytes enumeration in spite of the fact that the technology is expensive both in terms of initial investment in sophisticated equipment and running cost. The newer techniques may be economical to procure and maintain. The latter are particularly intended for countries with limited resources. WHO conducted a workshop to orient the nationals about these technologies and integration of a quality system into routine testing, at Siriraj Hospital Bangkok. The report describes the status of CD4 testing in these countries. While Indonesia, India and Thailand have developed a good infrastructure for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka have made a beginning in this direction. The workshop focussed on principles of various techniques and imparted a hands-on training for performing the same. The issues regarding selection of technology, procurement of equipment and their maintenance; ensuring continuous supply and economical use of reagents and biosafety in laboratory were discussed and have been presented in this Report. references/10665-97885.sec-013.8.json export: BibTeX · RIS · CSL-JSON · DC XML | S-12 (Sassani et al., 1991) 3.2 Immune responses to revaccination Studies have examined presence of antibodies prior to and following the second dose of mumps vaccine. In a prospective study, <1% of subjects were seronegative before a second dose of mumps vaccine and, following the second dose, IgM was detectable in only 2% of individuals, suggesting that most vaccine recipients had mounted a secondary immune response to revaccination (LeBaron et al., 2009). Although up to 30% of individuals were reported to be seronegative prior to revaccination in other studies, 75% to 97% seroconverted following the second dose of mumps vaccine. 10665-97885.sec-013.9 · extracted · source: references/10665-97885.sec-013.9.json export: BibTeX · RIS · CSL-JSON · DC XML | There was no assessment to determine if seronegativity was due to primary vaccine failure, or having antibody below the level of test detection (Broliden et al., 1998; Gothefors et al., 2001). 10665-97885.sec-013.10 · extracted · source: references/10665-97885.sec-013.10.json export: BibTeX · RIS · CSL-JSON · DC XML | Among individuals with neutralizing antibodies prior to receipt of a second dose, an increase in antibody levels generally occurred following revaccination. 5615.doc: There are currently few data on HSV2 prevalence from many parts of the world, including Asia, South America and many …
5615.title: There are currently few data on HSV2 prevalence from many parts of the world, including Asia, South America and many …
5615.content: There are currently few data on HSV2 prevalence from many parts of the world, including Asia, South America and many parts of Africa. HSV2 incidence data are also scarce [Kamali et al., 1999; McFarland et al., 1999; Hayes et al., 2001]. Prevalence and incidence data are necessary: i) to estimate population attributable fractions (PAFs) for HIV; ii) as background data to inform future intervention studies, such as HSV2 4. EPIDEMIOLOGY AND NATURAL HISTORY OF HSV2 treatment and vaccine trials; iii) to evaluate the need for changes in syndromic management of GUD due to presence of genital herpes; and iv) to evaluate the need for regular HSV2 seroprevalence surveys. EPIDEMIOLOGY AND NATURAL HISTORY OF HSV2 treatment and vaccine trials; iii) to evaluate the need for changes in syndromic management of GUD due to presence of genital herpes; and iv) to evaluate the need for regular HSV2 seroprevalence surveys. 5959.doc: S-12 (Sassani et al., 1991) 3.2 Immune responses to revaccination Studies have examined presence of antibodies prior …
5959.title: S-12 (Sassani et al., 1991) 3.2 Immune responses to revaccination Studies have examined presence of antibodies prior …
5959.content: S-12 (Sassani et al., 1991) 3.2 Immune responses to revaccination Studies have examined presence of antibodies prior to and following the second dose of mumps vaccine. In a prospective study, <1% of subjects were seronegative before a second dose of mumps vaccine and, following the second dose, IgM was detectable in only 2% of individuals, suggesting that most vaccine recipients had mounted a secondary immune response to revaccination (LeBaron et al., 2009). Although up to 30% of individuals were reported to be seronegative prior to revaccination in other studies, 75% to 97% seroconverted following the second dose of mumps vaccine. 14071.doc: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen…
14071.title: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen…
14071.content: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen the Greek letter representing its type, for example IFN-a for alpha interferons. Non-allelic variants can be indicated by an arabic number or capital letter (sometimes subscripted) attached to the Greek letter. The prefixes “Hu” and “Mu” may be used to represent “human” and “murine” respectively. For example: MulFN-y HulFN-B — HulFN-c4. Interferon nomenclature. Journal of immunology, 1980, 125:2353. 14791.doc: Isotopic labelling The symbol for the isotope introduced is placed in square brackets directly attached to the part o…
14791.title: Isotopic labelling The symbol for the isotope introduced is placed in square brackets directly attached to the part o…
14791.content: Isotopic labelling The symbol for the isotope introduced is placed in square brackets directly attached to the part of the name to which it refers (e.g. sodium ('4C]formate); appropriate arabic numerals and prefixes are added as necessary (e.g. L-[2-C]leucine). For simple molecules, chemical formulae may be used (e.g. 4#CO,). Square brackets should not be used when the isotopic symbol is attached to a word that is not a chemical name (e.g. “!*C-labelled”). Terms such as “'![-labelled albumin” should not be contracted to [3!T]albumin since native albumin does not contain iodine. 15175.content: Oncogenes Oncogenes are usually designated by three-letter italic terms, often taken from the names of the viruses with which the genes are WHO Editorial Style Manual associated. A roman prefix may be added: “v-” for viral, “N-” for nuclear and “c-” for the gene’s cellular counterpart (proto-oncogene). Other prefixes and various suffixes are common. For example: Ha-ras-1 N-ras v-erb B yes c-abl fes/fps. 16241.title: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen…
16241.content: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen the Greek letter representing its type, for example IFN-a for alpha interferons. Non-allelic variants can be indicated by an arabic number or capital letter (sometimes subscripted) attached to the Greek letter. The prefixes “Hu” and “Mu” may be used to represent “human” and “murine” respectively. For example: MulFN-y HulFN-B — HulFN-c4. Interferon nomenclature. Journal of immunology, 1980, 125:2353. 16425.doc: Genital herpes can also be due to HSV1 infection, and a study in Scotland found that 40% of genital herpes was due to…
16425.title: Genital herpes can also be due to HSV1 infection, and a study in Scotland found that 40% of genital herpes was due to…
16425.content: Genital herpes can also be due to HSV1 infection, and a study in Scotland found that 40% of genital herpes was due to HSV1 in 1991 [Ross et al., 1993]. Both HSV1 and HSV2 are able to infect and reactivate in the same anatomic area, although the natural history of these infections is markedly different, with HSV2 recurring more frequently than HSV1, so most clinical reactivations are likely to be due to HSV2 [Sucato et al., 1998]. In developing countries, the proportion of genital herpes caused by HSV1 is unknown, although assumed to be low. 17041.title: Genetics Genes and chromosomes The International Committee on Standardizing Human Gene No-menclature has developed a …
17041.content: Genetics Genes and chromosomes The International Committee on Standardizing Human Gene No-menclature has developed a system knownas the International System. for Human Gene Nomenclature, but this is not universally accepted. Human genes are generally denoted by italicized symbols composed of capital letters, sometimes with the addition of an arabic numeral (e.g. CF, G6PD). Lower-case letters are commonly still used in blood-group symbols (e.g. Fy, Rh). Phenotype symbols are set in roman type (e.g. ADA 1). 17363.title: CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; NPA= nasopharyngeal aspirate. Methodological quality Studies evaluating Xpert Ultra on spu…
17363.content: CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; NPA= nasopharyngeal aspirate. Methodological quality Studies evaluating Xpert Ultra on sputum specimens (15 studies) In the patient selection domain, for MRS, we judged the risk of bias as low for most studies (13/15, 86.7%) and high for two studies (2/15, 13.3%) because in one study participants with definitive tuberculosis were excluded (Liu 2021) and in the other, the sampling method was retrospective and by convenience (Enimil 2022). Regarding applicability, we judged low concern for most studies (12/15, 80%). We judged high concern for two studies (2/15, 13.3%) because participants were enrolled exclusively as inpatients in tertiary care centers. We judged unclear concern for one study (1/15, 6.7%) because the setting was undefined. Issued2022 Typedocument As printedCSF = cerebrospinal fluid; NPA= nasopharyngeal aspirate. 18691.content: Nahmias et al, 1990 1 (f) females; (m) males 2 Age-weighted sample: younger age-groups were over-represented HSV2 AS A MARKER FOR SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR As HSV2 is more readily transmitted sexually than HIV, HSV2 serology may be a useful marker for changes in sexual behaviour in HIV intervention studies. However, the persistent nature of the infection implies that seroprevalence may not be a sensitive marker of behaviour change, although it will be more discriminating at the lower prevalences seen in younger age groups [Obasi et al., 1999]. HSV2 seroincidence would be a preferable marker of behaviour change, especially in countries in sub-Saharan Africa where there is high incidence among young people. 19432.title: Términos redactados
19432.content: Bootstrap terms . | término | etiquetas alternativas | definición | . | Nodo | — | Un archivo, o una parte de un archivo direccionable mediante un fragmento de IRI, nombrado por un IRI. | . | Referencia | — | La designación que un Nodo hace de otro Nodo por su IRI. | . | Esquema de nodo | — | Un esquema contra el que se puede validar un Nodo: un JSON Schema, o un esquema externo publicado como el de BPMN. | . | Tipo de nodo | — | Un nombre emparejado con un Esquema de nodo. | . | Subtipo | — | Un Tipo de nodo cuyo Esquema de nodo exige todo lo que exige el de otro Tipo de nodo, de modo que todo Nodo que lo satisface satisface también el otro. | . | Instancia de nodo | — | Un Nodo que nombra su Tipo de nodo, en $schema o en el preámbulo, y satisface el Esquema de nodo de ese tipo. | . | Tipo de grafo | — | Un conjunto con nombre de Tipos de nodo. | . | Declaración | — | Un documento JSON, <name>.json, que da un nombre y enumera entradas de directorio y entradas de archivo. | . | Extensión | — | Un campo de una Declaración, o de una de sus entradas, que no se define aquí. Un lector que no reconoce el campo lo ignora, y el resto de la Declaración conserva su significado. | . | Subgrafo | — | Una entrada de directorio de una Declaración: un id, un directorio y los Tipos de grafo a los que pertenecen los tipos de sus Instancias de nodo. | . | Recurso | — | Una entrada de archivo de una Declaración: un archivo sobre el propio repositorio, cuyo campo role indica para qué sirve. | . | Grafo de conocimiento | — | Los Esquemas de nodo, las Instancias de nodo y los Recursos que enumera una Declaración, en una versión dada del repositorio. Publicadas como JSON-LD, las afirmaciones de las Instancias de nodo de cada Subgrafo forman un grafo con nombre. | . | Dependencia | — | Una entrada needs de una Declaración que nombra otro Grafo de conocimiento. Las Referencias pueden apuntar desde las Instancias de nodo de este grafo hacia el nombrado, nunca en sentido inverso. | . | Contenido | — | Instancias de nodo que describen el objeto de un Grafo de conocimiento, como registros, documentos, catálogos y sus términos, y no cómo trabajar con él. | . | Tarea | — | Una unidad de trabajo, expresada por lo que necesita para comenzar y lo que produce. | . | Actor | — | Una persona, un agente o un programa que puede llevar a cabo Tareas. | . | Habilidad | — | A Node Instance stating a responsibility an Actor carries out to complete a Task: as natural-language instructions to follow, as a contract to be tested against, or both. (sin traducir) | . | Rol | — | Una Instancia de nodo que nombra un papel que un Actor asume para llevar a cabo Tareas y enumera las Habilidades que ese papel necesita. | . | Nodo de proceso | — | Un nodo de flujo BPMN: una actividad (una tarea o una actividad de llamada), una compuerta o un evento. | . | Flujo de secuencia | — | Una conexión dirigida en un proceso BPMN de un Nodo de proceso al siguiente. | . | Proceso | — | Una Instancia de nodo que contiene un proceso BPMN que coordina Tareas: sus Nodos de proceso, unidos por Flujos de secuencia, se sitúan en carriles que nombran cada uno un Rol. | . | Arnés | — | Un Grafo de conocimiento cuyos Subgrafos contienen Habilidades, Roles o Procesos: aquello que un Actor usa para trabajar con un Grafo de conocimiento, incluido él mismo. | . Todos los demás términos redactados, de la A a la Z . Folio Assistant platform terms (cat-harness) . | término | etiquetas alternativas | definición | . | arnés asociado | — | Un arnés que este conoce por nombre, sitio y repositorio, y que nunca carga, construye ni copia. 19453.title: computable adjudication and agentic test harness
19453.content: Computable adjudication and agentic test harness. Also written: caaat-harness, ca&at-harness, .c&at-harness, c@t-harness . Please be introduced to a cat who acquires things, for whatever purpose — maybe somebody knows. Scope: the platform — skills, schemas, processes, the MCP server and the pipeline. Not what a folio IS (that is folio-assist-core), and not any folio’s own content, which lives in its own repository. | cat-harness, in the source Its own repository since the cutover; the in-tree copy is archived in folio-assistant’s fsh-guts. | RTFM — the cat-harness docs The agent–user interaction model, and what this harness is for. | The work plan is where you say what you are doing Claim a bean before you work, so a sibling session does not pick up the same item. | Make your first folio This repository is the platform; your content lives in its own. | Know which kind of thing you are writing A document is structured prose; a paper adds the block kinds whose assertion is a formal claim. | The documentation you will never read All of it. The honest expectation is that you arrive from a search engine when something breaks. | .

19454.title: What a folio is
19454.content: The knowledge graph is four sub-graphs, and a layer declares which of them it holds. Content is what somebody authors and a reader reads — this layer’s subject. Skills are the instructions an agent follows to do the work. Processes are the BPMN diagrams that say who does what, in which order, and where the gates are — they are executable, not illustrations. Tools are what an agent can call. Getting anything in is acquisition: unstructured and semi-structured sources arrive through uploads/ or through the conversation, and are ingested into library/. It is a step rather than a graph typology of its own — there is no fifth directory to look for. Scope: the content model — what a folio IS. Not the skills and tools that operate on it, and not any particular folio’s chapters. | Content A document is structured prose; a paper adds the block kinds whose assertion is a formal claim. | Skills Every skill and role, and how they fit together. | Processes The BPMN diagrams, which are the source of truth rather than a picture of it. | Tools What an agent can call, served over MCP. | Acquisition How a source gets from uploads/ into library/. | RTFM — folio-assist-core Its scope, in and out, and why it declares no directories yet. | .

19463.doc: Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph
19463.title: Steps
19463.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Write dublin-core.jsonld (the record of truth)Task_Dublin | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | One standalone Dublin Core record per folder. dcterms is already this corpus’s JSON-LD vocabulary, so this extends a live context rather than introducing one. | . | Write manifest.jsonld referencing itTask_Manifest | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Write manifest.jsonld for the folder: its @id, @type folio:SourceDocument, what it contains and its provenance, referencing the standalone dublin-core.jsonld as the record of truth rather than copying its fields. | . | Record assets[] — local path or remote URLTask_Assets | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | kind / role / url-or-path / checksum / retrieved. A SIBLING of library:, never inside it: LibraryRef is regenerated from the tree, so an authored URL placed there is dropped on the next sync. | . | Bind the folder to its bibliography slugTask_Bind | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Bind the folder name to the document’s bibliography slug, so library/<bib-slug>/ and its citation key are the same string: a citation resolves to a directory without a lookup table between them. | . | Read glossary into candidate termsTask_Glossary | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | glossary-terms | The source’s glossary and abbreviations sections become candidate terms of a folio-glossary/v1 scheme with the Tool glossary-from-source, verbatim, each with source file#line, and an acronym as the notation of the term it expands. Terms a person owns are never changed, and only a person moves a term to authored. A source with no such section skips this step with nothing written. | . | Extract reference listsTask_References | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | Each reference list of the source (a References, Bibliography or Further reading section, in any of the six UN languages) becomes folio-reference/v1 nodes with the Tool references-extract: one node per cited work, provenance extracted, derivedFrom the section it was read from, and printed the entry exactly as the source prints it. Only fields read without guessing are set (address, DOI, ISBN, year, access date); a cited IRIS item the library holds gets heldAt. The nodes are the document’s own bibliography on the bibliography page. A source with no reference list skips this step with nothing written. | . | Link L1 nodes into the corpus graphTask_Link | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Anything in library/ is L1 source content. A knowledge-graph reference from any artefact – paper, L2, L3 – resolves to it through library/. | .

19468.title: Steps

Mechanical and cheap; the checksum is what makes a remote asset verifiable. | . | Narrative description per image, localizedTask_Image | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Applies equally to an image EXTRACTED FROM A PDF (Task_FiguresTables), not only to an uploaded one. An agent opens every image and vector render and records a verdict in the library’s image-verdicts.json: role (figure, logo or decorative), the reason, and a draft description in English plus ar, zh, es, fr and ru, which the apply-image-verdicts.ts arm lays over images.json on every ingest. Images judged figure are kept as WebP, quality 80, at most 1600 px; logos, decorative fragments and page scans are not. Every description stays a draft until a person confirms it with bun run cat narratives. Method: skill document-intake, “Figures and captioned tables: describe, keep, transcribe”. | . | Transcribe and translate audioTask_Audio | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | No Tool yet; the method, and the choice of recogniser, is skill audio-transcription. | . | Sheet names, headers, shape, narrativeTask_Tabular | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Tools tabular-csv and tabular-xlsx, as CSVW (skill tabular-metadata). CSV and spreadsheet: tabs, column and row headers, sizes, and what the dataset is about. | . | Extract figures and tablesTask_FiguresTables | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | The pdf-images.py, pdf-vector-labels.py and pdf-vector-figures.py arms extract the raster images and the figures drawn as vectors (grouped and rendered). For every table the document’s structure declares, an agent reads the rendered page, checks cell text against the text layer, and writes tables/<label>.csv plus tables.csvw.json (folio-tabular-csvw/v1), with a draft description in the six UN languages; pdf-tables.py’s grid is a cross-check, not the answer. Owner, 2026-11-11 (who-iris): “actually extract the figures” and “any tables too”. 19488.title: Every initialization step, as the declarations name them
19488.content: Skill initialization-steps: Walk every initialization step the declarations name (the layer’s own and each one it needs), check each before doing anything, do what can be done, ask for what only a person can do, and report every step as done, not done, could not determine, or stated. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are making sure a harness’s initialization is complete: right after installing it (initialize-harness calls complete-initialization), or because you were dispatched to do exactly this with nothing but the diagram and the repository. Either way the steps are the same, and they are not listed in this file. They are named by the declarations.

19489.title: Where the steps come from
19489.content: Read <name>.json at the root, then each name in its needs, from a sibling checkout at ../<name>/<name>.json. Each step below names the declaration that names it, so a reader can see why it is there. | step | named by | done when | . | declaration | the file itself | <name>.json parses and its name is its file name | . | needs:<name> | needs | the dependency is beside it, and its declaration parses | . | instructions:<name> | FR-4 | stated: <name>/docs/bootstrap/initialization.md was read and followed | . | schemas:staged | each $id / @id under iriBase (FR-11) | the site build stages every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document at its IRI | . | schemas:published | the same IRIs (FR-11) | every one of those IRIs answers | . | directory:<id> | directories[] | the declared path exists | . | asset:<id> | assets[] | the declared file exists | . | readme | FR-8 | the root has a README.md | . | readme-sections | the README’s own markers | every section the README opts into is current | . | site:workflow | repository | a workflow commits the rendered site onto gh-pages | . | site:branch | repository | a gh-pages branch exists — it must, before Pages can be switched on | . | site:enabled | repository | Pages is on, serving gh-pages | . | site:live | iriBase, else the Pages address | the address answers | . The two schemas: steps are the primary ones. They are checked first once the declarations are read, and the report leads with them: publish-documents. A harness above bootstrap names more steps the same way. A work-plan store it declares as a directory is a directory: step, and a harness’s own set-up instructions are its instructions: step. Bootstrap does not need to know which harness declares what. The site steps are in publish-site.

19490.title: Four states, not two
19490.content: . | done: checked, and it holds. | not done: checked, and it does not. Say exactly what to do next. | could not determine: the check could not run (no forge CLI, no network). Never reported as done. A check that could not look is not a pass. | stated: the declarations name it but nothing can observe it (reading and following a harness’s instructions). Follow it, say you did, and leave it stated. | .

19491.title: Idempotent by construction
19491.content: Check before doing, every time. A done step is left alone, so running the process twice changes nothing the second time, and an interrupted run is resumed by running it again. Performing is not the same as done: after you do a step, check it again, and only the check says done. Replace nothing. A step that would overwrite what somebody wrote (an existing README, a Pages site built from a branch, a declaration that disagrees with the directories on disk) is a step for the person. Ask through human-agent-discussion, with the exact step written out. Do not create an empty declared directory to make its step pass. Git does not track an empty directory, so the check would pass on your machine and fail on every clone. Put its first file in it, or ask whether the entry should go.

19492.title: Where tools are available
19492.content: A toolset may perform the checks for you — for example https://github.com/litlfred/bootstrap-tools, whose init command reads the same declarations, does what a tool can (regenerating README sections; switching Pages on when an authenticated gh is present), and prints each step in these four states with what to do next: . bun run scripts/init.ts --root ../<instance> # from a toolset checkout beside it bun run scripts/init.ts --root ../<instance> --dry-run # check only . Where no tools are available, do the same by reading files. The diagram is the same either way, and so is the report.

19493.title: The report
19493.content: One report through log-message, led by the primary step’s state (the JSON Schemas and JSON-LD at their IRIs): then every step, the declaration that named it, its state, what was seen, and for anything not done, what to do and who does it. End with the counts (done, not done, could not determine, stated). An initialization that finished with steps open says which. It is not hidden behind “installed”.
