19833.title: Adopting a methodology, and choosing between them
19833.content: Skill methodology-adoption: How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Options analysis, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, SWOT situation analysis, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Record agent step, Review-log watch, IRIS CDN initial load . A methodology is somebody else’s work, adopted whole. It is not a house process with a citation bolted on. The graph carries them as a distinct kind so that adopting one, replacing one and removing one are all ordinary operations. Methodologies are parallel ways of achieving the same process, chosen by context; each is formalised on its own and kept independent, so that other skills can incorporate it as a sub-graph.

19834.title: Parallel, not composable
19834.content: Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them. A composite — this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter — is a house method that cites nobody, and it inherits none of their authority while claiming all of it. So: pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.

19835.title: Choosing which applies
19835.content: First: is this a judgement, or a process? . Ask before the ladder. The ladder below is about how to decide something; a request for a change is not yet a decision but work needing agreed requirements before anything is built. Sent down the ladder, it lands on the catch-all rung and produces an options analysis for a question nobody has framed yet. Is somebody asking for a change, such that requirements have to be agreed before it is built? . If yes, the question is who is asking, and does the answer depend on what a folio says? . | A change to the platform’s own capability — a tool, a schema, a pipeline, a skill, a gate — raised by somebody building the tooling, whose answer does not depend on any folio’s subject matter → the software-development process methodology. | Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, tied to a folio’s domain → the stakeholder requirements methodology. | . Both answer request → agreed requirements, so they are parallel and must not be blended — the refusal below applies to this pair first and hardest. Which is which is stated in each one’s applies-when, not here, for the reason in §”Why this skill does not name them”. If no — the change is agreed and the question is how to decide something within it — continue to the ladder. Then the ladder . Ask in this order. The first yes decides. | Do the criteria recur, with the same inputs having to produce the same answer? → the computable methodology. A one-off tabled as if it recurs asserts a repeatability it does not have. | Is the question the certainty of a body of evidence behind a recommendation? → the evidence-grading methodology. Note this is about evidence, not about a design choice that happens to be uncertain. | Is the context a work item recording a decision? → the decision-record methodology. It constrains the record, not the method, so it composes with (1) or (4) rather than competing. | Otherwise — a one-off choice among candidate options → the decision-analysis methodology. | . If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence. Say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit: either is how a house method gets in. Why this skill does not name them . Naming each methodology here would couple this skill to the set, and the set is meant to be extractable: a methodology can be lifted out, or replaced, without a prose edit here. So the declared set is the contents of the methodology graph, read from the layer’s declaration. Ask for it; do not remember it.

19836.title: Node, skill, or both?
19836.content: An adopted methodology can produce up to two artefacts: . | you are writing | it is a node in the methodology graph | it is a skill | . | what the method IS — its vocabulary, its constraints, what it refuses | ✅ | ❌ | . | how to PERFORM it here — the extension element, the gate, the procedure | ❌ | ✅ | . | a house process with no external origin | ❌ | ✅ — and do not dress it as an adoption | . Most adoptions produce both, and the split is the same every time: the node is the method, the skill is this platform’s application of it. The skill names the node and does not restate it, because two files carrying one definition is two copies free to drift. Three worked cases: . | raci — both. The four letters and the one-Accountable rule are the method (node); reading R from the BPMN lane, the cat-harness.processes:raci element and check:raci are this platform’s application (skill). | crdm — both (methodologies/crdm.md). PHII’s three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, swimlane Task Flow Diagrams, and PATH’s activity-linked requirement structure are the external method (node, backed by library/phii-2023-crdm, library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, and library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm); agentic facilitation, 7-dimension code impact analysis, work-item decomposition, and pull-request merge sign-off are this platform’s adaptation (crdm-requirements-workflow and crdm-requirements-template). | swot — both. | . A methodology in use with no node is invisible to the graph: check:methodology-evidence and every other reader of the methodology graph count nodes, not skills.

19837.title: Adopting a new one — the ingestion process
19837.content: . | Establish it is external and named. A methodology has an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body. If it has none, it is a house process — write it as a skill and do not dress it as an adoption. | Render it faithfully, and say where the rendering stops. The file carries what the method says, not a summary of what we liked. Where this platform adopts part of a method and refuses part, both halves are stated with the reason — a silent omission misrepresents the standard. | Declare its applicability. applies-when in the front matter, phrased so the selection question above can reach it, and saying what it is not for. | Place it by ownership, not by convenience. A domain-neutral method belongs to the harness; a domain method belongs to the repo that owns the domain. The separation plan decides, and the placement must make extraction literal — the directory lifts out, its declaration entry goes with it, and nothing else moves. | Declare the directory. A methodology outside a declared directory is invisible to every tool that reads the graph. | State its refusals. The part of a method a platform must not do is as load-bearing as the part it follows, and it is the part a later agent will breach first. | Ingest the source and cite it as evidence. origin names the work; evidence: library/<bib-slug> points at a copy a reader can open from this checkout. Use literature-search to find it and library-ingestion to bring it in. Where the source cannot be fetched, that is an outcome to report — a located-but-unreachable document, never a missing one — and the node keeps its origin with no evidence until somebody closes the gap. | .

19838.title: Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools
19838.content: A source that presents a method through an implementation is presenting two things, and only one of them is the methodology. Render the method first, then decide which tools — existing or to be added — this platform should use to perform it. A node that adopted the source’s tool stack would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method, and it could never be falsified: the tools would work and the method would never be examined. hybrid-llm-deterministic is the worked case. Its source demonstrates the method in one tool with one model and one expression language; the node renders the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards and the bounded-truncation technique, and §”Where this rendering stops” names every tool it declined to adopt and why. The method survives replacing all of them, which is the test of whether you extracted a method at all. Ask it as: what would still be true if they had built it differently? What survives is the methodology. What does not is their engineering, and it belongs in the skill if anywhere — where this platform’s own tool choices already live. And say what the source does NOT establish. A demonstration is not an evaluation. Where a paper shows an approach working once, with no baseline and no measurement, the node records that no performance claim rests on it. Doing otherwise manufactures a finding the authors did not make — the same failure as §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”, arriving through a citation instead.

19839.title: An origin nobody can open is not evidence
19839.content: A methodology’s justification is being somebody else’s named, external work, so its origin must resolve to a source a reader can open. bun run cat check:methodology-evidence is the axis that makes this visible, and test/results/methodology-evidence.qa-results.json is where it is recorded. It reports and does not gate on a missing source: whether a methodology whose source nobody can open may still be used is the owner’s call, and a gate failing on the whole corpus at once would be switched off. It does fail on front matter that does not validate, and on an evidence pointing at a bib-slug no library holds, because a citation that claims to resolve and does not is worse than none. The evidence is an input to SELECTION, not only to adoption. options-analysis.bpmn’s A_CheckEvidence reads it before the chosen methodology is applied. Adoption happens once; selection happens at every decision, and a source can stop being reachable in between. A contested origin is recorded as contested. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: the usual attribution is repeated everywhere and its own source says no academic reference supports it, so the node declines to name an inventor: flattening that into a fact would carry the authority of a citation while resting on nothing.

19840.title: Refusals
19840.content: . | Never blend two methodologies into one procedure. Parallel means parallel. | Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A citation with no rendered method is an appeal to authority that no reader can check. | Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform adopts the structure and refuses the arithmetic: a total reads as a measurement, and the weights were invented. This is the same rule as never quoting a count from prose as though it were evidence. | Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. Whichever methodology was used, the alternatives and why they lost are part of the output — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted. | Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched. Read the source, or say you read it through another and mark each attribution second-hand. See literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. | .

19848.title: Remote-mount a dependency
19848.content: Process_MountDependency · strict · 6 step(s) . Laying a harness — and every layer it needs — down from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories, with a lock that says exactly what arrived. You are in this process whenever a folio or harness needs a layer it does not hold: a downstream folio built on a content layer above this harness, a separated layer whose foundation lives elsewhere. The downstream names the harness, its repository and a 40-character pin as a source.remote layer in its root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration, never both); everything else is read from the harness’s own declaration at that pin. Every layer reached ends in one of three states — mounted, missing, could-not-determine — and the third is never reported as the first. The skill is remote-mount. i i i i i i

19854.title: Mount a declared subgraph

A remote subgraph is another repository’s tree at a pinned commit, laid down by Process_MountDependency and read-only here. 19860.title: Multi-locale translation
19860.content: Process_MultiLocaleTranslation · advisory · 13 step(s) . Translate one or more layers into several locales at once, as a team: one source-language lead, one translator per locale, an untainted round trip, and the owner’s merge window. The result is unofficial, on main, and kept current by a watcher. You are in this process when more than one locale is being produced from the same source at the same time. translation-workflow is the machine half for one catalogue and human-translation-workflow is the path to an official, signed-off translation; this process is the team around them. It extracts ONCE: every locale starts from the same templates, merged to main in one source PR before any locale begins, and no translator re-extracts. Each locale then lands as its own PR to main, never into the source branch, and a source PR’s branch receives nothing after it merges. Two things are never done in a translation: fixing the source (a source-text error is reported as one issue to the lead), and editing a FHIR resource inline (terms go into one CodeSystem supplement per locale). Officiality is not decided here: every catalogue is written unofficial, and a person makes it official through human-translation-workflow. i i i i i i i i i i i i i

19861.title: How it connects
19861.content: . | Called by: Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route | Calls: Translation round trip (untainted) | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

19862.title: Lanes — who acts
19862.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Owner | user | Decides which layers and locales are translated, and when locale PRs may be merged. The merge window set here binds the lead’s merge step and the refresh watcher alike. Official sign-off is also this person’s, and is a separate process. | . | Source-language lead | translation-source-lead | The one party that touches the source. It extracts every template once, merges that source PR first, collects source-text errors into one issue, validates and merges each locale PR inside the owner’s window, and keeps the watcher that runs translation-refresh. | . | Locale translator (one per locale) | locale-translator | One lane for every locale: each step here runs once per locale, in parallel, and each locale’s work is its own branch and its own PR. A translator starts from the merged templates, never from its own extraction, and reports a source error rather than translating around it. | .

19863.title: Steps
19863.content: Every one of the 13 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Set locales, scope and merge windowTask_ML_Scope | Owner | — | Which layers, which locales, which assets (pages, diagrams, glossary, FHIR terms), and the window in which locale PRs may be merged. | . | Extract every template onceTask_ML_Extract | Source-language lead | shared step GT_ExtractPottranslation-manager | Scan the source content and write the translatable strings to .pot files at the configured granularity: segment prose by paragraph, shield what must not be translated (math, code, labels, Lean companions) as placeholders, normalise whitespace, and extract metadata such as titles, alt text and captions. Tool: the translation_extract MCP tool.Once, for every locale: the .pot templates for the pages, the diagrams (translate-bpmn --extract) and the glossary schemes, each by the layer’s own extractor. A locale that would need a different template is a defect in the extraction, not a reason to extract again. | . | Merge the one source PR to mainTask_ML_SourcePR | Source-language lead | translation-manager | All the templates in one PR to main, merged before any locale starts, so every translator branches from the same main. Once it has merged, its branch receives nothing more: a later fix to the source is a new PR. | . | Schedule the refresh watcherTask_ML_Watcher | Source-language lead | translation-refresh | Schedule a fresh session that follows translation-refresh on each layer, so a template that moves after today is caught by its check failing, not by a reader. | . | Translate one localeTask_ML_Translate | Locale translator (one per locale) | translation-manager | From the merged templates, with the locale term base: translations/<locale>/**.po, a translation-node manifest beside each (official: false, generatedBy: "agent"; no status.json), and the FHIR terms as CodeSystem supplements, all in one file for the locale rather than edits inside the resources. | . | File the source errors as one issueTask_ML_SourceIssue | Source-language lead | translation-manager | One issue for every source-text error the translators found, each with its location and the reading the translator took. Never fixed in a translation: a fix to the source is a source PR, and the next refresh carries it to every locale. | . | Run the deterministic gatesTask_ML_Gates | Locale translator (one per locale) | translation-manager | Template currency, catalogue coverage, placeholder, tag and URL preservation, officiality, kg:locale, and the locale’s supplements compiling with no SUSHI error and passing their structural checks. | . | Untainted round trip on a sampleCall_ML_RoundTrip | Locale translator (one per locale) | calls Translation round trip (untainted) | The sample: every diagram label, the personas and scenarios, and a seeded random fraction of the rest. | . | Check glossary consistencyTask_ML_Glossary | Locale translator (one per locale) | translation-manager | translation:glossary:check, against the layered term base: the normative reference glossaries first, then each layer in the order the index config lists it, the layer’s own glossary last and never overriding. Never into the source branch. | . | Fix each drift on the PRTask_ML_FixDrift | Locale translator (one per locale) | translation-manager | Correct each string the adjudicator ruled drift, on the locale PR, and note the fix beside the ruling in the QA report. | . | Validate and merge in the windowTask_ML_Merge | Source-language lead | translation-manager | Read each locale’s QA report, confirm the PR is green, and merge it inside the owner’s merge window. 19866.title: normative-statements
19866.content: Named by: Authoring a document . Carry a recommendation, requirement or rule in a document folio — the thing an L1 health-policy guidance note, a standard, or a terms-of-reference document exists to state.

19867.title: The problem this addresses
19867.content: A normative statement is the block readers cite, implementers trace to, and reviewers sign off individually, so it needs a label, a stable identity and a place in the dependency graph. It is not a theorem: nothing proves it, and its authority is the issuing body’s.

19868.title: What to do
19868.content: Use a recommendation block: one statement per block, with a label, a title, and its strength as a code. // folio/<slug>/<chapter>/rec-cold-chain-audit.ts import { recommendation } from "@folio/schemas/builders"; export default recommendation({ label: "rec:cold-chain-audit", title: "Audit the cold chain quarterly", strength: { list: "grade-recommendation-strength", code: "conditional" }, uses: ["rec:scope", "prose:cold-chain-terms"], about: ["hi:cold-chain-management"], }); . The block’s .md holds the statement itself, and its label becomes the anchor every cross-reference targets ([see](#rec:cold-chain-audit)). | label: a prefix of your folio’s own choosing, kept consistent across the corpus. The platform reserves none: the kind’s node says prefixEnforced: false. rec: is recognised, never required. Pick a prefix once and write it down in the folio’s own AGENTS.md. | title: the short form the document’s index and any cross-reference will show. | strength: a code in a declared code list, not free text. Core declares two: . | grade-recommendation-strength: strong or conditional, GRADE as the WHO handbook for guideline development applies it; | rfc2119-requirement-level: must, must-not, should, should-not, may, from BCP 14. | . A folio whose issuing body grades differently declares its own folio-code-list/v1 in its code-lists/ rather than editing these. The check is “resolves in the scheme”: strengthFinding in folio-assistant-core/schemas/recommendation-strength.ts. State the strength in the prose too, in the issuing body’s own words, because readers read the prose. | uses[]: the blocks a reader must have read to act on this one. That means definitions of terms it uses, the scope statement it sits under, and the evidence summary it rests on. This is what makes “what else changes if this recommendation changes?” answerable. | about[]: optional labels of the DAK health-interventions this recommendation is about. It is a link, not a merge: the two vocabularies stay separate, and nothing in this one depends on the DAK adapter. | . Keep one statement per block. A block holding three recommendations cannot be cited, reviewed, superseded or traced individually, and splitting it later means renumbering everything that referenced it. Converting a labelled prose block. Change the builder call from prose to recommendation and add strength. The label, title, uses[] and .md stay as they are, so no reference breaks.

19869.title: When the statement comes from a source
19869.content: A normative statement or requirement that a SOURCE makes is already a node in that source’s L1 entry (l1-document-ingestion, “Requirements and normative statements”), with the source’s own number in meta.source_number. Cite that node from the block’s meta.source, and keep the source’s number in the title or prose. Do not mint a new id that looks like the source’s: a reader cannot tell the two apart.

19870.title: What not to do
19870.content: . | Do not use definition. It is a math kind: its lean field is required, so the block will not validate in a document folio at all. | Do not use a bare prose block. It validates, but no criterion can tell it is normative. | Do not use theorem or proposition for a good-practice statement. They are outside this profile and content_profile_check rejects them. | Do not encode the recommendation number in the label alone. Numbers are renumbered between editions; the label must survive that. Put the published number in the title or the prose. | .

19872.title: NPM Knowledge Graph Distribution
19872.content: Skill npm-kg-distribution: Package, release, distribute, and retrieve Knowledge Graphs using npm tooling and tarballs: declare package.json as an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph, build .tgz packages via bun pm pack, record publications as folio-binary-release/v1 state documents hosted on GitHub binary releases, and retrieve remote Knowledge Graphs using npm install for both unhydrated source graph and hydrated materialized graph views. Named by: Mount a declared subgraph . Knowledge Graphs in the folio ecosystem can be distributed and consumed as npm packages — packaged tarballs (.tgz) containing either the authored source graphs, pre-compiled hydrated graph views, or both. |   | where | . | the packaging tool | pack-tarball (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts) | . | the retrieval tool | kg-retrieve-npm (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts) | . | the release schema | schemas/sdlc/binary-release.ts (folio-binary-release/v1) | . | asset verification | cat-harness-tools/scripts/check-declared-assets.ts | . | related skills | remote-mount, kg-export, package-release (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc), kg-subscription | .

19873.title: 1. package.json as an authored pre-packaging asset in the KG
19873.content: A file that is not declared in <instance>.json is a file no check verifies, so package.json is declared as an authored Knowledge Graph asset that defines package identity, exports, dependencies, scripts, and the tarball inclusion whitelist (files array). Each layer that publishes an npm package declares package.json under assets in its <instance>.json: . { "id": "npm-manifest", "src": "package.json", "role": "package-manifest", "title": "package.json", "description": "The npm pre-packaging source manifest declaring package identity, exports, dependencies, scripts, and tarball whitelist." } . Why declare it under assets . | Verification at commit and mount time: check:declared-assets verifies that every declared asset exists on disk. | Remote mount resolution: remote-mount.ts and mount-from-lock.ts check out, lay down, and verify declared layer assets so that mounted dependencies carry their package identity. | Single source of packaging truth: package.json’s files field acts as the authoritative whitelist for what is bundled into the distribution tarball. | .

19874.title: 2. Packaging via bun pm pack & folio-binary-release/v1
19874.content: An npm package is built as a compressed tarball (.tgz) using bun pm pack: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts --root <instance-root> --destination <out-dir> . The packaging process: . | Reads the authored package.json to verify package identity (name and version). | Invokes bun pm pack --destination <dir>, which respects .npmignore and the files array in package.json. | Computes the exact file size in bytes and the SHA-256 digest of the .tgz tarball. | Generates and validates a folio-binary-release/v1 state node recording the release event. | . The folio-binary-release/v1 state node . A published tarball is represented in the Knowledge Graph as a folio-binary-release/v1 document (schemas/sdlc/binary-release.ts). A release record captures the publication event, never the binary payload itself: . { "$schema": "folio-binary-release/v1", "release": { "id": "cat-harness-v1.0.0", "version": "1.0.0", "tag": "v1.0.0", "publishedAt": "2026-10-08T18:30:00.000Z", "url": "https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/releases/tag/v1.0.0" }, "origin": { "kind": "github-release", "repository": "litlfred/cat-harness" }, "assets": [ { "name": "cat-harness-1.0.0.tgz", "bytes": 524288, "digest": { "algorithm": "sha256", "digest": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855", "verifiedAt": "2026-10-08T18:30:00.000Z" }, "fetchedFrom": "https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/releases/download/v1.0.0/cat-harness-1.0.0.tgz", "contentType": "application/gzip", "disposition": "published" } ] } . Key invariants: . | Never the bytes: The schema is .strict(). Content and blobs are rejected. | Verifiable fixity: SHA-256 digests and byte counts are required. | Provenance: fetchedFrom must state where the binary can be retrieved. | Dispositions: An asset’s state after publication is tracked (published, superseded, deleted-before-deploy). Any deliberate removal must provide a dispositionReason. | .

19875.title: 3. GitHub binary releases hosting .tgz tarballs
19875.content: Published Knowledge Graph tarballs are hosted on GitHub Releases: . | The git tag (v<version>) marks the exact source commit in the repository. | The .tgz package is uploaded as a release asset attached to the GitHub release. | The release URL follows the canonical scheme: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/v<version>/<package>-<version>.tgz | . This provides: . | High availability via CDN. | Immutability tied to the release tag. | Checkable fixity against the folio-binary-release/v1 document. | .

19876.title: 4. npm install as an alternative retrieval Tool for remote KGs
19876.content: Remote Knowledge Graphs can be retrieved into a workspace or consumer environment through three distinct mechanisms, each serving a specific architectural need: . | tool / mechanism | transport | granularity | best when | . | remote-mount | Git shallow blobless fetch at 40-char SHA | Transitive dependency closure of declared directories | Developing against dependencies whose TypeScript/code is imported directly | . | kg:subscribe | Substrate snapshot via HTTP | Selective subgraphs and on-demand assets through 5 gates | Consuming large external reference datasets (WHO IRIS, FHIR) | . | kg-retrieve-npm (npm install) | NPM package tarball (.tgz) via registry or GitHub release | Pre-packaged bundle with whitelisted files and optional pre-built views | Distributing versioned Knowledge Graph packages with immediate consumption | . Unhydrated source graph vs. Hydrated materialized graph views . When an npm package distributes a Knowledge Graph, it can provide two distinct graph views: . 1. Unhydrated source graph view . The authored source files as they exist in the repository: . | package.json pre-packaging manifest. | <instance>.json layer declaration. | Authored source directories: skills/ (markdown instructions), schemas/ (Zod/TS definitions), processes/ (BPMN diagrams), methodologies/, text-based metadata. | Binary media assets excluded: PNGs, JPGs, PDFs and figures under library/ and uploads/ are excluded via .npmignore during unhydrated packaging, keeping the base package compact (~2-5 MB). | Packaged as <package>-<version>.tgz. | Ideal for agents and developers authoring new knowledge, extending skills, or compiling the graph locally. | . 2. Hydrated materialized graph view . The complete, materialized Knowledge Graph artifacts and binary assets: . | Binary media assets included: Losslessly optimized library PNGs, figures, and covers. | Named subgraph JSON-LD (docs/subgraph/<instance>/<path>/index.jsonld). | Fully dereferenced hydrated JSON-LD (index.hydrated.jsonld). | Metadata indexes, RDF N-Quads, and pre-computed search indices. | Packaged via pack-tarball --hydrated as <package>-<version>.hydrated.tgz. | Ideal for read-only consumers, visualizers, semantic search engines, and portal deployments that require immediate access without installing compilation toolchains or running offline export pipelines. | . 3. The subgraph index package — one per pin . A third, narrow package carries a pin’s subgraph index files and nothing else: <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>, built by the subgraph-index-package Tool through pack-tarball and released as subgraph-index-<sha> on every push to main. A hydrated remote mount reads it; see remote-mount §”Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package”. Using kg-retrieve-npm . To retrieve and inspect a remote Knowledge Graph tarball or package: . # Retrieve and inspect both graph views from a tarball bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz # Retrieve and verify integrity against a folio-binary-release/v1 document bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --release path/to/release.json # Retrieve only the unhydrated source graph view into a target directory bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --view unhydrated --destination ./deps/my-kg # Retrieve only the hydrated materialized graph view bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --view hydrated --destination ./static-kg . When verified against a folio-binary-release/v1 document, any mismatch in byte size or SHA-256 digest immediately refuses the package, preventing corrupted or tampered graph data from entering the consumer environment.

19878.title: Opening brief — brief the topic before you touch anything
19878.content: Skill opening-brief: Brief a work item or a topic BEFORE touching anything: what you are doing and why it is worth doing, what you already know and with what provenance, how you plan to do it and what would falsify the approach. Scales with irreversibility, not line count. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Options analysis, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, SWOT situation analysis, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Record agent step, Review-log watch . This skill governs what you say before the work; turn-reporting.md (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) governs what you say during and after it; todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) keeps the work item mechanics.

19879.title: Opening brief
19879.content: Claiming a work item records the work. Briefing it is what makes the work resumable. Both are required, and the brief comes first — before the first tool call, in the chat, not in the commit. AGENTS.md §”Opening a bean or a topic” states the rule and when it applies. This is the shape. When it applies — proportionality, so this does not become ceremony . The trigger is irreversibility and surprise, not line count. | A one-line fix with an obvious route needs no brief. Say what you are doing and do it. | Anything touching a shipped gate, a shared artefact, a formal declaration with consumers, or a number a reader sees — brief it. | Anything where you expect to be wrong some of the time — brief it, and say where you expect to be wrong. Research is the case this is most valuable for and most often skipped, on the grounds that the outcome is unknown. The unknown outcome is the reason to write down the route, not a reason to skip it. | . Why it is a rule and not a style preference . Sessions end mid-thread. Containers are reclaimed, context windows fill, a branch is picked up days later by an agent with none of the reasoning that produced it. The work item body and the commit are durable; the chain of inference that made them sensible is not, unless it is written down at the point where it was still obvious. An agent resuming cold should be able to read the brief and continue — not reconstruct its predecessor’s rabbit hole first. It catches wrong work before it is done rather than after. A route stated in advance can be corrected by the author in one line. The same route discovered in a finished diff costs a review cycle and, often, a revert. It is the same discipline as the question frame in interaction-modality §4.1, applied to work instead of decisions: a terse start, like a terse question, makes the author go and find context the agent already had. The four parts . 1. The problem, stated for someone who was not here. Expand every identifier on first use. Not “fixing qou-93hu” but “bean qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent conjecture carrier, whose only field is (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12, a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so the class constrains nothing.” . 2. What you know, and how you know it. Every number with its provenance: . | provenance | how to say it | . | measured this session, on this tree | “measured just now: 22 of 22 seeded, 0 missed” | . | measured this session, on a DIFFERENT tree | “grepped 0 on claude/x before branching — not re-run here” | . | carried from a prior session | “recorded 2026-08-24 as 43 drifted; not re-measured” | . | asserted by a work item or a doc | “bean qou-q7lf says X — unverified” | . The last row is the one that bites hardest. A sibling’s work item is not a primary source, and neither is a source file’s ## Status note; both go stale, and a specific, recent, confidently-worded work item is exactly the kind that gets believed. “Measured this session” is not the safe case. A measurement is scoped to the TREE it was taken on, and git switch invalidates every earlier one without saying so. The number is real, recent, and yours; only the tree underneath it moved. So say which tree, and re-run anything load-bearing after a branch change — the re-run costs one command and it is the same command. Part 2 includes the result of the collision review in coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Starting new work”: the siblings that overlap, or “no overlap found” and what you checked. 3. The route and the gate. How you plan to do it, what you will verify against, and what would falsify the approach. A plan with no failure mode is not a plan; it is an intention. If the gate is a script, name it and its expected output. 4. What you are NOT doing. The adjacent defect you are leaving, the scope you decline to widen into, the thing you will flag rather than fix. Stating it up front is what stops it becoming either silent scope creep or a silent omission — and it puts the scope call where it can still be argued with, which is before the diff. Briefing a sibling or a subagent — pass interaction-modality on (STRICT) . When a coordinating session writes a brief to launch a child session (create_session, send_message) or a background subagent (Agent, invoke_subagent), the brief is the child’s only prompt until it reads the graph. A child whose brief omits how to ask the owner will default to asking in plain prose when it hits a permission wall or a design call. Every sibling brief and subagent prompt written by a coordinating session MUST carry the interaction-modality contract explicitly: . | If the child can reach the person directly (a sibling session with its own chat surface): every question to the owner goes out twice, in order — first the full question in chat (context, what differs, every identifier expanded, at most four numbered or lettered options with pros, cons, downstream impact and reversibility, recommended option first and marked (Recommended), and the stated default on silence), and second the tappable card (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, ask_question, or post_widget) carrying the same option labels. Never ask in prose alone, and never ask the person to type. | If the child is a background subagent or a sibling running beside a live discussion: it does not ask the person in prose either; it returns any owner-facing decision to the coordinating session in the hand-back-to-discussion schema format so the coordinator presents both the full chat block and the tappable card. | Pass it on: if the child itself spawns a helper or a subagent, its brief to that child must carry the same interaction-modality block. | . Before you offer options, check whether it is already ruled (STRICT) . Part two of the brief is what do I already know, with each measurement’s provenance. This is the half that gets skipped, because an unsettled question is more interesting than a settled one and nothing in a checkout announces that a decision exists. Presenting options for a settled question is worse than presenting none. It reopens a decision, spends the owner’s attention on it a second time, and the options offered will not be the ones already weighed. Four places to look, in this order: . | The proposals — the design corpus. They live in the docs/ of the layer whose stub needs them; today that is cat-harness/docs/proposals/ (opt-in cat-harness.proposals), and its index.md is where to start. Resolve the directory rather than remembering this sentence — a stub’s docs/ is where its proposals are, and this path is an example of the rule, not the rule. | The owner’s rulings, in work items and in the declarations that quote them verbatim. A _comment field in a *.json is frequently where a decision was recorded, because that is where it had to be obeyed. | The skill that owns the area — and read it, rather than recalling it. | The commit history — git log -S "<symbol>" over the file you are about to change, and a beans list | grep <topic> that does not filter to open items. A decision that shipped is invisible to every instrument that looks for pending ones — and a recent one is exactly when you are most confident your own reading is current. One git log -S answers it. | . Cite what you read, never what you remember. A half-remembered line used as an authority is the fake-reference failure activity-names-skill exists to prevent, one level up: it is unfalsifiable by the reader, because it sounds like something this repository would say. Worked example . Starting qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent §3b-cond hypothesis class in lean/QOU/AlgebraicSubstrate/ConditionalClasses.lean. The problem. Its single field is alpha_three_eq_four : (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12 — a closed numeral identity with the values already substituted in, so no exponent variable occurs in it and rfl proves it whatever the physics. Four sibling carriers in the same file are vacuous too, but they are at least the right shape (parameter-quantified inequalities); this one has no quantifier and no free variable at all. What I know. Measured this session: bound as [C] in 5 files; the probe baseline records it proved-vacuous; the class’s own docstring already claims “α = 4/3”, so the target value is not something I need to invent. Not measured: whether any downstream proof depends on the field’s current type. Route. Make α a class parameter — class CriticalExponent (α : ℝ) : Prop where alpha_eq : α = 4/3. A Prop class cannot carry data, so α must be a parameter, not a field. Gate: lean-direct exit 0 on all three affected modules, plus a content probe proving ¬ CriticalExponent 2 — because inhabitability at 4/3 alone would not show the class constrains anything. Falsifier: if ¬ CriticalExponent 2 will not go through, the encoding is not doing what I claim and I stop. Not doing. The other four carriers need analytic setup their docstrings only gesture at — the author’s mathematics, not a cleanup. Also leaving the separate CriticalExponent in core-levi-form.lean, a different carrier in a different namespace. ~200 words, and it would have let a reader stop the work, redirect it, or pick it up cold. What a thin brief looks like, and why it fails . Starting qou-93hu — fixing CriticalExponent. Names the work item and nothing else. It does not say the field is a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so a reader cannot tell whether this is cosmetic or load-bearing; it does not say the class signature changes, so nobody can warn that every binder in two consumer modules moves with it; and it does not say what “fixed” will be checked against, so the agent is free to declare victory on a compile. Each of those omissions is a place the author could have intervened for the cost of reading one sentence. The failure this prevents . An agent that has spent an hour inside a problem writes in the private vocabulary it built along the way, and a reader — the author, or the next agent — has to reconstruct that vocabulary before evaluating anything. The brief is written at the one moment when the agent still knows which parts are non-obvious, because it has just finished finding them out. Cheapest correct move when you do not want to spend the words: do not start the topic. A task you cannot brief is one you have not understood well enough to begin. The brief’s durable form is the PR description. Once the work exists, pr-description (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) answers the same questions for a reader who arrives after it.

19881.title: Options analysis
19881.content: Process_OptionsAnalysis · strict · 5 step(s) . A decision reached by a NAMED methodology, with its rejected options recorded. Called as a subprocess, never run on its own. WHEN IT APPLIES: the trigger is opening-brief’s — IRREVERSIBILITY AND SURPRISE, not size. A reversible choice needs no subprocess; an irreversible one cannot skip it. A subprocess fired on every decision becomes ceremony, and ceremony is how a gate stops being read. WHY IT IS ONE SUBPROCESS AND NOT A BRANCH PER METHODOLOGY: the methodologies are parallel tracks selected by context, and the selection is a judgement made inside A_Select rather than a gateway. A gateway per methodology would assert the choice is computable from data, which is the claim dmn says to make only when the criteria recur. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not decide. It produces the options, their trade-offs and a recommendation; the decision and its authorisation belong to whoever owns the calling step. i i i i i

19883.title: Lanes — who acts
19883.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Business analyst | business-analyst | This lane’s deliverable is the recommendation together with the rejected options — a rejected option with no record is a dead end the next agent walks back into — but it never authorises anything; A_Record hands both to whoever called the subprocess, and the decision stays theirs. Answering GW_Trigger no is not a skipped step either: End_TriggerNotMet is recorded as a distinct outcome from a completed comparison, because a caller unable to tell “not needed” from “we chose X” cannot audit either one. | .

19884.title: Steps
19884.content: Every one of the 5 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Frame the decision and check the triggerA_Frame | Business analyst | opening-brief | One sentence naming the KIND of thing being chosen, not the options — “which cache strategy”, never “A or B”. Then the trigger: is this irreversible, or would the answer surprise someone? If neither, say so and stop; the calling step decides without this subprocess. Stopping here is a correct outcome, not a skipped step. | . | Select the methodology by contextA_Select | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | Ask the selection question in order, first yes decides: do the criteria RECUR with the same inputs having to produce the same answer; is this the CERTAINTY of a body of evidence behind a recommendation; is the context a BEAN recording a decision; otherwise a one-off choice among candidates. If none fits, that is a finding — say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit.The declared set is the contents of the methodology graph. Ask for it; do not remember it. | . | Check the selected methodology’s evidence baseA_CheckEvidence | Business analyst | literature-search | Before applying a methodology, establish that the thing being applied is what it claims to be. A methodology is adopted because it is somebody else’s named, external work; this step checks that the origin it cites resolves to a source in a declared library, and reads the methodology-evidence QA sidecar for it.WHY THE CHECK IS HERE AND NOT AT ADOPTION. Adoption happens once; selection happens every time a decision is made. A source that was reachable when the methodology was adopted can stop being so, and a methodology adopted before this axis existed was never checked at all. Measured 2026-09-22: six methodologies cited an origin and NONE had that source in any library, so every selection made until then rested on an unverifiable citation.WHAT A GAP DOES AND DOES NOT DO. A missing source does NOT block the decision, and this step has no branch that stops the process — that would make a documentation gap into an outage, and the owner decides whether an unbacked methodology may still be used. It does two things: it runs literature-search to try to close the gap, and it puts the evidence state into the record A_Record writes, so a reader can tell a decision made on a verified method from one made on a citation nobody could follow.The third state is the one that matters. “Source ingested”, “source located but unreachable from here” and “no source found” are three different facts, and literature-search exists largely to stop the middle one being reported as the last. | . | Apply it, and state each option’s trade-offsA_Apply | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | Follow the selected methodology as written — adopted whole, not blended with another. At least two real options: one option is not a choice, and a straw option is worse than a short list because it makes the analysis look thorough while narrowing it.Never quantify the comparison to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform takes the structure and refuses the arithmetic: the weights are invented and a total reads as a measurement. | . | Record the chosen option AND the rejected onesA_Record | Business analyst | decision-audit | The rejected options and why they lost are part of the output, not an appendix. A rejected option with no record is a dead end nobody marked, and the next agent walks into it — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted.In a bean context the form is MADR’s. Which methodology was followed is named here, so a reader can check the method rather than take the conclusion. | .

19885.title: Decisions
19885.content: Every one of the 1 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Irreversible or surprising?GW_Trigger | A_Frame has always ENDED with this question — “is this irreversible, or would the answer surprise someone? If neither, say so and stop; the calling step decides without this subprocess. Stopping here is a correct outcome, not a skipped step.” Until this gateway existed, the diagram gave it NO WAY TO STOP: A_Frame’s only outgoing edge went to A_Select, so the prose promised a branch the model did not have.Found by adding the second caller, not by reading. With one caller the straight line looked fine; wiring editing-hci-validation made every write in that process run all four activities, and its corpus-gate tests failed with “Task_RecordDecision is not enabled. Enabled now: A_Frame.” That is the ceremony this process’s own documentation refuses — “a subprocess fired on every decision becomes ceremony, and ceremony is how a gate stops being read” — and it was unreachable as a criticism while the subprocess had a single caller.DELIBERATELY NOT DMN-BACKED, unlike the gateways that are. Irreversibility and surprise are judged, not computed: dmn says to claim computability only when the criteria recur with the same inputs having to produce the same answer, and “would this surprise someone” does not. So the outcome is supplied by whoever is at the step, exactly as Gateway_EditorDecision takes one. | yes → Select the methodology by contextno → Trigger not met — the caller decides without an analysis | .

19892.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
19892.content: Skill placement: Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which layer, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two “stub” conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Code node review, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which layer owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

19893.title: Step 1 — which layer?
19893.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the layer from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

19894.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that layer put it?
19894.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every layer declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this layer, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. A layer that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the layer that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong layer’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . A layer inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-layer skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

19895.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
19895.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

19896.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
19896.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this layer publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real layers. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

19897.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
19897.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this layer genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

19898.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
19898.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

19899.title: Checklist
19899.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Layer — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

19901.title: The platform’s own gates — run what CI will run
19901.content: Skill platform-gates: bun test passing is not the gates passing. What to run before you push, why the list is derived from the CI workflow rather than written down, and what a *:check failure is actually telling you to do. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Record agent step, Review-log watch, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them . Run it before you push, not after CI tells you.

19902.title: The CI workflow is the list
19902.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

19903.title: bun test green is not the gates green
19903.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

19904.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
19904.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

19905.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
19905.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

19906.title: Fast versus full is job membership
19906.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | .

19907.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
19907.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

19908.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
19908.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

19909.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
19909.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

19910.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
19910.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

19911.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
19911.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.
