20260.title: Skills and Tools — the skill says what, the Tool says how
20260.content: Skill skills-and-tools: A skill states a capability generically; a Tool node carries the concrete mechanism. Read before writing or editing any skill, and whenever a skill is about to name a vendor, a CLI, a binary or an API endpoint. Named by: Code node review . A skill is a capability stated generically. A Tool content node is one concrete way to exercise it. One skill may be satisfied by several Tools; a Tool names the skills it satisfies through its satisfies field. This is the standard operating procedure for every skill in the harness, not a guideline for new ones. A skill that names GitHub, names the beans binary, or embeds a shell invocation has swallowed a Tool, and the swallowing is what makes a layer un-portable. Schema for the Tool node: schemas/tools/tool.ts in the tools layer; carrier convention (Zod authoritative, JSON-LD and JSON Schema generated) in directory-conventions §”What lives in the schemas graph”.

20261.title: The test, in one line
20261.content: Would this sentence still be true on a different forge, a different binary, a different machine? If yes it is skill. If no it is Tool. Applied: . | sentence | verdict | . | “Open a change proposal as soon as there is one commit to hang it on.” | skill — true anywhere | . | “gh pr create”, or the REST call it wraps | Tool — one forge, one transport | . | “Claim the item before you work, so a sibling session does not pick it up.” | skill | . | “beans update <id> --status in-progress” | Tool | . | “If the CLI is unavailable, the store is still writable by hand.” | skill — the fact is portable | . | “Edit the status: line in the front matter of beans/defs/<id>--*.md.” | Tool | . That last pair is the one people get wrong. Having a fallback is a property of the capability; performing the fallback is a mechanism. The skill must say a fallback exists and when to reach for it, because an agent that does not know one exists will stop. What it must not do is spell out the edit. When the mechanism is itself a procedure, it is the Tool’s subprocess (§”A Tool may describe its own subprocess”). The Tool node names the BPMN in subprocesses (process ids, checked by check:tools), conventionally under processes/tools/; the skill keeps the portable sentence. See bpmn-processes.

20262.title: Every bean skill has (at least) two Tools
20262.content: The work-plan skills are the worked example: . | Tool | when | . | beans CLI | normal case — installed via scripts/install-beans.sh | . | hand edit / scripts/beans-fallback.ts | CLI absent or cannot be installed here | . Both satisfy the same skills. Neither is the skill. A fresh container has no beans on PATH, so an agent that only knows the CLI reads the plan and touches nothing. The fallback is a second Tool with equal standing, and the skill must present it that way. An external project is a candidate Tool before it is anything else. When somebody asks whether another project could do a skill’s job — Beads for the work plan, say — that survey is research, not a proposal and not a skill edit: it files under <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/ per placement, dated, with each project’s health measured rather than recalled (for example research-and-analysis/prior-art.md). Only if a candidate is adopted does it become a Tool node, with the selection its derived alternatives call for, below.

20263.title: Substitutable Tools are derived, and each says how to choose
20263.content: A pair like that is substitutable: same job, different mechanism, pick one. Nobody declares it. Two Tools are alternatives when they satisfy a common skill AND have the same I/O signature — the same input names, types and required flags, the same outputs, the same renders and maintains (deriveAlternatives in schemas/tools/tool.ts). A shared skill alone is not enough: most skills with several Tools have complementary ones, steps rather than choices, and their I/O is what tells them apart. So the discipline moves to the ports. Type and name a port for what it really takes and gives. A CSV reader and a workbook reader typed Text would derive as alternatives; DelimitedTextPath and WorkbookPath keep them apart. Two generators whose output is a bare pages would too; naming each output for what it writes does not. Each Tool with a derived alternative then carries selection — three fields, all required together (check-tools fails one without it): . | field | answers | . | when | the case this Tool is the right answer to | . | limits | where it stops, and which sibling picks up | . | cost | what having it available costs | . Do not skip limits: without it an agent reaches for the tool and discovers the boundary by failing. State it even when it is “none”, for the same reason install.none exists — so “no limits” is distinguishable from an unfinished record. cost is not install. install says how to obtain the tool; cost says what having it costs — CI minutes, a wheel needing a C toolchain, a network round trip. Two Tools can be equally easy to install and very differently expensive to keep. Not in description. It is projected verbatim as the MCP tool description and into the exported graph, and answers “what does this do”; comparative prose about cost does not belong there, because it would degrade the surface an agent reads when choosing among tools. Sharing a skill does NOT make two Tools alternatives . Most skills with several Tools have complementary ones: workflow-list, -start, -next, -gate and -complete are five steps of process-state, not five ways to perform it. Only Tools that also share an I/O signature are alternatives, and scripts/check-tools.ts checks that the relation is mutual, because a one-sided one means an agent arriving at the silent end never learns a choice exists. Keying substitutability on a shared skill alone would demand comparative prose where there is nothing to compare, and an author obliged to write it writes noise. The worked pair: stdlib vs extensions . ingest-stdlib and ingest-extended both satisfy library-ingestion, and the split falls where the dependency boundary actually is rather than on principle: . |   | ingest-stdlib | ingest-extended | . | install | nothing (install.none) | PyMuPDF, pypdf + Pillow, tesseract | . | covers | archives, CSV/spreadsheets, technical metadata, content routing | PDF outline, page text, OCR, images | . | runs in CI here | yes | no — CI installs ruff and nothing else | . Reading a zip’s central directory, sniffing magic bytes and parsing an xlsx’s XML are all in the Python standard library; rendering a PDF’s text layer is not and never will be. An agent picks by what the machine has, not by what the document is — and the stdlib arm refuses a PDF outright rather than half-ingesting one, so the choice is never made silently. This is also the shape to reach for whenever a capability has a heavyweight backend: two Tools, one skill, the dependency posture legible on each node, instead of a repository-wide yes/no that no reader of a skill can see.

20264.title: The harness assumes no MCP — and knows how to emit one
20264.content: agentic-harness must work with no MCP server running. Everything it needs is files in directories the layer declares: skills in the kg graph, Tool nodes beside them, the work plan in the beans graph. An agent with nothing but a filesystem and <name>.json can read all of it. MCP is acknowledged as a future transport, not assumed as the present one. Where a downstream layer runs a server, skill_list / skill_fetch / work_plan_prime are a convenience over the same files — and ToolDefinition accordingly declares invoke.mcp as one optional arm beside shell and container. A Tool whose only invocation is an MCP call is not usable by the harness that defines it. Editing a skill goes through skill_update, not a raw file write. Where the server runs, it is the write side of skill_fetch. It refuses unless every gate passes: . | the skill resolves as skill_fetch serves it; | the file is tracked in this repository, so not another layer’s skill and not a mounted copy; | the file is not generated; | a policy grants skill-update to the actor (no default policy does); | the file is unchanged since it was read; | the front matter parses and keeps the skill’s name; | every link the edit adds resolves. | . A gate that cannot decide refuses. The Tool writes the working tree, and the caller commits the change. That is a statement about dependency, not about ignorance. MCP is an output of this harness: mcp-projection is how an agent takes a Tool node describing a CLI and produces a working MCP service from it, mcp-assembly covers composing several into one namespace, and mcp-contract checks the result still matches its sources. The harness is the thing that knows the mapping; it just does not need the result in order to run. It is what makes the harness bootstrappable: the layer that defines what a Tool is cannot require a tool server to read its own definitions without arguing in a circle. It is also why sovereign-compute and air-gapped operation are reachable later without a second design — a layer with no server loses a transport, not a capability. So when this skill says “reach a Tool through the graph”, the floor is: read <name>.json, find the kg entry, open the directory. Anything richer is an optimisation a layer may offer.

20265.title: GitHub is a Tool node, not a layer
20265.content: The PR-choreography skills — prepare-merge-auto, pickup, watch, coordinate — assume a forge, but most of their text is portable: “pull request”, “PR”, “GitHub” as a noun. Only a few lines are concrete invocations. So forge-specificity is isolated at the Tool layer: the skills stay in the harness, stated generically, and Tool nodes carry the invocations — one per forge operation (table below). Adding another forge is more Tool nodes satisfying the same skills, not a repository or a fork. The forge operations, one Tool node each . One Tool node per forge operation, using the fields Tools already have. A skill names the operation in neutral words, and this table is where an operation meets its nodes. An agent picks the node for the forge the checkout’s remote is on; each pair is a derived alternative carrying selection (check:tools holds it). These Tool nodes sit in the opt-in integrations sub-graph (integrations/tools/): a layer that uses them lists cat-harness.integrations in its enableSubgraphs. | operation (as a skill names it) | GitHub | GitLab | . | list change proposals | github-pr-list | gitlab-mr-list | . | read change proposal (body, comments, reviews) | github-pr-view | gitlab-mr-view | . | read change proposal (check runs) | github-pr-checks | — | . | list changed files | github-pr-files | gitlab-mr-files | . | comment on change proposal | github-pr-comment | gitlab-mr-comment | . | request review | github-pr-request-review | gitlab-mr-request-review | . | resolve review thread | github-pr-resolve-thread | gitlab-mr-resolve-thread | . | list branches | github-branches | gitlab-branches | . A dash is a known gap. Two GitLab nodes run a script rather than glab directly: glab mr diff has no --name-only, so gitlab-mr-files reads the paths out of the raw diff; and glab mr update --reviewer NAME replaces the reviewers, so gitlab-mr-request-review passes +NAME, which adds one. Its names are GitLabUsernames, since GitLab usernames do not fit Login. Branches alone are also listable with git ls-remote --heads origin, which needs no forge. Subscribing to a change proposal’s activity is not a forge operation. It is the session platform’s (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription), so no forge Tool node offers it, and a skill says so rather than naming a forge for it. A Tool may describe its own subprocess . When one mechanism takes several steps, they belong to the Tool, not to the general skill: the Tool lists subprocesses (process ids, each the stem of a .bpmn the checkout declares), and a general diagram’s call activity is bound by it. General skills name the Tool, never its steps. Example: render-kg-to-cdn is the general step (render a Knowledge Graph for a CDN at a publication root URL; output a status and a message), and gh-pages is one Tool for it whose subprocess is bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn — declared below the harness, so the reference points down. Vocabulary — name the concept, not the vendor’s word for it . GitHub calls it a pull request; GitLab calls it a merge request; Gerrit calls it a change. A skill that says “pull request” has picked one vendor’s noun, which is a milder form of the same defect. Prefer the neutral term on first use and the local term thereafter, rather than scrubbing every occurrence — a skill written entirely in invented vocabulary is unreadable, and unreadable is worse than mildly GitHub-flavoured. The rule is that an agent must never have to resolve a vendor noun to act: it is fine for a skill to say “pull request (PR)” once and use PR after it; it is not fine for the only statement of what to do to be gh pr create.

20266.title: Writing or editing a skill — the checklist
20266.content: . | Grep your own draft for vendor names, binaries, endpoints, file paths under a tool’s control, and flag characters. Each hit is a Tool that has not been declared. | State the capability first, in a sentence that survives the mechanism being replaced. 2b. If an input reaches a command line, give it a type that cannot be a payload — and put free prose on stdin. See untrusted-input; check:tools fails CI on a violation. | Say a mechanism exists and where to find it — never inline it. A Tool is reached the same way a skill is: resolve the kg graph from the layer’s declaration and read from the directory it names. Not a remembered path, and — see below — not necessarily a tool call. | Say when each Tool applies if there is more than one, because choosing between them is judgement and judgement is skill. | Name what happens when no Tool is available. Three states, as everywhere here: the Tool worked, the Tool is absent and here is the fallback, and we could not tell — which is never rendered as success. | .

20267.title: The Tool schema, and the remaining debt
20267.content: schemas/tools/tool.ts (in the tools layer) defines a Tool, tools/ holds the nodes, and bun run cat check:tools fails when a satisfies names a skill that does not exist. ToolInput.repeated marks a list input (rather than a list type per scalar type, which would multiply the shared $defs and break the identity property the shared vocabulary exists for). invoke.inProcess names a TypeScript function for a Tool with no shell equivalent; it is runnable by the harness directly, and is the projection source rather than something to proxy, so the refusal of an mcp-only Tool does not reach it. Many skills still carry their invocations inline. Most of the remainder is fine — a great many skills are pure judgement (interaction-modality, one-voice-style-guide) and have no mechanism to name. check:tools reports the coverage count rather than failing on it, for exactly that reason. What it cannot tell you, and what needs a human eye, is which of the uncovered skills describe an action — those are the ones whose mechanism is still swallowed. A satisfies edge is checkable against the skill’s own contract . satisfies is the one part of a Tool node a schema cannot check, and it was being written on judgement alone. bun run cat check:tools compares a Tool’s io against the input contract of every skill it claims — the contract the skill names in its own front matter (input:), never one found by directory name. Two rules: every required property of the contract must appear as an input on the Tool, and where a Tool input and a contract property share a name, their JSON types must agree (an integer port may serve a number property). If either fails, the Tool cannot exercise the skill and the edge is false. What is compared, and what is not. A skill’s contract is free-form JSON Schema; a Tool’s io is named ports referencing shared $defs IRIs, so they meet only at names and at the JSON type each port’s vocabulary type projects to. The type rule is weak — nearly every contract property here is a bare {"type": "string"} — but not vacuous: it catches an array contract served by a string port, which the name rule passes. A mismatch that is “only” a naming difference — path against targetPath — is a finding, not a false positive to suppress. Two names for one input, across a skill and the Tool claiming to implement it, means an agent reading the contract cannot call the Tool. Three states, as everywhere. No contract (the common case, not a defect) is undefined; a contract requiring nothing is [] and passes; a contract that is declared but missing or unparseable is reported and fails, never counted as agreement. An external https:// contract is not fetched by this offline check. For example, a Tool that validates a .po against its .pot does not satisfy content-validate, whose contract requires targetPath: validating translations is not validating a folio’s content. Which uncovered skills actually need one — bun run cat tools:coverage . The count alone does not say which. A grep for shell blocks over-reports, because a skill may legitimately QUOTE a command while stating its capability generically. The corpus carries a better signal — BPMN task type. A process step is a serviceTask (runs without a person) or a userTask (performed by one), and the diagrams already say which. Triaged on that, plus an I/O contract under schemas/skills/, the tiers are A (automation evidence), B (userTask-only), C (ambiguous) and D (nothing), and only C needs a human read. Run it for the numbers; do not quote them from prose: a count in prose is a claim that nothing re-checks, and it drifts unnoticed. Many skills are both: two activities name interaction-modality, a serviceTask that reads the preferences file — a mechanism — and a userTask about how to frame a question — judgement. The question is not “is this skill a Tool?” but “which PART of it is.” . A skill with both halves is not mis-modelled. Migrating it is a split: the mechanical half becomes a Tool, the judgement half stays as prose. Expecting a clean move makes the migration look bigger than it is. So when you write or edit a skill: follow the checklist above and reference a Tool. When you read one that inlines gh pr create or beans update, that is the debt, not the pattern — do not propagate it. Authoring a Tool node: tools/<id>/<id>.json, one folder per Tool, a "$schema": "tool-definition/v1" document validated against the Tool schema; the loader lives in the tools layer. io ports reference the shared vocabulary in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts by its type name ("$type") — never a free-form string, because a reference nothing checks is eventually wrong. For the end-to-end guide on authoring, implementing, packaging, and registering concrete tools across separated repositories, see tool-authoring. For runtime conventions, test preloading, and TypeScript configuration, see bun-use (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

20268.title: Covered is not reachable — see its own skill
20268.content: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing, and check:tools reports it as covered and is right to. That discipline, the two questions it keeps apart, what to do when you meet one, and the two reasons not to write maintains: covered-is-not-reachable.

20270.doc: Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file
20270.title: Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file
20270.content: Process_SliceSqlitePublish · strict · 7 step(s) . Build one named slice of a knowledge graph as a SQLite file a browser mounts without parsing, and publish it beside its manifest and its payloads. The contract is kg-export §”Per-slice SQLite”; the builder is the slice-sqlite Tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-slice-sqlite.ts), one table-driven builder with one definition per slice; the search is one page, slices/search.html?slice=<name>. THE SIZE IS MEASURED BEFORE THE SLICE IS WIRED. A slice that is wired first and measured afterwards ships whatever it weighs, because by then a manifest, a gate, two deploy steps and a page depend on it. The budget gateway sits between measuring and wiring so that an oversized slice stops with its measurement reported, rather than arriving on a reader’s connection. NO BINARY IS COMMITTED. The file is built at deploy from the tree being published, so the gate cannot compare against a committed copy; it proves determinism (two builds, one sha256) and a row-content digest read back from the file against one computed from the source. i i i i i i i

20276.title: Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history

20284.title: Signature — one optional string in, a reviewable list out
20284.content: Other processes invoke this skill, and so does a person typing /staging-review, so the contract is stated formally: one left in prose is one each caller re-derives. Input . |   |   | . | type | string | . | cardinality | 0,1 — optional, and at most one | . | meaning | what the reader wants to look at, in their own words | . | absent | the whole preview: every page this branch changed | . Keep the wording verbatim wherever the output echoes it — the same rule goal-review (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) applies to a goal: a request the agent paraphrased is a different request, and the reader cannot tell which one the list was built for. It narrows; it never adds. “The navbar” gets the pages carrying it, not a page that mentions it. An ask matching nothing that changed is said, not answered with the whole preview — a list that silently ignores its input is worse than an empty one, because the reader believes it was answered. Output . Markdown, in this order. Every part is required; an absent part is stated, not dropped. | What changed, in prose — a short narrative, before any link: what a reader of the site will now see or do differently, in plain sentences, and why (the request it answers, in the requester’s words where there are any). One paragraph per PR or per coherent change. A table of URLs tells a reviewer where to look; only the narrative tells them what they are looking for, and a reviewer who has not read the code cannot reconstruct it from a filename. | Where to start — one line, one URL: the one that best answers the input, or the page with the most change behind it when there was none. A reader opens one thing first whether or not you choose it for them. | The comparison table below — before (main), after (staging), what to review. Links are deep — to the page, and to the anchor on it where the change sits (…/#harness-cat-harness), never the site root with “scroll down”. | The pictures — a before/after pair for each visual change, SHOWN to the reviewer (sent as images where the surface allows it), not only linked. A link asks the reviewer to do the comparison; a pair does it for them. How to make a fair pair is before-after-preview (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). If a pair could not be made, say which and why — that is part 5, not a silent gap. | What could not be checked, per the three states below. | . The third column is the one with value . What changed must be phrased as something to look at, never as a restatement of the filename. Build it by mapping changed files to published surfaces: . | what changed | which page | what to say | . | a stylesheet or client script | every page that loads it | the affordance that changed, and the gesture to make | . | a template or include | the pages that include it | where on the page to look | . | generated content | the page it generates | what it was generated from — a stale generator and a correct one look identical on the page | . | a schema, a test, a gate | none | say so, and point at the diff | . | folio content (block manifests and prose) | the page each block renders on | the ChangeSet’s aspect: reworded, moved, renamed, added, removed. See below. | . Where a change is only visible after an interaction — a control behind a disclosure, a mode a reader turns on — say WHICH interaction. A reviewer who cannot find the thing reports it as missing, and a gate that sweeps the page without opening the view misses a defect behind it. You can open it yourself — the publish ref is a git branch . Everything above composes URLs for a reader. The agent writing them usually cannot open them. From inside a session container: . | route | result | . | curl https://<owner>.github.io/… | 403 — CONNECT tunnel failed (policy denial) | . | WebFetch | EGRESS_BLOCKED | . | Playwright / Chromium | net::ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED | . A browser is not a way around it — Chromium is proxy-configured too, so “use Playwright” fails identically. Without another route, nothing in the repository can look at what deployed, and a defect only a click reveals ships past every green gate. But the site is published to the gh-pages BRANCH, and git works. So the deployed bytes are readable with git show, and a Playwright route handler can serve them at their real path: . const blob = (p: string) => { try { return execFileSync("git", ["show", `origin/gh-pages:${ROOT}/${p}`], { maxBuffer: 1 << 28 }); } catch { return undefined; } // absent is a FINDING, not a 200 }; let missing = 0; // REPORT THIS. See below. await page.route(`${ORIGIN}/**`, (route) => { const u = new URL(route.request().url()); let p = u.pathname.startsWith(BASE) ? u.pathname.slice(BASE.length) : u.pathname; p = p.replace(/^\/+/, ""); if (p === "" || p.endsWith("/")) p += "index.html"; const b = blob(p) ?? blob(`${p}/index.html`) ?? shared(p); if (!b) { missing++; return route.fulfill({ status: 404, body: "not in the publish ref" }); } return route.fulfill({ contentType: typeFor(p), body: b }); }); . A preview that shares with the live site falls back to it. A preview (cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-share.ts) stores only the files that differ from the live site, and its staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live root in the browser. So when branches/<slug>/staging-sw.js is in the ref, a file absent from the preview is the live site’s file at the same path, and shared(p) must read it from the root (blob with ROOT set to ""). Without that, every shared file reads as missing. Where there is no staging-sw.js, shared returns undefined and an absent file is a finding. The worker also puts the banner and fa-staging back on a live page it serves, which the route handler does not, so judge banner presence on the preview’s own pages. ROOT is "" for the canonical deploy and branches/<slug> for a preview, so the same handler gives you the before/after pair this skill is about — and a count, not an impression. Fetch the ref first (git fetch --depth=1 --filter=blob:none origin gh-pages); blobs are then fetched on demand. Serve it under the real BASE. A page served at the origin root cannot reveal a missing baseurl, because “composed against the base” and “not composed at all” are the same string there, so an e2e at the root stays green over a missing baseurl. And BASE is NOT the site’s base when you are reading a preview. A preview is published at <origin>/folio-assistant/branches/<slug>/, so that whole prefix is what its pages compose hrefs against — BASE and ROOT carry the same staging segment, one in the URL and one in the ref: . | reading | ROOT (in the ref) | BASE (in the URL) | . | the canonical deploy | "" | /folio-assistant | . | a branches/ preview | branches/<slug> | /folio-assistant/branches/<slug> | . Getting that wrong doubles the segment — branches/<slug>/branches/<slug>/... — and every asset 404s. Report the absent count, and read it before anything else . A run that could not fetch the page’s assets has established nothing, and its other numbers are actively misleading: a wrong BASE on a correct deploy reports zero tiles, which looks like the very defect being checked for. The rule outranks every other number the run prints: . missing > 0 is COULD NOT DETERMINE. Not clean, and not a finding. Discard the run’s other counts rather than reading them, fix the rig, and re-run. Scanning nothing and reporting it broken is as wrong as reporting it clean, and costlier: an agent acting on it goes looking for a defect that is not there, or “fixes” one. What this does NOT verify, and it matters . It serves the bytes in the publish ref. It is not the live host, so it cannot see: . | redirects, headers, or anything else the host decides at request time | Pages’ own 404 handling, or its directory-index rules where they differ from the handler above | whether the deploy has actually published — a ref can hold bytes that Pages has not served yet (§”Say how long”) | . So a green result here means “the published bytes are right”, never “the site works”. Report it in those words. When it stops applying . The technique rests on one assumption: publishing goes to a branch. If publishing moves to the Pages artifact API, git fetch origin gh-pages fails and there is nothing to read. Report that as could not determine, never as a clean run — an empty ref and a correct deploy are opposite facts. The third state, here as everywhere . “Could not determine” is never rendered as clean — and a change with no rendered surface is not a failure, it is the useful answer. | case | report it as | . | not deployed yet | not deployed, with the timing from §”Say how long” — never a link to where it will be | . | a changed page absent from the publish ref | a finding — the build dropped it, or it is not a page | . | no rendered surface | reviewed in the diff, naming the files | . The middle row is the most useful thing this skill can report, and composing its URL anyway would hide exactly that — §”Before you report a staging URL as broken”. The commit in the bot’s comment is NOT your branch head . On a pull_request trigger the stage job builds refs/pull/<n>/merge — your head merged into the base — so the commit the comment names never equals your head and is not even in your clone. Comparing the two reports a stale preview on every PR. Resolve it instead. The merge commit’s second parent is the head it was built from: . git fetch origin "refs/pull/<n>/merge:refs/remotes/origin/pr-<n>-merge" -q git log --format="%h %p" -1 origin/pr-<n>-merge # <merge> <base> <YOUR HEAD> . Stale means that second parent is not your head — nothing else does. This is the same fact bun run cat gates exists around: CI tests the merge, and so does the preview, so a branch behind its base is previewing a tree nobody will have. A stub where a layer should be is the cone, not a broken build . A composed layer the branch cannot reach is replaced by a one-page stub pointing at the published copy. Which layers a preview carries is decided by the staging cone (feature-staging §7), and the build log prints each decision with its reason. Before reporting a missing IG as a defect, read that line. If the cone left out something your change does affect, the fix is a missing writer or derivedFrom on the directory’s declaration, not a rule to always carry it.

20285.title: Which pages to list: the Change Set’s rendered list
20285.content: When the change is a Change Set, do not choose the before/after pages by judgement: take them from its rendered list (skill rendered-impact (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)), every content page on it, and say which inputs the renderer could not place. A page the list does not name and you add anyway is fine; a page on the list that you leave out is a gap the reviewer cannot see.

20286.title: When to provide before/after URLs
20286.content: Provide before/after URLs in every interaction where: . | Content has changed on a feature branch (authoring, editing, translation) | CRDM feature development — once requirements are agreed and a staging preview exists | Review/feedback sessions — when the user asks to review changes | Translation review — comparing translated vs source pages | .

20287.title: Before/after URL schema
20287.content: Every feedback response involving rendered content must include a stagingComparison object: . interface StagingComparison { /** Feature branch name (e.g. "claude/206-staging-preview"). */ branch: string; /** URL to the branch on GitHub. */ branchUrl: string; /** PR number if one exists. */ pr?: number; /** Pairs of before (main) and after (staging) URLs for changed pages. */ pages: Array<{ /** Page title or path. */ title: string; /** URL on the main (production) site. */ before: string; /** URL on the staging preview site. */ after: string; /** What changed on this page. */ summary?: string; }>; } . Example output . When reporting changes to the user: . ### 📋 Staging comparison | Page | Before (main) | After (staging) | What changed |---|---|---|---| Landing page | [main](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/#languages) | [staging](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/branches/claude-206-staging-preview/#languages) | Added French translation badge (the landing page itself changed, so its root is the page; the anchor is where the badge sits) | French landing | — | [staging](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/branches/claude-206-staging-preview/fr/index.html) | New page | Agent onboarding | [main](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/docs/cat-harness/guides/agent-onboarding.html) | [staging](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/branches/claude-206-staging-preview/docs/cat-harness/guides/agent-onboarding.html) | Language switcher added | .

20288.title: URL construction
20288.content: Main (before) . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/<path> . Read from the layer’s config (its index.config.json entry) → readme.pagesBaseUrl, or construct from the repo’s GitHub Pages URL. Staging (after) . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/<path> . The <branch-slug> is the branch name with non-alphanumeric characters replaced by hyphens (the same transform as feature-staging.yml). Deriving the slug . function branchToSlug(branch: string): string { return branch .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9._-]/g, "-") .replace(/-{2,}/g, "-") .replace(/^-|-$/g, ""); } .

20289.title: Integration with CRDM
20289.content: In the CRDM requirements workflow (Phase 5: implementation), once a staging preview is deployed: . | Post the staging URL on the GitHub issue as a comment. For a folio, post the review page too, branches/<slug>/review/, and name it as the page a reviewer opens first. The folio-staging workflow’s PR comment carries both links. The page lists every changed block, not only every changed page. Posting the site root alone sends a reviewer hunting through a 300-page document for a one-word edit. | Include before/after table for every changed page | Link from the PR body to the staging preview | Remind reviewers that staging uses the magenta “FEATURE BRANCH” banner | . The staging preview is part of the acceptance criteria: stakeholders must review the rendered output, not just the code diff.

20290.title: Integration with content authoring
20290.content: When an author has made content changes on a feature branch: . | Compute the ChangeSet, not a file list, when the branch touches a folio’s folio graph: the folio-changeset Tool, with --folio <folio dir> --base origin/main --head <branch>. Its command line is the Tool node’s invoke, declared by the content layer that defines the folio graph kind; this skill names the Tool, not that layer’s path. It says, per block, whether it was added, removed, reworded (prose), edited (manifest), moved or renamed. A file list cannot: a prose-only edit changes no .ts, and a move changes two files that look unrelated. Rank “where to start” by it. For a large document, the section with the most changed blocks is where a reviewer’s time goes first. | Construct before/after URLs for each changed docs page, and for each page carrying a changed block | Present the change to the author in the Output order above: the narrative first, then the deep-linked comparison table, then the before/after pictures themselves | Offer to run the staging workflow if not already running | . Finding your way on the review page . A 300-page review needs to know where it is, and to move in one key or one click. The review page has a navigation pane, beside the list on a wide screen and above it on a narrow one: . | Outline. Each document’s chapters and sections, in manifest order, from the outline.json the folio’s site build writes. | A section with something to review is a button that moves focus to it, with word badges (“2 changed, 1 comment, QA failing”). | Any other section links to its published page. | It is on the review page only; normal pages carry no table of contents. | . | Minimap. One cell per block, in order. It is one tab stop: Up and Down move, Home and End jump to either end, and Enter opens the block. Each cell is labelled in words and marked with glyphs (Δ changed, + added, ● open comments, ! QA failing), so colour is never the only signal. | Where am I. Every move announces “document › chapter › section › block” in the page’s one live status line. | . Keys, each with a visible button twin: . | key | button | goes to | . | j | Next | the next item | . | k | Previous | the previous item | . | n | Next with comments | the next block with open comments | . | p | Previous with comments | the previous block with open comments | . | u | Next unreviewed | the next changed block with no reviewer verdict on its CURRENT version | . “Unreviewed” means no verdict on this version, not “no comments”. A block whose only verdict is on an earlier version is unreviewed, and says so in words (“1 verdict on an earlier version, not counted”). A build whose review-comments.json carries no verdicts says “No verdict data on this build” rather than treating every block as unread. Typing into a selector is never navigation. Tests. the tools layer’s test/review-nav.e2e.ts drives all of this with the keyboard alone. It uses no mouse, no click and no hover. The review page, and choosing how to see a change . A folio’s preview carries review/index.html: every changed block, grouped by section, with its reviewer comments (the review-comments skill). Each changed block has a “Show this change as” selector, and one at the top applies to every block: . | renderer | shows | the default for | needs | . | Word diff of the source | the Markdown with removed words struck and added words marked: exactly what the author typed | any kind not listed below | the block’s prose | . | Inline, as rendered | the block as a reader sees it now, with the change marked in place | prose, remark, definition, example | the block’s prose | . | Pictures, before and after | a picture of the block on each side, the changed pixels marked, and the share changed in words (visual-diff (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) | table, figure, diagram, equation, simulator | visual-diff.json from the folio-block-screenshots Tool | . | Side by side | main and the preview next to each other, each scrolled to the block | the same kinds, as the second choice when a build published no pictures | a page on either side | . | Where the data comes from. The ChangeSet step’s --text-out writes changeset-text.json: the source and rendered prose of each listed block, on each side that has it. The pictures step writes visual-diff.json and visual/. With neither file, only side by side is available, and the page says so. | Two renderers may default for one kind. Order is preference: the page opens a block on the first renderer that lists its kind AND can run. | A renderer that cannot run on a block is listed, disabled, with the reason. For example, a manifest-only change has no prose to diff. If the page-level choice cannot run on a block, that block falls back to one that can. | The page-level choice is remembered for this viewer in localStorage. A private window just gets the defaults. | The renderers and the registry are cat-harness-tools/scripts/review-renderers.ts, cat-harness-tools/scripts/word-diff.ts (no diff library; about forty lines, tested) and cat-harness/schemas/ui/diff-renderers.ts. To add one, declare it in the registry with what it needs and which kinds it defaults for, add its function to review-renderers.ts, and add a case to the page’s renderInto. | .

20291.title: Staging retention
20291.content: A MERGED pull request’s preview goes away. Everything else is retained by default, subject to the size cap below. The distinction is about where the content lives, not about how confident anyone is: . | the PR was | the preview is | so | . | merged | the same thing the MAIN SITE now shows | redundant on the instant, and removed automatically — no label | . | closed, unmerged | the ONLY rendering of that work | the last copy, and retained unless a person says otherwise | . The store therefore drains: what remains is bounded by concurrent reviews, not by cumulative history, so a size warning stays a signal rather than becoming a permanent verdict. This applies deletion-requires-confirmation; it does not relax it. The merge is the confirmation: a person decided this content belongs on main. What the label guards is the case where nobody decided anything. Removal is one preview directory at a time. Which mechanism depends on whether the PR is still open. Three cases, and the label cannot reach a closed PR: . | Merged — nothing to do. cleanup reads github.event.pull_request.merged off the close event and removes without a label, recording the reason as merged. | While the PR is open, and it will not be merged — add the staging:cleanup label. cleanup in feature-staging.yml fires on pull_request_target: closed and reads the labels off that event, so the label has to be there before the PR closes. | Once the PR is closed unmerged and unlabelled — run feature-staging.yml from the Actions tab with cleanup_slug: <slug> and cleanup_confirm: <slug>. The confirmation repeats the slug so that it names the artefact it confirms, and the job re-checks that nothing is still using the preview before it removes anything. | . Labelling a closed PR does nothing, and re-running its old workflow run does nothing either — a re-run replays the stored event payload, which still carries no label. So for an orphan the health sweep’s staging-preview-orphans finding names, option 2 is the remedy. If you find yourself reaching for a hand-pushed gh-pages commit instead, stop: that is the unilateral removal deletion-requires-confirmation exists to stop, and option 2 exists so you do not have to. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by total size, not count, because preview sizes vary widely and a count bounds the total only while preview size holds still. GitHub Pages deploys gh-pages as-is, and past its 10 GB artifact limit the live site stops deploying. Every removal path above is per-preview and event-driven; none bounds the total. What the stage job does, on every deploy, before its one push: . | Sums the size of the previews under branches/, including the one it is staging, and keeps them within 3 GB. The number lives once, as MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES in cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts. | Keeps the newest that fit and removes the rest, oldest first — strictly by recency. An older small preview never outlives a newer one that did not fit, so a preview’s age alone says whether it is still there. One 780 MB preview displaces several small ones; that is what a size budget means. “Last updated” is the branches/<slug>/.staged-at stamp the job writes on every stage, falling back to the latest rendered render-log entry, then the record’s builtAt, then git. The preview being staged is never removed. | Never touches branches/_retired/ or anything that is not a preview directory. | Leaves a record for each removal — a removed render-log entry with the reason, the preview’s staging-preview.json retired into _retired/, and a line in the commit message and the job log giving slug, age and size. | . This DOES reach open pull requests. Under the cap, the oldest preview goes whatever its PR’s state; the owner’s cap is the confirmation deletion-requires-confirmation asks for, given for the class. It is recoverable because a preview is a build, not content: the next push to that PR’s branch re-stages it, and the run that re-stages it can never rotate it off. So when a reviewer’s preview link 404s, check _render-log/ on gh-pages for a removed entry for its slug before calling it broken — if it says “rotated off”, push to the branch (an empty commit will do) or re-run the PR’s Feature Staging workflow. A closed PR is not an abandoned preview . staging-preview-orphans does not ask “is there an open PR?”, and neither should you. A session that reuses one branch across successive pull requests has no open PR for the whole gap between one merging and the next opening. Liveness is three signals, any one of which means leave it alone: an open PR, a branch on the remote carrying work not in the default branch, or a tip commit in the last 30 minutes. scripts/staging-cleanup-preflight.ts --slug <slug> answers the same question on demand, and the dispatch above runs it before removing.

20292.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)
20292.content: A staging URL is not a deliverable until you have checked the ref, and it is never “live” on your say-so. The bot’s comment says a workflow pushed, not that a site serves. Three states, and conflating any two of them is the defect: . |   | observable from a container? | how | . | the stage job succeeded | yes | the check run on the PR’s head | . | the files are in gh-pages | yes | read branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages | . | the URL serves them | NO | see below | . The third is not available to you, and curl will not make it available. The proxy blocks github.io, so a fetch returns 000 and says nothing either way. And where Pages is configured as Deploy from a branch — as it is here — its builds produce no workflow runs at all (event: page_build returns total_count: 0, and there is no pages-build-deployment workflow to query). So there is no API answer either. So: verify the ref, and report the third state as unverified rather than inferring it. Listing branches/<slug>/ on gh-pages and finding index.html proves the build ran and what it published; it does not prove Pages has rebuilt. Those are different claims and only one of them is yours to make. LIST the directory. Do not FETCH the page. A staging page is ~100 KB of rendered HTML, a context window spent to learn a fact the directory listing gives for free. The listing returns a name and a byte count per entry; index.html present and non-zero is the whole check. Request only the name and size fields. Say how long, and come back . A person handed a URL with no timing either refreshes a 404 or walks away. Give them the number and the follow-up, in the same breath as the link: . | The stage job takes about 22 minutes, plus its wait at the rate limit (derived artefacts, the knowledge-graph export, mounting, Jekyll and checks). Drafts are staged too, from the first push. The job then waits until gh-pages has gone 5 minutes without a staging push and 10 without a main-site one (feature-staging §7), and its PR comment says queued with an earliest push time and a live-by time while it waits. Quote those times; they are the job’s own estimate. | Pages propagation is on top of that, and GitHub documents it as up to ten minutes. Since it is unobservable from here, quote the bound rather than a guess: “give it ~5 minutes; up to 10 if Pages is slow.” | Then actually check back. Schedule it rather than promising it — the same mechanism that watches a PR. Re-list the ref, and if the person reports a 404 after the window, that is a real finding worth chasing; before it, it is the window. | . Never present a URL as though it is already serving. “Deployed to gh-pages, should be live in ~5 minutes” is the honest sentence and costs nothing. Check for newer cleanup commits on gh-pages . Before declaring a preview good, check the gh-pages commit log for any staging(cleanup) commit touching that slug that is newer than the last staging(...) publish: . git log -n 5 --oneline origin/gh-pages -- "branches/<slug>" . If a staging(cleanup) commit appears newer than the last staging(...) publish, or if the directory was deleted within the hour, flag it immediately. A preview whose slug was recently deleted and re-published is vulnerable to cancelled Pages builds: if Pages cancelled the re-publish build, the site continues serving the deletion (a 404) even though the publish ref has the files. A preview whose slug was deleted within the hour is not in the ordinary propagation window. Re-publishing without a code push . When a preview needs to be rebuilt or re-published — because a previous Pages build was cancelled, or because a slug was deleted by cleanup from a preceding PR — you do not need an empty code commit or push. Dispatch the staging workflow directly with the branch name: . gh workflow run feature-staging.yml -f branch=<branch> . This triggers feature-staging.yml via workflow_dispatch for that branch, building and deploying a fresh preview to branches/<slug>/ on gh-pages and queueing a new Pages build.

20293.title: Do not
20293.content: . | Do not hand over a staging URL without listing branches/<slug>/ on gh-pages first. The bot’s comment says a workflow pushed, not that a site serves. | Do not declare a preview good without checking the gh-pages commit log for newer cleanup commits. A staging(cleanup) commit newer than the publish means a cancelled Pages build leaves the live site serving a 404. | Do not say a preview is “live”, “up” or “deployed and ready” unless someone has loaded it. You cannot see that from here. | Do not provide before/after URLs without checking the staging workflow has run. A URL that 404s is worse than no URL. | Do not remove a staging preview by hand without confirmation. Apart from a merged PR’s preview and the size cap’s rotation, a person confirms every removal — the label while the PR is open, or the dispatch with its repeated-slug confirmation once it is closed. | Do not read “no open pull request” as “abandoned”. It is true of a live branch for the whole gap between one PR merging and the next opening. | Do not assume all pages are at the root. Guides are under guides/, reference under reference/, French under fr/ etc. | Do not omit the comparison table. Even for a single page change, show the before/after pair — it is the whole point of staging. | .

20294.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
20294.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — docs/<stub>/proposals/x.md publishes to /proposals/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

20295.title: staging-review (skill)
20295.content: The skill staging-review as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/staging-review.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

20296.title: Sub-KG lifecycle — staged here, separated later
20296.content: Skill sub-kg-lifecycle: A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own layer, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA layer that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Record agent step, Review-log watch, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Skill id: sub-kg-lifecycle · Package: graph-management Process: sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn Stages 6 to 13 are drawn as the phases it shares with kg-separation: authorise, move and cut over. A sub-KG created inside a folio or harnessed repository can move to its own repository later: once it is staged for separation, a new repository is created and the staged contents are copied into it.

20297.title: Which skill, this one or kg-separation?
20297.content: | the graph | use | . | holds data — an artefact index, generated pages, a library, a folio — and leaves whole | this skill | . | holds data and the code that writes it, and the two must become a content repository and a tools repository | kg-separation — its fourteen stages, the pair, FR-7 | . | is not yet a graph at all — tangled into its host | graph-detanglement first | . The two share their gates on purpose. Ready to seed? here is the same decision table, seed-readiness-gate.dmn, evaluated by the same command, and the owner’s confirmations here are the same rule, deletion-requires-confirmation. What this skill adds is the part kg-separation does not cover: a sub-KG born in the host, with no tools pair, that leaves in one piece.

20298.title: How a sub-KG is born — the intent question
20298.content: A content type’s own creation skill asks whether the new thing goes in a new repository or inside this one, and routes here for the second answer. For a folio in general that is getting-started’s add-folio branch. A harness above this one may own a creation skill for its own kind of graph; ask skill_list for it rather than improvising. In-repository is the cheaper default whenever the session is already in a harnessed repository. Every stage up to 6 is reversible with git revert, and nothing outside the repository changes until stage 7. A new repository is the first irreversible, outward-facing act, and this lifecycle puts it behind a confirmation rather than at the start.

20299.title: The stages
20299.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and what decides that it is done. A stage is done when its check is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | done when | . | 0 | Brief, claim the work item (opening-brief) | authoring-agent | work item claimed with bun run cat beans:claim | . | 1 | Declare it in place | authoring-agent | the declaration parses; instance-repositories.test.ts green | . | 2 | Grow it in place | authoring-agent | the content type’s own gates | . | 3 | Push generic down | platform-authoring-agent | check:import-direction, check:reference-direction, check:process-bindings add nothing | . | 4 | One import seam | platform-authoring-agent | every climb out of the directory goes through <name>/platform.ts | . | 5 | Rehearse self-contained | build-pipeline | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse | . | 6 | Report what would move | authoring-agent | the report is in the work item (as kg-separation stage 9) | . | 7 | Owner confirms: create the repository | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 8 | Create the repository | administrator | it exists, empty, and was read before writing | . | — | Ready to seed? | build-pipeline | seed-readiness-gate.dmn answers settled | . | 9 | Copy the staged contents in, with history | authoring-agent | a reviewed PR on a branch of the new repository | . | 10 | Re-point the declaration | platform-authoring-agent | the host is green consuming the new repository | . | 11 | Verify on a fresh clone | build-pipeline | the new repository’s gates green from git clone in an empty directory | . | 12 | Owner confirms: delete the in-repo copy | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 13 | Cutover commit | administrator | one commit, revertable (as kg-separation stage 13) | . 1 · Declare it in place . A directory <name>/ at the host’s root, with <name>/<name>.json: . { "name": "<name>", "repository": "<owner>/<name>", // the PLANNED home; IRIs key on it "livesAt": { "repository": "<owner>/<host>", "path": "<name>" }, // where it sits TODAY "version": "0.1.0", "needs": ["<the harness it instantiates>"], "directories": [ /* only directories that exist, each with its graphTypologies */ ] } . | repository differs from livesAt.repository — that difference is what makes the directory a staged layer, and it is what the separation guard and seed:ready read. Nothing lists the staged layers by hand. | The directory may sit anywhere — a root sibling is the convention, but the tools read livesAt.path, so folio/<name>/ works the same. | Scaffold it with init-folio --staged <path>: . bun run cat init-folio --staged <path> --title "<title>" \ --repository <owner>/<name> --needs <harness> # --host-repository when origin cannot say . It writes exactly two files, <path>/<name>.json and an empty <path>/platform.ts, and nothing at the host’s root; init-folio-staged.test.ts snapshots the whole host tree to hold that. Never --instance inside a host: it writes a repository’s worth of scaffolding (AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, a work items store, a session hook; 15 files, measured with --dry-run). --instance is for stage 8’s repository. | Declare a directory with its files, in one commit: a declared-but-absent directory is scanned as empty and reported clean. | . 3 · Push generic down — before the seam, not after . Move everything generic into the harness below, consolidate what the sub-KG needs into its own harness, and only then seed. The other order copies generic code into a repository that has to give it back. Wrong-direction edges hide in declarations and data, not only in imports: a skill definition naming a package one layer up, a dependsOn, a publication target enumerated in an input schema, prose links, a needs edge to an empty layer. So run all three direction checks, not one. 4 · One import seam: <name>/platform.ts . Every symbol the sub-KG uses from the platform is re-exported from one file, and nothing else in the directory climbs out of it. On the day it leaves, re-pointing the platform is a one-file edit instead of a sweep. cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/instance-separation-imports.test.ts is the guard. It covers every layer whose repository differs from its livesAt.repository, not only those that opted in, because an opt-in guard is silent for exactly the layer that has no seam. Layers other layers build on are an explicit, checked exemption, and a layer that still climbs has a ceiling that may only fall. Create the seam at stage 1, not here. It costs one file on day one, and every later climb is a reroute. A merge from main is where new climbs arrive, so a red guard after one is the expected signal to reroute, not a regression. 5 · Rehearse self-contained — run the gates, do not scan . bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . It copies the layer and what it needs into a scratch workspace of sibling directories and runs the tests there. It is a run rather than a reading because: . | a static import scan misses files the gates load at run time — a JSON code list read by URL, for one; | renaming the directory can change every generated page, when a URL prefix or a chrome lookup keys on the directory name. Take the identity from the declaration’s name, never from the path, and check for that before seeding into a different directory name. | . 7 and 12 · The two confirmations . Both are userTasks in the administrator lane, marked relaxable="false", and both follow deletion-requires-confirmation: the agent reports what would happen, how large it is and how it is undone, then waits. Silence is not a yes. The questions are numbered, four options at most, the recommended one first, with a stated default: . Before stage 8: . <name> is staged and rehearses green: N files, M MB, history of K commits. Creating <owner>/<name> is visible outside this repository and is not undone by a revert. May it be created? . | Yes — you create it, and tell me when it exists (recommended) | Yes — I create it (only if this session has that permission) | Not yet — keep it staged here | . Default if you do not answer: 3. Nothing is created. Before stage 13: . <owner>/<name> is green from a fresh clone and the host consumes it. The in-repo copy is N files. Deleting it is one commit, revertable. | Delete the in-repo copy now (recommended) | Keep it until the new repository’s first release | Show me the file list first | . Default if you do not answer: 2. Nothing is deleted. When the repository must be created by someone with credentials this session lacks, the hand-over is agent-handoff: one work item, one sentence for the person to relay. 9 · Copy the staged contents in, with history . The staged directory becomes the new repository’s content with its history: git subtree split --prefix=<name> in the host, then git subtree add (or a merge of the split branch) in the new repository. It goes in on a branch, as a draft PR, never straight to main. The new repository’s own root files — its declaration at the root, its config, its README — are a second commit in the same PR, so the copy itself stays byte-identical and reviewable. Ready to seed? comes first, at seed time, because the tree has moved since the rehearsal: every open PR touching the layer when the copy is taken is orphaned. Its criteria and thresholds are in kg-separation §”Ready to seed?”, and not restated here. 10 · Re-point the declaration . | what changes | how | . | livesAt | removed in the new repository — absent means “sits at the root of repository” | . | the seam | platform.ts points at wherever the platform now is: a remote-mounted path, or a sibling checkout | . | the host | remote mount if the host imports code from the sub-KG — a source.remote layer in the host’s root index.config.json (remote-mount; never a submodule); subscription (kg:subscribe) if it only reads its content | . | pins | the host pins a commit while staging, a version once released (upstream-version-adoption) | . | its site | the new repository publishes and previews itself (feature-staging, Which site): "site": { "agentRun": true } in its index.config.json when an agent publishes it, plus whatever workflow its publisher layer’s own creation skill requires (an IG’s AST-cache refresh, for one) | . | its checks | .github/workflows/harness-pr-checks.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml, so its gates run on every pull request | . | its QA record | when it declares a qa directory with storage (test/results/, cat/cat-harness/qa-reports, keyed by commit): .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-qa-publish.yml, so every push to main and every pull request publishes its results to its own qa-reports branch, and test/results/ in .gitignore. A host reads them at the commit it pins. Without the job, the declaration names a store nothing writes | . | .gitignore | the mount block, written by the mount tool between its own markers. Never typed: a hand-written marker makes remote-mount.ts refuse (markers unpaired) | . Copy these from a sibling repository of the same kind; never type them. A repository scaffolded by hand misses them, and its site cannot be built until each is copied in. The host keeps its own copy through this stage. The re-point is additive. 11 · Verify on a fresh clone . bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <seeding branch> --text # exit 0 green, 1 red, 2 unknown . The Tool sub-kg-verify-clone clones the new repository into an empty scratch directory with its submodules (and each --sibling beside it), installs, and runs its own gates script, else its test script. An empty tree, a failed clone or a repository with no gate is unknown, never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a test that climbs out (Cannot find module '../../../<harness>/…') fails here. A rehearsal in the host’s scratch space is not this check; it shares the host’s node_modules and network. The new repository’s own site is part of this check: bun run cat stage:local --repo . --dry-run from the fresh clone must build. A refusal names what stage 10 left out.

20300.title: Stage 13: the frozen copy
20300.content: After cutover the host keeps a frozen copy in fsh-guts, not a refreshed mirror and not a deletion. Step 12 asks (1) move to fsh-guts now, (2) keep in place until the first release, (3) show the file list first, default (2). Step 13 deposits the directory into the PARENT’s fsh-guts as a verified archive (not plain trees, which CI would audit as live content), then removes it from main. The deposit is the one state:seed --cutover makes for a state graph: an archive that must extract to the exact tree being removed, plus a provenance note (movedFrom, movedOn, sourceCommit, tree), and the removal commit is made only once it has landed. A separation targets the parent’s fsh-guts rather than the departing layer’s, which --cutover does not yet do. The live copy is the remote mount (index.config.json source.remote), npm package retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm), or subscription (kg:subscribe) from stage 10; the frozen one is never refreshed and never rendered. How checks treat a frozen subtree . This is the one place the rule is stated; scanners point here. A frozen subtree is one retired item, and its sibling note is the node that answers for it. Every reader of fsh-guts — the fsh-guts.jsonld export, the fsh-guts page, the render-pipeline and bean-reference tests, check:materialized-fixity — reports the note and does not enter the directory. The page shows it as one row in the via sidecar state. | Recognised by declaration, never by path. A directory is frozen because <name>.md beside it declares $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1 and kind: separated-instance (isFrozenSubtree in schemas/kg/fsh-guts.ts). A copy dropped in with no note, or under a note of another kind, is walked like any directory, so its files fail self-declaration loudly rather than vanishing from every check. | The note must carry all four stage-13 fields — movedFrom, movedOn, repository, matchesCommit — because it is now the only thing any check reads about thousands of files. Those beyond the common set are exported under the node’s data. | Materialization records inside are not judged. They claim bytes in the repository the graph now lives in, which the copy deliberately does not carry. | The note’s bean: resolves against main’s work plan, with no pending escape. So the deposit lands on the fsh-guts branch in the same step that merges the PR carrying that work item, never before it; a deposit pushed ahead of its PR turns every PR’s CI red. | .

20301.title: Anti-patterns
20301.content: . | Creating the repository first. It is the one irreversible step; everything that can be done in place is done before it. | A seed with no history. A one-commit seed severs blame for every line, and the history is cheap to keep. | Re-pointing by sweep. If more than one file changes when the platform moves, the seam was skipped. | Reading the rehearsal as the fresh-clone check. They catch different things: the rehearsal catches climbs, the fresh clone catches everything the host’s environment was quietly supplying. | Deleting the in-repo copy because the new repository is green. Green is the precondition for asking, not the answer. | Committing mounted directories to the host repository. Remote mounts populate layer directories locally. If .gitignore does not ignore the mounted paths, external files pollute downstream git status. index.config.json must generate gitignore entries for all remoteMounts. | Breaking dependents when dependencies fold. If a dependency layer folds into another (e.g. cat-openapi into cat-harness), downstreams that still reference the folded layer fail unless FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES maps them. | Separating before resolving withheld asset clearance. If library items are withheld or unpermitted in the separated repository (as with the IRIS replica), materialization results in broken links. Clearance must be verified at seed time. | .

20303.title: A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository
20303.content: Process_SubKgLifecycle · strict · 11 step(s) . Create a knowledge graph inside a harnessed repository as a layer of its own, grow it there, and when it should leave, stage it for separation and move it whole into a new repository. Declared in place with a planned repository and a livesAt saying where it sits today; staged by one import seam (<name>/platform.ts), the separation guard and a self-contained rehearsal; then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, the repository is created, the staged contents are copied in with their history, the declaration is re-pointed, a fresh clone is verified, and the in-repo copy is frozen in the kept trashcan. The light sibling of kg-separation, which splits a graph into a content and a tools repository; this moves a data layer whole, and shares kg-separation’s seeding gateway and decision table. DRAWN IN PHASES (owner, 2026-11-08, Q-B1-3 A): it keeps its own grow-in-place and staging steps, and calls the authorise, move and cut-over phases it shares with kg-separation. i i i i i i i i i i i

20309.doc: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph
20309.title: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph
20309.content: Process_SubscribeKg · strict · 11 step(s) . Subscribe a folio or harness to an external knowledge graph pinned to a full commit SHA, then take each chosen part from referenced to materialized through materialize-remote and instantiate each chosen harness once its needs are held, so the harness appears in the subscriber’s navbar. A SUBSCRIPTION IS NOT A NEW MECHANISM, and this diagram is where that claim is kept honest. Every byte that arrives does so through Process_MaterializeRemote, called once per chosen subgraph or asset; every held copy is refreshed through Process_RefreshMaterialized. Neither is re-described here. What this process adds is only the walk: pin, validate, choose, and then carry each chosen part from referenced to materialised one at a time. A SUBSTRATE is a repository whose root declaration meets bootstrap’s schema requirements and declares at least one harness. Both are answerable from the declaration file alone, so validating one never needs the whole repository. WHERE IT LIVES: library/processes/, beside Process_MaterializeRemote and Process_RefreshMaterialized, which it calls, naming the kg-subscription and materialize-remote skills in library/skills/large-datasets/; every ref stays inside the harness. STRICT. The pin and the five gates are the reason: an unpinned subscription is how two subscribers see two graphs under one name, and a gate that only warned is a gate nobody fails. i i i i i i i i i i i

20315.title: Surprise to corpus — notice it, filter it, then ask
20315.content: Skill surprise-to-corpus: What was unexpected in that task, and does it belong in the corpus? Logical surprise is the detectable kind, recurrence is the filter that stops this generating noise every turn, and the agent PROMPTS — it never writes corpus guidance unasked. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . Skill id: surprise-to-corpus · Package: folio-core . When something unexpected happens during a defined process that runs often, it may be worth a new skill, guidance or tool refinement: prompt the person to add it to the corpus. Three clauses: notice, filter by recurrence, prompt. The first alone is a diary; the first two are an agent rewriting the corpus on its own authority; the third without the second is a prompt every turn until people stop reading them.

20316.title: 1. What counts as a surprise
20316.content: Ask it as an after-action review asks it: . What did you expect to happen, what actually happened, and why the difference? . This makes the surprise articulable BEFORE you know whether it matters. “Something felt off” is not reviewable; “I expected the tracer to read the mask as ink and it read the ground” is. The filter in §2 then operates on a statement rather than on a feeling, so it can be applied consistently. Only LOGICAL surprise is detectable. Statistical surprise implies a base rate, and the corpus carries none — nothing records how often a gate fires, a merge conflicts, or a selector breaks. Do not claim a statistical surprise: it would assert a distribution nobody measured. Logical surprise needs no baseline. It is any of: . | A premise turned out false. You believed something about the system, acted on it, and the system disagreed. | A gate fired for a reason nobody predicted — including a gate that passed when you expected red. | A command failed and the failure was invisible, because whatever ran next produced plausible output anyway. | Two things that looked like one thing, or one thing that turned out to be two. | . Examples of the general shapes . | the surprise | the general shape | . | potracer treats ZERO as foreground — the inverse of what the name suggests | a library whose convention is the opposite of its name | . | Image.crop past the edge pads with BLACK, which a tracer reads as ink | a default that is invisible until another tool interprets it | . | a CSS class used as an IDENTITY is reused by a second button as a box class, breaking every selector at once | a name doing two jobs, discovered when the second arrives | . | an id sliced one character short fails silently behind a tail -1 | a truncated identifier that still LOOKS like an identifier | .

20317.title: 2. The recurrence filter — the part that stops the noise
20317.content: A surprise inside a one-off is an anecdote. The same surprise inside a process that runs often is a defect in the process. Without this filter the rule fires every turn, because every non-trivial turn contains something somebody did not expect. With it, the question is narrow and answerable: . Did this happen inside a defined process that runs often — and would the next agent running that process hit it too? . Both halves. A rare process can still be worth guarding if its failure is expensive, but then say that rather than claiming a recurrence you have not seen. “The next agent would hit it too” separates a fact about the system from a fact about your own mistake. Three ways a candidate fails the filter, all of which end in silence rather than a prompt: it happened once, in a process nobody runs twice; it was your own slip and the system behaved as documented; or the corpus already says it and you had not read that part. The third is the common one, and checking costs one grep. Read the slip blamelessly . A finding is about the SYSTEM rather than about the person. “My own slip” fails the filter only when the system behaved as documented AND nothing about the system made the slip easy. Where the system DID make it easy, would the next agent hit it too is true, and the candidate passes. A mis-copied id is not just a slip: a truncated id is still a well-formed id, and a | tail -1 hides a non-zero exit — both properties the next agent meets unchanged.

20318.title: 3. PROMPT, never write
20318.content: The agent proposes; a person decides. This is deletion-requires-confirmation pointed the other way: that skill governs removing a durable artefact on your own initiative, this one governs ADDING durable guidance on your own initiative. The corpus is read by every future session, so the person who has to live with a line in it should be the one who agreed to it. What a good prompt contains — the same parts interaction-modality §4.1 binds every handed-over decision to, and the test is identical: can the reader answer without opening anything? . | What happened, concretely, with the measurement or the error text. | Which process it happened in, named. | Why it will recur — the filter above, argued rather than asserted. | What you propose: a new skill, a line in an existing one, or a tool change. Say which, and where it would live — where-does-this-go is how you answer that. | Your recommendation, marked as such. | What happens if they say nothing: nothing gets written, and the candidate is filed as a work item so it is not lost. | . A work item is the third state — recorded, unactioned, findable — so silence is not expensive and an unanswered prompt is something the next session can pick up rather than rediscover.

20319.title: 4. When to run this
20319.content: At the end of a task, not continuously: one pass over what actually happened. Most turns produce nothing and should say nothing — a loop that reports “no surprises” every turn is a loop people stop reading. It pairs with turn-reporting (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc), which governs the shape of the report you were already writing.

20320.title: What this skill deliberately does not do
20320.content: . | No severity scale. Ranking surprises would invite filing the low ones, which is the noise the recurrence filter exists to prevent. A candidate either passes the filter or is worth a work item at most. | No automated corpus change. A mechanism that could write guidance would be used to write guidance. | No timeline reconstruction. The agent was present for the whole turn, and the transcript is the timeline. | No routing method. Where a surprise goes is where-does-this-go, which needs an index rather than a taxonomy at its size. | .
